papers.node_id: 65tullrev1323!!ARTICLE: WHEN THE BORROWER AND THE BANKER ARE AT ODDS: THE INTERACTION OF JUDGE AND ARBITRATOR IN TRANS-BORDER FINANCE.
papers.title: ARTICLE: WHEN THE BORROWER AND THE BANKER ARE AT ODDS: THE INTERACTION OF JUDGE AND ARBITRATOR IN TRANS-BORDER FINANCE.
papers.abstract:
Lenders and borrowers traditionally have gone before judges rather than arbitrators to resolve controversies arising out of international loan agreements.  Arbitration has been relatively rare, even ill-favored, in financial dispute resolution.  Exceptwith respect to performance guaranteesand securities,arbitrators seldom decide controversies arising out of financial transactions.  The disfavored status of arbitration in banking contrasts sharply with arbitration's position as the preferred adjudicatory mechanism in trans-border commercial relationships.
The banker's customary hesitation about arbitration should not be surprising.The financial muscle often exercised by international lenders has led to loan forum-selection clauses granting exclusive competence to courts of the banker's own jurisdiction.  Hometown justice is always best -- at least for the hometown boy or girl.  Moreover, a court proceeding may be quicker and less expensive than arbitration when nothing significant is in dispute except the borrower's willingness or ability to make payment on a promissory note.  It would be startling, for example, if an English bank did not prefer to sue a defaulting borrower before an English judge in London rather than to bring a claim before an arbitrator in Geneva.
Bankers also resist arbitration clauses because they may sometimes operate to bar the benefits of the summary procedures available to lenders under many national legal systems.  Thedroit cambiaireof France, for instance, provides for court-ordered payment procedures that simplify the enforcement of commercial-paper obligations.Moreover, some jurisdictionsmay consider interim measures of protection (such as pre-award attachment of assets) as incompatible with arbitration agreements covered by the New York Arbitration Convention -- at least if the parties are silent on the matter in their arbitration agreement.
Finally, bankers tend toward a herd mentality (not always unjustified) that sometimes leads them to fear the hex effect of innovation: "If it ain't broke, don't fix it." Changes in old forms selecting courts that have worked fairly well in the past, so it seems, will likely bring bad luck.
Nevertheless, legal counsel in the financial services industry are increasingly aware that things are no longer so simple, particularly in international transactions.  Several considerations occasionally impel the inclusion of an arbitration clause in a credit agreement: (i) difficulty in enforcing foreign judgements; (ii) the "act of state" and sovereign immunity defenses raised by foreign borrowers; (iii) developing countries' leverage in debtrescheduling and project finance; and (iv) the epidemic of "lender liability" litigation in the United States.
, when bankers contemplate court adjudication, they presume enforceable judgments.  But foreign judicial decisions are not always as easily enforced as domestic ones.Sometimes debtors have assets in jurisdictions that are not party to any bilateral or multilateral recognition-of-judgment treaty with the dispute-resolution forum.  Arbitral awards, however, will usually benefit from recognition and enforcement in more than eighty countries under the 1958 New York Arbitration Convention.Therefore, in some cases arbitral awards may be more enforceable than foreign court judgments.
, two peculiarly international defenses are increasingly invoked against enforcement of trans-border loans: sovereign immunity and the act-of-state doctrine.  These defenses add a special dimension to international financial risks that requires a more nuanced analysis of the costs and benefits in arbitration of credit disputes.Recent statutory enactments reducing the sting of both defenses give arbitration a specialraison d'etrein any loan implicating a foreign borrower.  The Foreign Sovereign Immunities Actand the United States Arbitration Actwere both amended in November 1988 to make arbitration awards more enforceable than court judgments.Bank counsel thereforecan be expected to show greater sophistication in drafting forum-selection clauses when loans involve sovereign debt or borrowers in countries that may impose exchange controls.
, in some cases, borrowers may give the creditor no alternative to arbitration other than the courts of the debtor's country.  Arbitration imposes itselffaute de mieuxwhen the size of a borrower's potential default, paradoxically perhaps, increases its leverage in rescheduling negotiations to the point that the lender's own courts are no longer an acceptable option for the choice-of-forum clause.
Finally, the American epidemic of "lender liability" actionsagainst banks has led several major lenders to insert arbitration clauses in credit agreements in the hope of reducing the risk of excessive jury awards.
This Article will discuss each of these considerations in turn, and then will examine the impact of the International Monetary Fund Articles of Agreement on arbitration of transborder loan disputes.  From a policy perspective, my modest conclusion is that the measure of financial arbitration's aggregate consequences -- social, political, and economic -- will be the extent to which the arbitral process increases the reliability of credit arrangements that promote world development.  In a more practical vein, the costs and benefits or arbitration as compared to court litigation will depend on how the relative predictability of judges weighs in against the greater enforceability of arbitral awards in disputes implicating exchange controls, foreign assets, and sovereign borrowers.  The only thing that seems beyond doubt is that for some time to come arbitration's role in financial dispute resolution will resist facile analysis.

matches.theme_name: Do tribunals and domestic courts' forum-selection and governing-law choices produce systematic ex-ante incentives for forum-shopping and strategic litigation in cross-border sovereign debt?
matches.specific_contribution: The article explains that lenders typically draft forum-selection clauses pointing to their home courts for “hometown justice,” but in cross-border loans—especially those involving sovereign borrowers or foreign assets—they may instead choose arbitration to secure broader enforceability under the New York Convention and to navigate sovereign defenses.
matches.generalized_contribution: Forum-selection and arbitration choices in cross-border lending create predictable ex-ante incentives to choose fora that maximize enforceability and home-court advantage.

matches.theme_name: How do domestic courts, international arbitration, and official institutions (e.g., IMF) interact to determine bargaining leverage and the legality of restructuring plans?
matches.specific_contribution: The article links developing countries’ leverage in debt rescheduling and the 1988 FSIA/FAA amendments to greater use and enforceability of arbitration with sovereign borrowers, and it promises analysis of how the IMF Articles of Agreement affect arbitration of transborder loan disputes.
matches.generalized_contribution: Interactions among domestic courts, international arbitration, and official-sector frameworks influence bargaining leverage and enforceability in sovereign-related loan disputes.

matches.theme_name: Can contractual drafting (currency clauses, pari passu, waiver language, amendment thresholds) be designed to reliably reduce cross-border enforcement uncertainty and interjurisdictional conflict?
matches.specific_contribution: By emphasizing that arbitral awards are generally more widely recognized than foreign court judgments under the New York Convention and that silence about interim measures in arbitration clauses can curtail remedies, the article shows how tailored dispute-resolution drafting can reduce cross-border enforcement risk in certain loans.
matches.generalized_contribution: Careful drafting of dispute-resolution clauses, including the use of arbitration and explicit treatment of ancillary remedies, can mitigate cross-border enforceability uncertainty.

matches.theme_name: How do cross-border legal conflicts-choice-of-law, extraterritorial reach, and conflicting forum judgments-shape enforceability and predictability in international financial contracts?
matches.specific_contribution: The article contrasts the broader recognition of arbitral awards with obstacles to enforcing foreign court judgments and highlights how sovereign immunity, act-of-state defenses, exchange controls, and interim-measure limits affect predictability and enforcement in international loan disputes.
matches.generalized_contribution: Cross-border legal frictions—including recognition limits, public-law defenses, and regulatory barriers—shape enforceability and predictability in international financial contracts, often making arbitration comparatively advantageous.

matches.theme_name: Do judicial doctrines-such as act-of-state, sovereign immunity, and abstention/comity-unduly limit creditors' remedies in cross-border disputes and require doctrinal reform to balance politics and predictability?
matches.specific_contribution: The article notes that sovereign-immunity and act-of-state defenses increasingly impede enforcement of transborder loans, while 1988 statutory amendments reduced their sting by making arbitration awards more enforceable than court judgments.
matches.generalized_contribution: Doctrines such as sovereign immunity and act-of-state can constrain creditor remedies, but legislative adjustments and reliance on arbitration can narrow those limits.

matches.theme_name: How do enforcement realities (asset location, capital controls, extraterritorial remedies) interact with contractual clauses to determine practical recoveries from sovereign or cross-border defendants?
matches.specific_contribution: The article underscores that asset location, exchange controls, availability of summary procedures and interim measures, and New York Convention recognition interact with forum-selection and arbitration clauses to determine the practical value of creditor recoveries.
matches.generalized_contribution: Enforcement realities and treaty-based recognition regimes interact with dispute-resolution clauses to shape actual recovery prospects in cross-border lending, especially where sovereigns or foreign assets are involved.

matches.theme_name: How do inconsistent conflict-of-laws rules and varying domestic adjudicative practices affect cross-border payment disputes, the localization of bank deposits, and asset-recovery strategies?
matches.specific_contribution: By citing France’s streamlined payment procedures, uneven availability of interim measures, and the patchy recognition of foreign judgments versus widespread recognition of arbitral awards, the article shows how differing domestic practices drive enforcement strategies in cross-border disputes.
matches.generalized_contribution: Inconsistent recognition rules and adjudicative practices across jurisdictions materially influence where and how creditors pursue payment and locate attachable assets in transnational cases.

matches.theme_name: Do dispute-resolution architectures that shift authority to international fora create unintended incentive distortions or enforcement gaps?
matches.specific_contribution: The article observes that choosing international arbitration may preclude access to summary court procedures and some interim measures in certain jurisdictions even as it enhances cross-border enforceability of outcomes.
matches.generalized_contribution: Shifting disputes from domestic courts to international arbitration entails enforcement trade-offs, closing some remedial avenues while expanding award recognition.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do doctrines of sovereign immunity, act-of-state, and international comity provoke forum-shopping and strategic litigation in cross-border sovereign debt disputes?
matches.specific_contribution: In international loan disputes, the growing use of sovereign-immunity and act-of-state defenses, together with 1988 U.S. statutory changes that make arbitral awards more enforceable than court judgments, pushes lenders to select arbitration and draft forum clauses accordingly in sovereign-related cases.
matches.generalized_contribution: Sovereign-immunity and act-of-state defenses steer parties toward arbitration and strategic forum selection to enhance enforceability in disputes involving sovereigns.

matches.theme_name: Do fragmented or indeterminate cross-border legal regimes create enforcement gaps that justify doctrinal or institutional reform for sovereign debt?
matches.specific_contribution: Because many debtor assets sit in jurisdictions lacking judgment-recognition treaties, foreign court judgments can be hard to enforce, whereas arbitral awards are broadly recognizable under the New York Convention, creating enforcement gaps that sometimes make arbitration preferable.
matches.generalized_contribution: Fragmented cross-border recognition rules create enforcement gaps for court judgments that arbitration, via the New York Convention, can partially bridge.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do legal ambiguities and doctrinal vagueness (e.g., in 'pari passu', 'loan' definitions, or damages measures) cause litigation, market uncertainty, and suboptimal contracting outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The article notes that some jurisdictions treat interim measures like pre-award attachment as incompatible with arbitration agreements covered by the New York Convention—especially if the clause is silent—contributing to banker reluctance to use arbitration.
matches.generalized_contribution: Doctrinal uncertainty and divergence over interim relief in arbitration can deter arbitration clauses and affect dispute resolution choices.

matches.theme_name: Does the extraterritorial reach of U.S. courts and U.S. law materially change enforceability and pricing of sovereign debt?
matches.specific_contribution: The 1988 amendments to the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act and the U.S. Arbitration Act increased the enforceability of arbitral awards relative to court judgments in cross-border sovereign-related disputes, and widespread U.S. lender-liability litigation spurred lenders to adopt arbitration to reduce jury-risk exposure.
matches.generalized_contribution: U.S. legal changes and litigation risks can materially shift cross-border financial contracts toward arbitration to improve enforceability against sovereigns and manage exposure.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do choice-of-law and forum-selection clauses determine the enforceability of claims against sovereigns?
matches.specific_contribution: In cross-border loans—particularly those involving sovereign borrowers or exchange controls—the selection between courts and arbitration determines enforceability, with arbitral awards enjoying broader recognition under the New York Convention and, after 1988 U.S. statutory changes, often being more enforceable than court judgments, prompting more sophisticated forum-clause drafting.
matches.generalized_contribution: Forum-selection choices between courts and arbitration materially shape the enforceability of claims against sovereigns, with arbitration frequently offering superior cross-border recognition and immunity-related advantages.

matches.theme_name: How does the legal enforceability of sovereign obligations and the practical cost of cross-border enforcement affect foreign investment and cross-border capital flows to sovereigns/markets?
matches.specific_contribution: Arbitral awards are often more enforceable across borders than foreign court judgments under the New York Convention, and 1988 amendments to the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act and the U.S. Arbitration Act further strengthen award enforceability against sovereign-related borrowers, making arbitration a tool to enhance the reliability of cross-border credit arrangements.
matches.generalized_contribution: Greater international enforceability of arbitration awards, particularly where sovereign defenses are present, increases the reliability of cross-border lending and can bolster investor confidence.

matches.theme_name: How do cross-border regulatory measures (sanctions, capital controls, deposit freezes) alter contractual rights, remedies, and the incentives of creditors and debtors?
matches.specific_contribution: Exchange controls and sovereign act-of-state/immunity defenses can impede enforcement of foreign court judgments, while arbitral awards benefit from broader recognition under the New York Convention and recent U.S. statutory changes, thereby shifting forum-selection and remedy expectations in cross-border lending.
matches.generalized_contribution: Public regulatory measures and sovereign defenses can curtail judicial remedies, making arbitration—with its wider international enforceability—more attractive and altering contractual rights, remedies, and incentives.

matches.theme_name: Does the extraterritorial reach of national legal regimes and conflicting jurisdictional claims produce distortive conflicts-of-law that affect capital flows and contract design?
matches.specific_contribution: Because foreign court judgments can be difficult to enforce across jurisdictions lacking recognition treaties, while New York Convention arbitral awards are widely enforceable and less vulnerable to act-of-state and sovereign-immunity defenses, the article notes that lenders increasingly include arbitration clauses in cross-border loan contracts.
matches.generalized_contribution: Cross-jurisdiction enforcement frictions and public-law defenses shape international financial contract design by steering parties toward arbitration-focused forum selection.

matches.theme_name: To what degree does forum-shopping and strategic exploitation of legal uncertainty alter creditor litigation strategies and restructuring outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The article explains that lenders have traditionally chosen home-court forum clauses to access speedy summary procedures and familiar courts, but increasingly shift to arbitration when cross-border enforceability advantages or exposure to U.S. lender-liability jury awards alter litigation payoffs, and that powerful borrowers in rescheduling contexts can compel arbitration.
matches.generalized_contribution: In cross-border lending, parties strategically select between courts and arbitration to maximize enforcement leverage and minimize litigation risk, with choices driven by enforceability gaps, liability exposure, and negotiating leverage.

matches.theme_name: How do market conditions and relative bargaining power among actors determine debt terms, restructuring allocations, and recovery outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The article observes that when a borrower’s potential default increases its leverage in rescheduling negotiations, lenders may accept arbitration rather than insist on litigation in their home courts.
matches.generalized_contribution: Borrower bargaining power in distress can shift forum-selection terms toward arbitration in debt contracts.

matches.theme_name: Does expanding statutory limits on sovereign immunity and allowing extraterritorial asset discovery materially increase creditor recoveries without destabilizing sovereign functions?
matches.specific_contribution: The article notes that 1988 amendments to the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act and the U.S. Arbitration Act reduce the bite of sovereign-immunity and act-of-state defenses and make arbitration awards more enforceable than court judgments in cases involving sovereign borrowers.
matches.generalized_contribution: Legal reforms that curb sovereign-immunity defenses and bolster recognition of arbitral awards increase the enforceability of creditor claims against sovereign-related debtors in cross-border finance.

matches.theme_name: Does the availability and legal treatment of cross-border asset attachment and situs rules determine creditor recovery probabilities and thus influence lending terms?
matches.specific_contribution: The article cautions that some jurisdictions treat interim protective measures like pre-award asset attachment as incompatible with New York Convention arbitration agreements unless addressed explicitly, making access to attachment a factor in choosing courts versus arbitration.
matches.generalized_contribution: Constraints on cross-border interim attachment in arbitration regimes influence expected recoveries and drive forum-selection in international loan agreements.

matches.theme_name: How do market conditions, bargaining power, and counterparty composition drive adoption and specific wording of non-price clauses (MAE/MAC, covenants, break fees) in M&A and lending contracts?
matches.specific_contribution: The article identifies concrete conditions—difficulty enforcing foreign court judgments, sovereign immunity and act-of-state defenses, developing-country leverage in reschedulings and project finance, and exposure to U.S. lender-liability suits—that increasingly lead parties to adopt arbitration clauses in international loan agreements, notwithstanding tradeoffs like loss of summary procedures and some interim measures and the greater predictability of judges.
matches.generalized_contribution: Adoption of dispute-resolution clauses in cross-border lending shifts with enforcement prospects, sovereign defenses, borrower leverage, and litigation risk, reflecting a tradeoff between judicial predictability and arbitral enforceability.

matches.theme_name: What practical limits do asset-sheltering, jurisdictional immunity, and political constraints impose on extraterritorial enforcement of claims against states?
matches.specific_contribution: Because arbitral awards benefit from the New York Convention and, after the 1988 amendments to the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act and the U.S. Arbitration Act, are more readily enforceable than court judgments, arbitration can in many sovereign loan disputes better navigate sovereign immunity, act-of-state defenses, and exchange-control complications than foreign court litigation.
matches.generalized_contribution: Arbitral awards generally face fewer extraterritorial enforcement obstacles against sovereigns than foreign court judgments, particularly under widely adopted arbitration enforcement regimes and modern sovereign immunity frameworks.

matches.generalized_contribution: Bargaining power asymmetries shape dispute-resolution terms in cross-border finance, with stronger parties securing home-court litigation and leveraged borrowers shifting disputes to arbitration.

matches.generalized_contribution: Conservatism sustains boilerplate forum provisions in financial contracts, yet enforcement risks can drive more tailored dispute-resolution drafting.

matches.generalized_contribution: Repeat-player legal intermediaries can add value by tailoring dispute-resolution clauses to enforcement realities and sovereign-risk defenses in international lending.

matches.specific_contribution: The article argues that arbitral awards generally enjoy broader international recognition and enforceability under the New York Convention and, after the 1988 amendments to the FSIA and U.S. Arbitration Act, can be more enforceable than court judgments in sovereign-related cases, though this advantage must be weighed against the greater predictability of judges.
matches.generalized_contribution: In sovereign-related disputes, arbitration offers broader cross-border enforceability than court litigation due to treaty and statutory frameworks, but its social desirability depends on balancing this enforcement benefit against the predictability of courts.

matches.theme_name: What is the role of governing-law clauses and the extraterritorial reach of major legal systems (e.g., US law) in constraining sovereign policy space?
matches.specific_contribution: The article explains that selecting arbitration leverages the New York Convention’s multijurisdictional recognition and U.S. statutory changes (FSIA and the U.S. Arbitration Act) to overcome sovereign-immunity, act-of-state, and exchange-control obstacles, increasing sovereign borrowers’ enforcement exposure across borders.

matches.theme_name: Why do standardized contractual clauses ('boilerplate') persist despite inefficiencies, and what institutional or market mechanisms overcome this lock-in?
matches.specific_contribution: The article explains that a herd mentality and reliance on familiar forum-selection clauses have sustained courts-over-arbitration boilerplate in international lending, but mounting pressures—difficulties enforcing foreign judgments, sovereign-immunity and act-of-state defenses, debtor leverage in reschedulings, and U.S. lender-liability exposure—are prompting more sophisticated drafting and selective adoption of arbitration clauses.

matches.theme_name: When and on what grounds should domestic courts review or abstain from adjudicating claims arising from foreign sovereign acts (act-of-state and comity doctrines)?
matches.specific_contribution: The article explains that sovereign immunity and act-of-state defenses complicate court enforcement of trans-border loans and that 1988 amendments to the FSIA and the U.S. Arbitration Act make arbitration awards more enforceable than court judgments in such cases.
matches.generalized_contribution: Limits on sovereign-immunity and act-of-state defenses can make arbitration outcomes more enforceable than domestic court judgments in disputes involving foreign sovereign acts.

matches.theme_name: How do legal and institutional shocks (financial crises, regime change, pandemics) drive changes in contractual practice and market pricing?
matches.specific_contribution: The article identifies several shocks—1988 statutory amendments favoring enforcement of arbitral awards, developing countries’ increased leverage in rescheduling, and the U.S. lender-liability litigation wave—that have prompted major lenders to add arbitration clauses to credit agreements.
matches.generalized_contribution: Legal and institutional shocks alter contractual practice by pushing cross-border lenders toward arbitration clauses to manage enforcement and liability risks.

matches.theme_name: Does statutory codification of contractual standards produce faster or qualitatively different change in drafting practice than incremental common-law evolution?
matches.specific_contribution: It reports that November 1988 statutory amendments to the FSIA and the U.S. Arbitration Act increased the enforceability of arbitral awards relative to court judgments, leading counsel to revise forum-selection drafting in sovereign-related loans toward arbitration.
matches.generalized_contribution: Statutory reforms that enhance award enforceability can trigger revisions in forum-selection drafting toward arbitration in cross-border finance.

matches.theme_name: Do standardized contract forms and drafting defaults systematically shape non-price deal terms and bargaining outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The article explains that standard lender-drafted forum-selection clauses typically channel disputes to the lender’s home courts for advantages like hometown justice and access to summary procedures, but that concerns over cross-border enforceability, sovereign defenses, borrower leverage in reschedulings, and U.S. lender-liability exposure can lead parties to substitute arbitration clauses instead.
matches.generalized_contribution: Standardized forum-selection practices tend to steer dispute resolution toward the drafter’s home courts, but shifts in enforcement risk, legal defenses, bargaining power, and liability exposure can prompt parties to adopt alternative terms such as arbitration.

matches.theme_name: How do norms, professional networks, and market practice diffuse contractual innovations (like new clause language) across jurisdictions and market segments?
matches.specific_contribution: The article explains that although banks have traditionally resisted arbitration and favored home-court forum clauses due to speed, summary procedures, and a herd-mentality aversion to innovation, developments such as broader enforceability of arbitral awards under the New York Convention, 1988 U.S. amendments enhancing enforcement against sovereigns, borrower leverage in reschedulings, and U.S. lender-liability exposure are prompting inclusion of arbitration clauses in some international credit agreements.
matches.generalized_contribution: External legal and strategic pressures—greater award enforceability, limits on sovereign-immunity defenses, borrower leverage, and litigation risk—can overcome entrenched norms favoring courts and drive diffusion of arbitration terms in cross-border financial contracts.

papers.node_id: 22upajbusl209!!ARTICLE: PROACTIVE RESOLUTION OF SOVEREIGN AND SUBNATIONAL DEBT
papers.title: ARTICLE: PROACTIVE RESOLUTION OF SOVEREIGN AND SUBNATIONAL DEBT
papers.abstract:
Sovereign nations urgently need help in resolving unsustainable debt burdens.Paying that debt would reduce a nation's ability to provide critical public services,whereas defaulting on that debt would further damage the nation's fiscal integrity and reputation and could even trigger a systemic shock that harms the broader economy.This dilemma is real and growing:the median public debt of the sixty low-income developing countries increased from 33.5% of gross domestic product ("GDP") in 2013 to 47% of GDP in 2017.Eight of these countries are already in debt distress,and sixteen are facing a high risk of debt distress.
This Article seeks to help solve this dilemma by examining "proactive" ways to resolve unsustainable governmental debt. In a separate article, I examined how proactive strategies could help systemically important financial firms resolve unsustainable debt.Whether addressing firms or governments, proactive-resolution strategies should follow the same principles: convert debt that is beginning to become unsustainable ("borderline unsustainable debt") into sustainable financing, through pre-planning; or try to prevent the debt from approaching unsustainability.
Proactive resolution differs from traditional resolution strategies, which are primarily reactive. Corporate bankruptcy, for example, merely helps firms react to debt burdens that already have become unsustainable.Sovereign debt restructuring strategies have likewise been reactive.Reactive resolution strategies are even less effective for sovereign debt than for corporate debt because sovereigns lack systematic legal mechanisms--suchas those provided by corporate bankruptcy law--for correcting collective action holdout problems and other market failures that impede debt restructuring.Nor are such mechanisms likely to be implemented in the foreseeable future.Waiting until a sovereign becomes financially troubled to restructure its debt is also problematic because the sovereign's loss of access to low-cost capital markets can exacerbate its debt burden.
The ongoing drama of Greece's debt restructuring, which already involves the largest sovereign bailout in history, illustrates these inefficiencies. That nation has been using billions of euros of bailout funds solely to pay interest on, without actually reducing, the principal amount of its debt.Furthermore, a portion of that bailout funding is conditioned on Greece taking certain creditor-imposed austerity measures, which may be benefitting its creditors more than the nation.
Changes in the sovereign debt markets are making proactive resolution even more important. Diversification of the types of creditors holding sovereign debt, for example, is creating uncertainty as to relative creditor priorities, further impeding the ability of parties to restructure unsustainabledebt.The growth of collateralized sovereign debt also "reduces room for maneuver in the event of a crisis, making [debt] restructurings more difficult."Recent defaults by the Venezuela government and PDVSA (Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A., Venezuela's state-owned oil company) highlight these changes. The diversified nature of their creditors has created uncertainty as to the relative seniority of their claims,and the fact that a large portion of Venezuelan assets is located outside that country has made it easier for creditors to seize collateral.These factors further undermine the ability to reach a successful debt restructuring.
This Article also examines the proactive resolution of unsustainable subnational debt--meaning the debt of political subdivisions of nations, such as states, provinces, and municipalities.The World Bank and the International Monetary Fund ("IMF") recognize the increasing urgency of subnational debt problems.Unsustainable subnational debt sometimes also contributes to sovereign debt burdens; the inability of the Provinces of Mendoza and Buenos Aires to pay their debt, for example, appears to have been a major factor in Argentina's 2001 debt default.
The Article proceeds as follows. Part I conceives and designs ananalytical framework for proactively resolving government debt, to prevent it from becoming unsustainable. Part II applies that framework to resolving sovereign debt. Part III applies that framework to resolving subnational debt. The Appendix briefly summarizes the resulting design recommendations, following the Article's more detailed discussion.
There are references throughout this Article to "unsustainable" debt. Although the definition of unsustainability can be elusive in a government-debt context, the following intuitive definition should suffice for analyzing proactive resolution: government debt is unsustainable if the government cannot continue paying principal and interest thereon and still be able to provide critical public services. This definition roughly follows the more technical definition used by the International Monetary Fund, which views government debt as unsustainable if the government is not expected to be able to continue paying principal and interest on its debt given its current levels of income and expenditures.
Because they are examined at length in other literature, certain routine debt practices that some might consider proactive are beyond this Article's scope. These include investing the proceeds of borrowings to try to generate a sufficient return for repayment (analytically, this Article assumes that some nations, like some companies, inevitably will face unsustainable debt burdens); the actions of the IMF as a lender of last resort to governments; and the longstanding dialogue about creating forums to try to facilitate sovereign-debt-restructuring conversations.Also, the Article does not purport to try to solve the "rollover risk" of short-term government debt--that a government will be temporarily unable to borrow sufficient funds to repay its maturing debt.Even proactive resolution strategies may be unableto control that risk.

matches.theme_name: What institutional design best balances creditor enforcement rights and debtor-state welfare during sovereign restructurings (e.g., new-money priority, funding of essential services)?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article designs an analytical framework for proactively converting borderline unsustainable sovereign and subnational debt into sustainable financing so governments can continue providing critical public services while avoiding the costs and austerity pressures of reactive restructurings.
matches.generalized_contribution: Proactive-resolution frameworks that convert borderline unsustainable obligations into sustainable financing can preserve debtor fiscal space and mitigate welfare losses during debt distress.

matches.theme_name: Would instituting a treaty/statutory Sovereign Debt Restructuring Mechanism (SDRM) reduce holdout litigation and crisis costs compared with reliance on ad-hoc private mechanisms?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article states that sovereigns lack systematic legal mechanisms to address collective-action and related market failures and that such mechanisms are unlikely to be implemented in the foreseeable future, motivating reliance on proactive alternatives rather than a formal SDRM.
matches.generalized_contribution: Given low political feasibility for a formal sovereign bankruptcy regime, proactive, pre-emptive tools are a more realistic path than an SDRM for managing sovereign distress and its litigation risks.

matches.theme_name: Do fragmented or indeterminate cross-border legal regimes create enforcement gaps that justify doctrinal or institutional reform for sovereign debt?

papers.node_id: 6chijintll177!!ARTICLE: SYMPOSIUM: SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING: Redesigning the International Lender of Last Resort
papers.title: ARTICLE: SYMPOSIUM: SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING: Redesigning the International Lender of Last Resort
papers.abstract:
Since the Mexican Debt Crisis of 1994-95, which gave rise to an International Monetary Fund ("IMF") bailout of unprecedented size, there has been a raging debate on how the IMF should handle sovereign debt crises. Despite the successful resolution of the crisis and Mexico's quick repayment of all its emergency debt, the sheer size of the intervention has raised worries that bailouts could cause significant sovereign debt market distortions. These concerns, in turn, have led to a reconsideration of the prevailing wisdom that the IMF can and should act as the de facto international lender of last resort ("ILOLR") by arranging bailouts in response to major sovereign debt crises. As is now widely recognized, the problem with a purely bailout-based policy is that it requires ever larger funds to be credible and successful. It also invites undesirable policies by debtor countries. The prospect of a bailout encourages sovereign debtors to borrow more than they should, and it tempts them to resort to highly risky fixed exchange rate policies as a quick fix towardsmacroeconomic discipline.Of course, the worst debtor misconduct can be controlled to some extent by imposing conditions on the debtor country before granting a rescue program, but more often than not, the IMF finds itself in a weak bargaining position at the onset of a debt crisis. How credible is the IMF threat to withhold a financial aid package when a potentially contagious debt crisis is about to erupt? And once the bailout has been granted, why should the debtor country abide by the conditions it agreed to?
Because of the potentially enormous financial commitment a pure ILOLR policy requires, and because of the moral hazard it may induce in sovereign debt markets, it is now widely understood that bailouts need to be supplemented by at least a partial "bailin" of the private sector. According to this view, the IMF's involvement in a debt crisis should be conditioned on debt reduction or rescheduling by private sector lenders. Private creditors should be required, that is, to share at least some of the costs of resolving a crisis. Despite this emerging consensus on the importance of private sector involvement, however, there is still considerable disagreement on the appropriate balancing between bailout and bailin, and on the best process for crisis resolution and debt restructuring.
The most ambitious overhaul of IMF policy contemplated so far involves the introduction of some form of bankruptcy institution for sovereigns and envisions a single forum where the extent of debt reduction and the size of new emergency lending would be decided simultaneously. There was considerable discussion and research of this strategy -- which the IMF calls a Sovereign Debt Restructuring Mechanism ("SDRM") -- from late 2001, when the IMF first announced its support for a sovereign bankruptcy framework, up to the G-10 meetings in April 2003, when the IMF's proposal was shelved. Despite all the writing and debates, many open questions were still unresolved at the time of the G-10 meetings, including the role of the IMF in an SDRM regime. No doubt these questions would have received further attention if the SDRM proposal had gone forward. But in the aftermath of the SDRM debate, no clear new role has been marked out for the IMF and no clear rules have emerged to direct the IMF's balancing of bailins and bailouts in future debt crises.
As a result, the IMF now finds itself at a crossroads. Should it be content with the status quo and accept that it will be less and less equipped to deal with major emerging market debt crises? Or, on the contrary, should its size beconsiderably expanded, possibly by granting a more powerful role to Japan, China and other East Asian countries that are sitting on massive idle foreign exchange reserves? Or, even more radically, should the IMF disclaim any role in crisis lending and confine itself to an advisory and forecasting function, as Chari and Kehoe, Rogoff, and others have urged?
In this paper, we argue that by establishing an adequate bankruptcy procedure for sovereigns, the international community could both fully address the problem of sovereign debt restructuring and redefine an ambitious crisis resolution role for the IMF. Far from stepping away from a crisis lending role, we argue that the IMF could, without increasing the size of its funding, enhance its ILOLR role within the framework of a sovereign bankruptcy procedure. How do we square this circle?
Corporate bankruptcy provides a useful analogy for describing the new role we envision for the IMF. When a nonfinancial corporation ends up in financial distress, it does not, as a rule, seek a bailout from the government. Instead it files for bankruptcy, thus receiving temporary relief from its creditors. This relief from creditors -- or "stay" -- is the characteristic of corporate bankruptcy that has been emphasized most in the sovereign context. But, in addition to a stay on debt collection, and more significant for our purposes, the distressed firm can also ask the court to approve new priority lending -- usually in connection with so-called "first day orders" that authorize the company to continue paying its employees and thus preserve its going concern value.When the bankruptcy court grants new priority lending, it is not extending its own funds, as the IMFdoes when it puts together a financing package for a distressed sovereign. All the court does is make way for new lending by the private sector -- often the same lenders that have already lent to the distressed firm in the past -- by granting the new loans higher priority status.
We suggest that, just as a bankruptcy court does for corporations, the IMF could play the role of granting first-day orders to distressed sovereigns in the context of a sovereign bankruptcy procedure. Importantly, the IMF would not need any new funding to exercise this authority. Thus, a major additional benefit of sovereign bankruptcy is that it could open the way for a new enhanced role for the IMF. This new role would indeed strengthen the IMF's hand, as it would enable the IMF to facilitate much larger emergency lending packages consisting not just of IMF funding but private lending as well. In addition, it would not give rise to the same concerns about moral hazard as does the current form of intervention that relies on publicly funded IMF bailouts. In particular, since the fund would no longer just be extending its own funds, it would be subject to greater market discipline. The private lenders that the IMF would invite to provide the new capital could be expected to do so only if there were a plausible financial rationale for extending the loans. Moreover, the IMF could not extend priority status too liberally without imperiling its very existence.
To achieve this restructuring of the IMF's role, the underlying sovereign bankruptcy framework would need to provide coherent and enforceable priority rules.In earlier work that did not envision this new role for the IMF, we argued that solidifying creditors' seniority rights may be the single most important benefit of establishing a sovereign bankruptcy regime.In this Article, we take the analysis a step further, to incorporate a reconceptualized role for the IMF -- a role that would avoid the increasingly real risk that the IMF might otherwise become obsolete.
The remainder of our article proceeds as follows. In Part II, we discuss the recent policy proposals for improving the sovereign debt restructuring process. We also consider the extent to which the benefits of a statutory procedure could be achieved through contractual alternatives, and briefly explore the implicationsof the recent debt crisis in Argentina. Part III maps out the new role for the IMF and assesses how IMF actions in debt crises may need to be circumscribed.

matches.theme_name: Should international financial institutions (IMF/World Bank) be given expanded mandates (stays, priority lending, formal restructuring roles) to manage sovereign-debt crises, and what are the trade-offs?
matches.specific_contribution: The paper proposes a sovereign bankruptcy regime that empowers the IMF to issue bankruptcy-style 'first-day' orders granting priority to new private lending, enabling larger crisis packages without expanding IMF resources and with reduced moral hazard.
matches.generalized_contribution: Expanding IFI authority to confer priority on new-money within a formal restructuring framework can improve crisis management while limiting moral hazard and additional public funding needs.

matches.theme_name: What institutional reforms of the IMF and other multilateral actors would improve coordination of sovereign restructurings without creating undue moral hazard?
matches.specific_contribution: It advances a reform in which a statutory sovereign bankruptcy framework with coherent, enforceable priority rules and IMF authority to approve priority new financing coordinates private-sector bail-ins with official support, curbing moral hazard.
matches.generalized_contribution: Creating a formal restructuring framework that equips the IMF to authorize priority interim financing can enhance coordination and legitimacy of restructurings while restraining perverse incentives.

matches.theme_name: Which institutional or doctrinal reforms (statutory sovereign bankruptcy, coordinated creditor fora, harmonized conflict-of-laws rules) are feasible and likely to improve restructuring speed, predictability, and fairness?
matches.specific_contribution: The article contends that a statutory sovereign bankruptcy procedure—with enforceable priority and a single forum—would more fully address restructuring needs than the status quo, and it considers which benefits can and cannot be replicated by contractual alternatives.
matches.generalized_contribution: A treaty-based sovereign bankruptcy regime with clear priority rules and centralized decision-making is likely to enhance clarity and effectiveness relative to piecemeal contractual approaches.

matches.theme_name: Would instituting a treaty/statutory Sovereign Debt Restructuring Mechanism (SDRM) reduce holdout litigation and crisis costs compared with reliance on ad-hoc private mechanisms?
matches.specific_contribution: By centralizing decisions on debt reduction and new emergency lending under a sovereign bankruptcy mechanism, the paper argues crisis resolution would be more orderly and less distortionary than ad hoc, bailout-led responses.
matches.generalized_contribution: A formal SDRM that coordinates restructuring terms and new-money decisions can lower crisis-management costs relative to ad hoc mechanisms.

matches.theme_name: Are negotiated, policy-oriented processes through multilateral institutions more effective than formal international-law doctrines in resolving sovereign debt crises?
matches.specific_contribution: It favors a formal sovereign bankruptcy regime—with IMF-administered priority for new money—over reliance on negotiated bailout conditionality as the primary tool for resolving crises.
matches.generalized_contribution: Formal international restructuring procedures are more effective than purely negotiated policy processes for managing sovereign debt crises.

matches.theme_name: What institutional design best balances creditor enforcement rights and debtor-state welfare during sovereign restructurings (e.g., new-money priority, funding of essential services)?
matches.specific_contribution: The paper designs a system in which enforceable priority rules protect new private financing approved by the IMF during a sovereign bankruptcy, allowing necessary stabilization funding while respecting creditor seniority and limiting moral hazard.
matches.generalized_contribution: Granting super-priority to interim sovereign financing within a statutory framework can balance debtor funding needs with creditor enforcement rights during restructurings.

matches.theme_name: What role do the IMF and other official-sector actors play in shaping restructuring bargaining, creditor incentives, and ultimate debt-relief outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: It reconceives the IMF’s role as approving priority status for new private lending in a bankruptcy-like process, which would strengthen its bargaining leverage, align creditor incentives through market discipline, and shape the scale and terms of relief.
matches.generalized_contribution: Official-sector authority to confer priority on interim financing can materially influence bargaining dynamics, creditor participation, and debt-relief outcomes.

matches.theme_name: What contractual and institutional devices most effectively protect 'new-money' or interim financing priority during sovereign restructurings?
matches.specific_contribution: The article argues that a sovereign bankruptcy framework must include coherent, enforceable priority rules and empower the IMF to grant priority to new-money, thereby protecting interim lenders and unlocking larger financing.
matches.generalized_contribution: Statutory priority mechanisms administered by official institutions effectively protect and mobilize new-money during restructurings.

matches.theme_name: How effective are international financial institutions (IMF/Bretton Woods) and official-sector actors in shaping restructuring incentives and practical outcomes relative to private creditors?
matches.specific_contribution: Because new lending would come from private creditors only when financially justified and under IMF-approved priority, the scheme relies on market discipline to shape participation and outcomes.
matches.generalized_contribution: Official-sector structuring of priority for interim financing can channel private-creditor behavior but remains constrained by private market incentives.

matches.theme_name: Can official-sector institutions (e.g., the IMF) and enhanced institutional capacity mitigate systemic contagion and improve sovereign-debt restructuring outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The paper proposes a sovereign bankruptcy framework in which the IMF authorizes priority status for new private lending, enabling larger crisis packages without expanding IMF funds, reducing moral hazard, and improving restructuring outcomes.
matches.generalized_contribution: Empowering an official-sector actor to grant priority to new private lending within a sovereign bankruptcy regime can improve sovereign-debt crisis resolution while mitigating moral hazard without larger public bailouts.

matches.theme_name: Are market-based restructuring instruments (debt-equity swaps, exit consents, buybacks) as effective and equitable as formal legal remedies in reallocating burdens during sovereign restructurings?
matches.specific_contribution: The article notes that while it considers how far contractual alternatives can replicate the benefits of a statutory sovereign bankruptcy process, it emphasizes the need for coherent, enforceable priority rules best provided by a formal regime.
matches.generalized_contribution: Voluntary contractual mechanisms can only partially substitute for a formal sovereign restructuring framework where enforceable priority structures are required.

matches.theme_name: Do fragmented or indeterminate cross-border legal regimes create enforcement gaps that justify doctrinal or institutional reform for sovereign debt?
matches.specific_contribution: It argues that establishing a sovereign bankruptcy procedure with coherent, enforceable priority and seniority rules is necessary to address restructuring problems and to support a redefined IMF role.
matches.generalized_contribution: Deficiencies in enforceable priority and seniority in sovereign debt warrant coordinated statutory reform through a sovereign bankruptcy mechanism.

matches.theme_name: Can contractual and financial innovations (debt-equity swaps, buy-backs, securitization, contingent payments) reconcile creditor recovery with debtor welfare and domestic policy goals?
matches.specific_contribution: By allowing the IMF to grant priority to new private loans under a sovereign bankruptcy regime, the proposal mobilizes emergency finance that preserves debtor functionality while imposing market discipline on assistance.
matches.generalized_contribution: Priority new-money lending within a sovereign bankruptcy framework can align creditor incentives with debtor stabilization without expanding public bailouts.

matches.theme_name: How do market conditions and relative bargaining power among actors determine debt terms, restructuring allocations, and recovery outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The abstract explains that the IMF’s threat to withhold aid is not credible during potentially contagious crises, leaving it in a weak bargaining position to enforce conditionality.
matches.generalized_contribution: Systemic-risk conditions can weaken official creditors’ bargaining leverage, undermining conditionality and shaping restructuring dynamics.

matches.theme_name: What are the welfare trade-offs of prioritizing orderly, negotiated restructuring (stability and debtor rehabilitation) over strict creditor protections?
matches.specific_contribution: The paper favors an orderly sovereign bankruptcy process that enables priority new lending to rehabilitate the debtor—even at the expense of subordinating existing claims—because it curbs moral hazard and strengthens crisis resolution.
matches.generalized_contribution: Prioritizing coordinated restructuring with mechanisms for priority new money can improve welfare despite diluting strict protections for existing creditors.

matches.theme_name: How do contractual provisions allocating priority for new/interim financing (new-money priority) affect incentives to provide rescue capital and the success of restructurings?
matches.specific_contribution: Within a sovereign bankruptcy procedure with coherent, enforceable priority rules, empowering the IMF to approve priority status for post-crisis private loans would catalyze sizable rescue financing without enlarging IMF resources and would temper moral hazard via market discipline.
matches.generalized_contribution: Enforceable new-money priority in sovereign restructurings can unlock private rescue capital, expand and improve crisis lending, and reduce moral hazard.

matches.theme_name: Can contractual devices (collateral, covenants, exit consents, priority clauses) effectively allocate and limit creditor risk in sovereign and cross-border transactions under information asymmetry?
matches.specific_contribution: By emphasizing that a sovereign bankruptcy regime must provide coherent and enforceable priority rules to support the IMF’s proposed role, the paper implies that purely contractual devices may not reliably secure creditor seniority in sovereign workouts.
matches.generalized_contribution: Reliable allocation of creditor priority in sovereign restructurings often requires enforceable statutory mechanisms rather than relying solely on contracts.

matches.theme_name: How do courts' use of emergency or adaptive doctrines in crises influence creditor protections and the enforceability of sovereign obligations?
matches.specific_contribution: Within a sovereign bankruptcy framework, the paper proposes that the IMF would authorize priority new lending akin to corporate “first-day orders,” enabling larger, market-disciplined emergency financing and reshaping creditor protections without expanding IMF funds.
matches.generalized_contribution: Embedding stay and priority-financing tools in a sovereign bankruptcy regime can recalibrate creditor protections and crisis bargaining by channeling senior new money without public bailouts.

matches.theme_name: How does heterogeneity in creditor rights and intercreditor priority influence restructuring feasibility, bargaining dynamics, and recoveries?
matches.specific_contribution: The paper argues that a sovereign bankruptcy regime must provide coherent and enforceable priority rules that solidify creditor seniority, thereby facilitating IMF-authorized priority financing, improving restructuring effectiveness, and reducing moral hazard.
matches.generalized_contribution: Clear, enforceable intercreditor priority rules enhance sovereign restructuring feasibility by enabling senior new financing and disciplining bailout-driven moral hazard.

matches.theme_name: How does the legal enforceability of sovereign obligations and the practical cost of cross-border enforcement affect foreign investment and cross-border capital flows to sovereigns/markets?
matches.specific_contribution: The article contends that a sovereign bankruptcy regime with coherent, enforceable priority rules would let the IMF authorize priority new-money lending that crowds in private finance, reduces moral hazard, and enables larger crisis packages without expanding IMF funds.
matches.generalized_contribution: Enforceable priority and restructuring rules in sovereign debt increase the availability of private crisis finance and mitigate moral hazard, thereby shaping capital access during crises.

matches.theme_name: Can private ordering, market-level contractual design, and intermediaries substitute effectively for statutory or multilateral interventions in solving cross-border collective-action problems?
matches.specific_contribution: While considering contractual alternatives, the paper concludes that only a statutory sovereign bankruptcy framework with enforceable priority rules can fully resolve restructuring problems and support an enhanced, market-disciplined IMF role, so private ordering cannot substitute effectively.
matches.generalized_contribution: Private ordering and standardized contracts cannot fully solve cross-border sovereign debt collective-action and financing problems; a statutory bankruptcy mechanism with priority rules is necessary.

matches.theme_name: Do contractual devices (insurance, covenants, staged payments, MAC/force-majeure language) adequately allocate risk for large, systemic shocks, or is public intervention required?
matches.specific_contribution: The paper maintains that resolving systemic sovereign crises requires an official bankruptcy framework in which the IMF authorizes priority financing, rather than reliance on ex ante contract terms alone.
matches.generalized_contribution: Managing large systemic sovereign shocks requires public legal frameworks and official coordination beyond what private contractual devices can provide.

matches.theme_name: Do dispute-resolution architectures that shift authority to international fora create unintended incentive distortions or enforcement gaps?
matches.specific_contribution: The paper proposes embedding an IMF role within a sovereign bankruptcy procedure where the Fund authorizes priority new lending, backed by coherent and enforceable priority rules, to reduce bailout-induced moral hazard and strengthen crisis-enforcement credibility without expanding IMF resources.
matches.generalized_contribution: A sovereign bankruptcy regime that empowers an international body to grant priority financing under enforceable priority rules can mitigate moral-hazard distortions and close enforcement gaps inherent in ad hoc bailout-based resolution.
