Although the document standardizes many aspects of the practice of swap trading, it also allows for a certain amount of flexibility and adaptation by its users through a "schedule" at the end in which the parties can specify some of the details to their particular relationship, such as how payments are to be made. Hence the task of the documentation people was to tailor the agreement to the needs of the bank and its counterparties by filling in the blanks in the form.
At first blush, it may seem odd to focus on this kind of legal work as an example of global private law. It has become commonplace in sociolegal studies to focus instead on the "creative capacities of lawyers"- in bringing clients together, inventing innovative solutions to business problems, pushing the development of law, and hence shaping the character of society. But the rote and repetitive work of the documentation people, defined by its precision and attention to detail rather than its creativity, and by its distance from legal theory, points to another, too little acknowledged modality of legal work.
All this mundane activity is relevant to the nature of global private law and to the question of the extent to which it operates outside or beyond the state in two senses. First, the ISDA master agreement is the work of a powerful global private organization of the kind that is now at the center of many debates about global private law.Second, within the field of global derivatives trading, collateralization is a legal technology that is paradigmatic of global private law solutions. Although collateral is an artifact of multiple kinds of national law,it is also a device for running an end-game around certain aspects of national law. In the event of bankruptcy, collateral gives swap counterparties a mechanism other than the priority system of national bankruptcy laws with its concerns for the interests of thirdparties through which to resolve disputes.Collateral is a self-help mechanism: in many jurisdictions the collateral holder may simply keep the collateral to satisfy the debtor's obligations, without going to court.Collateral emerges as a solution to a practical problem of transnational governance, therefore. The problem is that the terms of the national bankruptcy laws of many of the countries in which derivatives trading occurs and the way these are interpreted and enforced by national bankruptcy judges do not always suit the global derivatives industry because they do not prioritize their claims ahead of others.
But collateral has many other advantages other than protection against bankruptcy. For example, it becomes a vehicle for the parties to privately steer their relationship through other turbulent waters: the ISDA Master Agreement lists a number of "events" short of bankruptcy that trigger the collateral holder's right to close out its positions and use the collateral to satisfy any residual debts.In this respect, collateral shares certain functional features with other private commercial practices such as the uses of barter in international trade,or the rules commercial banks have developed for letter ofcredit practices.We might say that collateral becomes, in a practical sense, a kind of private constitution for the parties' ongoing relationship.
For some, claims about the global production of private law of this kind become an urgent object of critique. These commentators seek to show that the "technical" quality of global private law is in fact highly politicized.They renew and expand longstanding critiques of the public-private distinction in domestic law to demonstrate that global private law is always dependent upon state legal institutions for enforcement.
It is certainly true, as these critics assert, that collateral is an artifact of multiple kinds of publicly created law.Collateral transactions in the privately traded derivatives markets raise particular problems of interface between multiple national legal systems, including problems of determining what law applies to any particular collateral transaction.The answers to these questions are murky,doctrinally arcane, and just as variable, from jurisdiction to jurisdiction, as is the law of collateral itself.Robert Wai terms these thornydoctrinal problems "touchdown points" in the relationship between global private governance and national law - points at which the efforts of private organizations such as ISDA to achieve "lift-off" from national regimes comes to rest on national law itself.
But this critique of global private governance is certainly not news to the proponents of global private governance institutions like ISDA. The legal experts with whom I worked understood full well that the private law of collateral is always only a partial global solution to their local legal problems.They were intimately aware, for example, that the terms of any collateral agreement must satisfy national requirements for creating a valid and enforceable security interest in order for the lender to be able to use the collateral, or again, that national bankruptcy law must recognize the primacy of the interest of "secured creditors" over other creditors if the collateral agreement is to have force once the debtor has declared bankruptcy. In fact, it was at these junctures that the legal actors I studied labored - these constraints created the legal work for them to do.
For example, where the terms in ISDA's standardized documents conflict with the norms enshrined in national statutory or judge-made law, ISDA actively works to supplant or change the latter so that it conforms to the former. ISDA hires local lawyers to investigate discrepancies between the terms of ISDA documents and national law, and where necessary, to lobby national governments to change national law to either conform to the terms of the Master Agreementor explicitly declare the ISDA documents enforceable.Partly at the urging of ISDA, and with active input from the organization, several transnational bodies are busy creating substantive legal rules concerning collateral that would apply in multiple jurisdictions and supersede national law. ISDA has pressed for the creation of a treaty - perhaps the ultimate example of global state law - that would mandate that national judges respect private parties' right to choose whatever law they wish to have applied to their collateral agreements.In response to lobbying from ISDA,the European Union has adopted a Directive on Financial Collateral Arrangements defining how security interests are to be created in EU Member States, and the rights of holders of collateral.And ISDA has also worked with UNIDROIT, the international body devoted to unifying private law globally,on a Convention on Harmonised Substantive Rules regardingIntermediated Securities to be adopted by individual nations as international law.ISDA members aim not only to create substantive legal rights through private contracts, but to influence the shape of those rights as they find expression in state law.
What Wai views as "touchdown points," then, were for my informants, projects - problems that demanded creative work, political mobilization, technical skill, and considerable devotion. What is interesting about typical artifacts of private global governance such as collateral, when viewed in practice, is not whether they are truly private (and outside the purview of the state), or actually public (and within state control), but rather how the impulse, the fantasy of a private market engenders particular kinds of practical projects, particular registers of engagement between lawyers working for private parties under the umbrella of transnational organizations such as ISDA, national and international law-makers, judges, and regulators.
Moreover, the view that private law is just a pass through to state power overlooks the role of the materiality of ISDA forms in the global private governance regime. The rhetorical force of the argument that judges will wreak chaos on the markets if they fail to honor market practices is perhaps different because of the sheer physical ubiquity of these documents. For example, in the early 1990s, the ISDA Master Agreement's procedures for closing out the agreement in the case of the bankruptcy of one party, and its delineation of the rights of the other party in such a scenario, arguably conflicted with the substantive rules and procedures of many national bankruptcy regimes. However, interviews suggest that the widespread use of the Master Agreement - the physical existence of thousands of such signed documents - transformed the question of what to do about substantive legal rules that industry members found unfavorable, a policy question, into a far more general and technical question of the enforceability of this contract in each national jurisdiction.
The sociological fact that material documents matter admittedly flies in the face of the longstanding assertion that the paper of the contract means nothing in itself, that it is the agreement between the parties, and not the document, that matters.But commentators have begun to pay attention to the consequences of standardized contracts such as ISDA documents for the authority, legitimacy and power of privatized law in a global market.Some even celebrate these standardized contracts as examples of "the changing paradigm of international commercial law" towards "privatized law-making."And indeed, for ISDA staff and members, collateral documents are crucial technologies of private transnational legal infrastructure - devices through which particular technical, institutional, political, legal, and economic arrangements gain solidity and durability.This is not to say that judges do not understand that a privately created document is legally meaningful only to the extent that a state-sanctioned court holds it to be enforceable. But what empirical observation of private law in action demonstrates is that in order for the transaction to "work" all sides (parties and judges alike) must be both aware of the "truth" that state power lies behind all private legal regimes and able to momentarily forget this fact to immerse themselves the practical and technical day to day experience of doing private law.

matches.theme_name: Can private ordering, market-level contractual design, and intermediaries substitute effectively for statutory or multilateral interventions in solving cross-border collective-action problems?
matches.specific_contribution: Using ISDA master agreements and collateral in the OTC derivatives markets, the article shows that private ordering provides day-to-day governance and self-help remedies but continually depends on, and seeks to reshape, state law through lobbying, directives, and treaties, so it does not fully substitute for public frameworks.
matches.generalized_contribution: Private contractual infrastructure can coordinate cross-border finance in practice but remains interdependent with, and often channels efforts toward, public-law harmonization rather than replacing it outright.

matches.theme_name: To what degree do soft-law norms, reputation, and market practice substitute for enforceable legal remedies in cross-border finance?
matches.specific_contribution: In OTC derivatives, standard industry documentation and collateral arrangements supply routinized self-help mechanisms—such as close-out rights and retention of collateral without court involvement—that guide relationships when formal enforcement is impractical, yet their effectiveness ultimately hinges on state recognition.
matches.generalized_contribution: Industry standards and self-help collateral practices can partially discipline cross-border financial relationships in the absence of immediate courtroom enforcement, but they depend on eventual legal enforceability.

matches.theme_name: What role do lawyers, underwriters, and other intermediaries play in creating, diffusing, and entrenching contractual innovations and standard clauses?
matches.specific_contribution: Based on participant observation, the article documents how ISDA staff, local lawyers, and in-house documentation personnel create, tailor, and circulate standardized master agreements and then lobby to align national laws with those templates, thereby entrenching those clauses across markets.
matches.generalized_contribution: Intermediaries and industry associations diffuse and entrench boilerplate by combining routine documentation work with legal and political efforts to align public law to standardized terms.

matches.theme_name: When do private ordering and standardized boilerplate generate negative externalities for third parties that warrant public-policy or regulatory intervention?
matches.specific_contribution: The article notes that collateralization lets swap parties resolve defaults and seize collateral outside national bankruptcy priority schemes designed for other creditors, effectively privatizing outcomes that affect third parties.
matches.generalized_contribution: Standardized collateral arrangements can bypass public insolvency distribution rules, shifting risks to nonparties and raising potential public-policy concerns.

matches.theme_name: Does the extraterritorial reach of national legal regimes and conflicting jurisdictional claims produce distortive conflicts-of-law that affect capital flows and contract design?
matches.specific_contribution: The article shows that inconsistencies and uncertainty across national laws governing collateral and conflicts of law shape contract drafting and spur ISDA to seek cross-jurisdictional fixes, including an EU directive and a treaty to ensure courts respect parties’ choice of law.
matches.generalized_contribution: Cross-border conflicts of law and divergent national regimes drive contract design choices and prompt industry-backed legal harmonization efforts.

matches.theme_name: Why do standardized contractual clauses ('boilerplate') persist despite inefficiencies, and what institutional or market mechanisms overcome this lock-in?
matches.specific_contribution: Drawing on observations of the swaps market, the article shows that the ISDA Master Agreement’s standardized, materially ubiquitous forms and routinized documentation work—reinforced by ISDA’s efforts to align national law—entrench boilerplate and give it practical authority.
matches.generalized_contribution: Boilerplate persists because the material ubiquity of standardized forms, routine production practices, and coordinated industry institutions entrench language and mobilize supporting legal change.

matches.theme_name: Can contractual devices (collateral, covenants, exit consents, priority clauses) effectively allocate and limit creditor risk in sovereign and cross-border transactions under information asymmetry?
matches.specific_contribution: In cross-border OTC derivatives, collateral arrangements under the ISDA framework function as self-help devices that permit close-out upon specified events and bypass aspects of national bankruptcy priority, thereby reallocating and limiting counterparty credit risk.
matches.generalized_contribution: Collateral mechanisms in international financial contracts can effectively limit and reallocate creditor risk by enabling self-help enforcement and event-triggered protections despite divergent national insolvency regimes.

matches.theme_name: How do cross-border legal conflicts-choice-of-law, extraterritorial reach, and conflicting forum judgments-shape enforceability and predictability in international financial contracts?
matches.specific_contribution: Participant observation reveals that murky and variable cross-border conflicts of law and enforcement for collateral drive ISDA to conduct legal due diligence and press for harmonization (e.g., EU Directive, UNIDROIT/treaty efforts) to improve predictability and enforceability.
matches.generalized_contribution: Cross-border conflicts of law and divergent national rules undermine predictability and enforceability in international financial contracts, prompting private actors to adapt documentation and pursue legal harmonization.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do legal ambiguities and doctrinal vagueness (e.g., in 'pari passu', 'loan' definitions, or damages measures) cause litigation, market uncertainty, and suboptimal contracting outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The article notes that applicable-law questions and collateral doctrines are “murky,” doctrinally arcane, and variable across jurisdictions, creating thorny problems that necessitate private legal work and harmonization efforts, reflecting practical uncertainty.
matches.generalized_contribution: Doctrinal ambiguity and cross-jurisdictional variability generate legal uncertainty that spurs costly private legal work and motivates standard-setting and harmonization initiatives.

matches.theme_name: How do enforcement realities (asset location, capital controls, extraterritorial remedies) interact with contractual clauses to determine practical recoveries from sovereign or cross-border defendants?
matches.specific_contribution: In the OTC derivatives setting, collateral under the ISDA Master Agreement operates as a self-help remedy that can bypass national bankruptcy priority rules in many jurisdictions, so practical recoveries hinge on both contractual close-out triggers and what domestic law permits.
matches.generalized_contribution: Self-help collateral mechanisms shape cross-border recovery prospects by coupling contractual rights with the permissions and limits of domestic insolvency law.

matches.theme_name: Do lawyers, deal teams, and legal intermediaries (as repeat players) add measurable economic value through drafting and structuring beyond mere documentation?
matches.specific_contribution: Through participant observation and ISDA practice, the article shows that routine documentation work and ISDA legal experts’ standard-setting, tailoring, and lobbying substantively structure rights (e.g., collateral and close-out) and enforceability, going well beyond mere memorialization of deals.
matches.generalized_contribution: Repeat-player legal intermediaries add substantive value beyond paperwork by designing, standardizing, and entrenching contractual architectures that allocate risk and influence enforceability.

matches.theme_name: To what extent does legal indeterminacy and doctrinal vagueness increase transaction costs and reduce cross-border capital flows?
matches.specific_contribution: The article reports that the applicable-law and bankruptcy rules for collateral are murky, variable, and doctrinally arcane across jurisdictions, creating interface problems that require ongoing legal work and harmonization efforts by ISDA.
matches.generalized_contribution: Cross-border legal indeterminacy around secured transactions generates coordination and compliance burdens that private actors seek to manage through standardization and lobbying.

matches.theme_name: Can contractual drafting (currency clauses, pari passu, waiver language, amendment thresholds) be designed to reliably reduce cross-border enforcement uncertainty and interjurisdictional conflict?
matches.specific_contribution: In derivatives markets, standardized ISDA documentation and collateral clauses provide a private infrastructure that mitigates some cross-border enforceability and insolvency conflicts, but their effectiveness is partial and depends on supportive national laws and public-law harmonization (e.g., EU directives, proposed treaties).
matches.generalized_contribution: Contractual architecture and standardization can reduce, but not eliminate, cross-border enforceability uncertainty and often require complementary public-law changes to be reliable.

matches.theme_name: How do inconsistent conflict-of-laws rules and varying domestic adjudicative practices affect cross-border payment disputes, the localization of bank deposits, and asset-recovery strategies?
matches.specific_contribution: Drawing on ethnographic observation of collateral practices in OTC derivatives, the article shows that murky, variable choice-of-law and bankruptcy rules across jurisdictions create practical “touchdown points” for cross-border collateral enforcement, prompting ISDA to secure harmonizing measures (such as an EU Directive, UNIDROIT work, and treaties to entrench party choice of law) to manage this uncertainty.
matches.generalized_contribution: Divergent conflict-of-laws and insolvency regimes impede cross-border collateral enforcement, leading private market institutions to pursue harmonized rules and robust recognition of party choice of law to coordinate outcomes.

matches.theme_name: Would greater doctrinal clarity (narrowed exceptions, precise rules) improve predictability enough to sustain cross-border lending and reduce costly strategic behavior?
matches.specific_contribution: The article notes that conflicts-of-law and collateral doctrines for OTC derivatives are murky and variable across jurisdictions and describes ISDA’s efforts to secure harmonized rules and treaties (such as the EU Financial Collateral Directive and UNIDROIT work) to make enforceability more predictable.
matches.generalized_contribution: In cross-border contracting, doctrinal uncertainty prompts industry actors to pursue clearer, harmonized rules to enhance predictability and reduce enforcement risk.

matches.theme_name: Do standardized contract forms and drafting defaults systematically shape non-price deal terms and bargaining outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: Drawing on participant observation in swap markets, the paper shows that ISDA’s standardized Master Agreement and collateral documentation routinize legal work, structure key non-price rights and remedies, and, through their ubiquity, influence how courts and policymakers treat these terms.
matches.generalized_contribution: Standardized contract forms and industry templates shape non-price deal terms and enforcement by organizing practice and leveraging widespread adoption to affect legal treatment.

matches.theme_name: How do norms, professional networks, and market practice diffuse contractual innovations (like new clause language) across jurisdictions and market segments?
matches.specific_contribution: The article describes how ISDA, a global association of derivatives dealers, produces standardized master agreements that are widely used across jurisdictions and are propagated through coordinated industry engagement and legal harmonization initiatives.
matches.generalized_contribution: Industry networks and standard-setting bodies diffuse contractual forms internationally by creating templates and coordinating with regulators and lawmakers.

matches.theme_name: Do legal-opinion practices and interpretive uncertainty among advisors increase transaction costs and systematically shape how contracts are drafted and priced?
matches.specific_contribution: Based on participant observation of swap-collateral documentation, the article shows that murky and variable national collateral rules and enforcement uncertainties lead documentation staff and ISDA lawyers to tailor boilerplate, consult local counsel, and lobby for harmonization, thereby shaping standardized drafting practices.
matches.generalized_contribution: Interpretive uncertainty across jurisdictions prompts sophisticated parties and their advisors to standardize and tailor contracts, seek local legal advice, and pursue harmonization efforts that shape drafting.

matches.theme_name: Can clearer, mandatory contractual defaults (e.g., standard voting rules, enforcement waivers) improve predictability without producing adverse distributional or moral-hazard effects?
matches.specific_contribution: The article details ISDA’s pursuit of supranational measures—such as the EU Financial Collateral Directive, collaboration with UNIDROIT, and a proposed treaty mandating party choice of law—to standardize collateral rules and enhance cross-border enforceability.
matches.generalized_contribution: Adopting harmonized, mandatory or uniform collateral rules through supranational instruments is used to increase predictability and enforceability in cross-border financial contracts.

matches.theme_name: When and to what extent should courts reinterpret or override standardized contract language to achieve equitable outcomes without sacrificing contractual certainty?
matches.specific_contribution: Interviews suggest that the widespread, material use of the ISDA Master Agreement shifted early clashes with national bankruptcy regimes from policy disputes to technical questions of contract enforceability, shaping judicial treatment of standardized terms.
matches.generalized_contribution: The ubiquity of standardized boilerplate can reframe judicial inquiry toward enforceability and away from substantive policy conflicts, influencing whether courts reinterpret or defer to standard terms.

matches.theme_name: What are the trade-offs between standardized boilerplate and bespoke drafting for transaction costs, liquidity, and fairness?
matches.specific_contribution: Based on ethnographic observation of ISDA collateral and Master Agreement practices, standardized boilerplate structures most swap relationships while allowing limited bespoke adjustments via schedules, and its ubiquity channels disputes into questions of contract enforceability.
matches.generalized_contribution: Widespread reliance on standardized contracts with narrow customization channels can shape how disputes are framed and resolved by focusing attention on the enforceability of boilerplate terms.

matches.theme_name: How does legal and drafting complexity affect transaction costs, negotiability, and the likelihood of litigation or deal failure?
matches.specific_contribution: The article describes routinized, compartmentalized documentation work, frequent reconciliation of confirmation discrepancies, and engagement with murky, variable national rules, indicating substantial ongoing transaction work inherent in drafting and implementing these deals.
matches.generalized_contribution: Complex, standardized-yet-detailed contracting practices require continuous reconciliation and legal interface work that materially affects execution and dispute handling.

matches.theme_name: Does diffusion of standardized contract clauses across jurisdictions reduce transaction costs and improve predictability for investors?
matches.specific_contribution: Drawing on participant observation of ISDA-based collateral and documentation in the OTC derivatives market, the article shows that globally diffused standardized master agreements and confirmations routinize documentation, reduce negotiation frictions, and, through their material ubiquity, stabilize expectations by channeling disputes into technical questions of enforceability and prompting legal harmonization.
matches.generalized_contribution: The global diffusion of standardized contract forms reduces documentation and negotiation costs and improves legal predictability by stabilizing expectations, framing disputes as technical enforceability issues, and encouraging cross-jurisdictional harmonization.

matches.theme_name: How do secondary markets and market-level standardization affect the diffusion of contract terms, the formation of expectations, and the potential for contagion across financial contracts?
matches.specific_contribution: Drawing on ethnographic observation of ISDA’s standardized Master Agreement and collateral documentation in the swaps market, the article shows that the widespread, material ubiquity of these boilerplate contracts entrenches their terms, coordinates participants’ expectations, and channels judges and policymakers to treat disputes as technical questions of enforceability across jurisdictions.
matches.generalized_contribution: Widespread adoption of standardized financial contracts anchors shared expectations and steers legal decision-making toward enforcing boilerplate terms, reinforcing the diffusion and authority of those terms across markets.

matches.theme_name: Does the availability and legal treatment of cross-border asset attachment and situs rules determine creditor recovery probabilities and thus influence lending terms?
matches.specific_contribution: Drawing on observations of collateralized OTC derivatives, the article shows that enforceability of security interests and the applicable law for collateral transactions vary across jurisdictions, prompting ISDA to navigate and lobby to harmonize national regimes because these differences affect whether creditors can realize on collateral without court involvement.
matches.generalized_contribution: Cross-jurisdictional variation in legal treatment and choice-of-law for secured transactions shapes creditors’ ability to realize value from collateral and spurs harmonization efforts.

papers.node_id: 64nyulrev733!!ARTICLE: EURODOLLARS, MULTINATIONAL BANKS, AND NATIONAL LAWS.
papers.title: ARTICLE: EURODOLLARS, MULTINATIONAL BANKS, AND NATIONAL LAWS.
papers.authors: PETER S. SMEDRESMAN * and ANDREAS F. LOWENFELD
papers.abstract:
In the good old days -- if there were any -- people put their money in the bank in a given place, and expected to be able to withdraw it in the same place, generally in the currency that was legal tender at that place.  In New York and Chicago banks dealt in dollars, in London banks dealt in pounds sterling, in Paris they dealt in francs, and so on.  Correspondingly, banks lent money, some said created money, in the same currency as that in which they accepted deposits.  There were of course international loans, and governments from time to time interfered with these transactions, sometimes for political, sometimes for economic reasons.Devaluations, freezing of assets, expropriations, and debt moratoriums took place in the pause between the two great wars, and even then the law, designed for a simpler era, failed to keep up.  Three more recent phenomena, each part cause, part effect of the other two, have come together in a way not foreseen by national lawmakers and only dimly andinconsistently understood by courts and commentators.
First,a new medium of exchange and storehouse of value, the Eurodollar, has grown up.  The Eurodollar has some links to the currency issued by the United States Treasury: at any given time U.S. $ 1 = Eur. $ 1.  But the Eurodollar is in many ways independent of the regulatory regime that embraces the national dollar -- reserve requirements, interest ceilings, deposit insurance, and indeed macro-economic policies turning on the supply of national money and credit.Second,the major banks have all become multinational, even when, as in the United States, they have been restrained from expanding within their own country.Third,the revolution in computers and telecommunications has not only made the search for the situs of intangibles more unreal than ever,but in the drive for speed in a high-volume, low-margin market, documentation for deposits (particularly in the "wholesale" market) has all but vanished.  When things go wrong and lawyers and judges are called upon to distribute the losses, the results are bound to be unsatisfying, and explanations about expectations of the participants or intent of the parties are bound to fall flat.
As we shall see, the problem appears in many shapes.  Basically, however, the question turns on the risks and expectations of the two parties to a bank deposit made at a foreign branch of a multinational bank -- the deposit taker, nearly always a bank, and the depositor, which may also be a bank, or may be a corporation or an individual.  Both the home country of a bank (notably the United States) and the host country of the branch may impose restrictions on use or withdrawal of the funds deposited.  Can the depositor reasonably expect the law of the branch to apply if it favors him, and still look to the home office if the law there applicable favors him?  Conversely, can the bank limit its exposure, so that if it follows the law applicable where the deposit is made it will be protected against double liability, and so that it is excused from application of conflicting law of the home country with respect to deposits made at foreign branches? Can the parties determine and allocate the risks by contract and rely on the effectiveness of such contracts?  Looking at the problem from a third side, to what extent are governments limited in the controls they can effectively impose on transnational banking transactions?
We do not claim to have found the Rosetta stone or the unified field theory that can bring together all the claims of depositors against banks at their head office because something went awry at the place where the deposit was made, or claims against branches when something wentwrong at the place of the bank's headquarters.  We are not satisfied, however, with the only rule that emerges from the recent American and English judicial decisions, a surprising number of them, that plaintiffs -- i.e., the depositors -- nearly always win.  We want to see whether the experience of a bank lawyer interested in international law and an international lawyer interested in banking might together develop some suggestions, distinctions, guidelines, or presumptions concerning the relations between multinational banks and their depositors.  We do not here address problems of bank secrecy and disclosure on the one hand,or common efforts to regulate banking practice, including adequate capital bases, on the other.These problems are clearly related to the causes mentioned above, and in some sense also to the task we have set for ourselves.  But one challenge is enough, at least at one time.  We note that all of the cases we discuss were decided in the 1980s.
Section I of this Article provides some basic background on the law of banking, the Euromarket, and the multinational operations of modern banks.  In Section II, we examine recent consideration by European courts of the validity of economic sanctions imposed by the United States and designed to restrain Eurodollar deposits in foreign branches of United States-based banks.  In Section III, we focus on the reverse question: whether the home office of a multinational bank may be liable for a deposit made at a foreign branch notwithstanding economic controls imposed by the country where the foreign branch is located.  The principal cases in both of these sections concern interbank transactions.  Another series of cases, not as important from an overall economic perspective, but raising some of the same issues as the principal cases, involves the closing of branches and the movement of refugees from Cuba and Vietnam.  Weaddress these cases, as well as two cases involving Mexican monetary controls, in Section IV, before offering some tentative suggestions in Section V.

matches.theme_name: How do inconsistent conflict-of-laws rules and varying domestic adjudicative practices affect cross-border payment disputes, the localization of bank deposits, and asset-recovery strategies?
matches.specific_contribution: Based on 1980s U.S. and English cases over foreign-branch deposits, the article observes that courts inconsistently apply home- and host-country laws, making the situs and enforceability of deposits uncertain, often with depositors prevailing, and offers tentative guidelines to allocate these risks.
matches.generalized_contribution: Divergent conflicts rules and adjudicative practices in cross-border banking produce unpredictable deposit localization and claim outcomes, frequently favoring depositors, and call for clearer risk-allocation norms.

matches.theme_name: How do cross-border regulatory measures (sanctions, capital controls, deposit freezes) alter contractual rights, remedies, and the incentives of creditors and debtors?
matches.specific_contribution: Surveying European court reactions to U.S. sanctions on Eurodollar deposits and cases involving host-country monetary controls (including Mexico), the article shows that such measures alter banks’ and depositors’ contractual rights and remedies—sometimes imposing head-office liability despite local restrictions—and tests the effectiveness of contractual risk allocation.
matches.generalized_contribution: Cross-border sanctions and capital controls reallocate private contractual entitlements and can override bargained-for remedies in transnational banking relationships.

matches.theme_name: How do enforcement realities (asset location, capital controls, extraterritorial remedies) interact with contractual clauses to determine practical recoveries from sovereign or cross-border defendants?
matches.specific_contribution: The article highlights that asset location uncertainties, host-state controls, and sparse documentation in the Eurodollar wholesale market can defeat contractual risk-allocation in foreign-branch deposits, shaping practical recoveries and exposing banks to potential double liability.
matches.generalized_contribution: Enforcement constraints and public controls can outweigh contract clauses in cross-border banking, determining creditor recoveries more than formal terms do.

matches.theme_name: How do cross-border legal conflicts-choice-of-law, extraterritorial reach, and conflicting forum judgments-shape enforceability and predictability in international financial contracts?
matches.specific_contribution: Through case studies of Eurodollar and foreign-branch deposit disputes, the article shows that conflicting choice-of-law rules and extraterritorial controls undermine predictability and shape enforceability in international banking contracts, and it offers tentative guidelines to improve clarity.
matches.generalized_contribution: Multi-jurisdictional conflicts of law and extraterritorial measures reduce predictability and drive enforceability outcomes in international financial contracting.

matches.theme_name: Does the extraterritorial reach of national regulatory regimes create irresolvable conflicts in cross-border financial enforcement?
matches.specific_contribution: By analyzing European courts’ consideration of U.S. sanctions aimed at foreign-branch Eurodollar deposits and clashes between head-office liability and host-country controls, the article demonstrates how extraterritorial assertions create direct conflicts that risk double liability and strain cross-border enforcement.
matches.generalized_contribution: Extraterritorial reach of national financial controls generates enforcement conflicts across jurisdictions, including exposure to double obligations and limits on unilateral regulatory effectiveness.

matches.theme_name: Does the extraterritorial reach of national legal regimes and conflicting jurisdictional claims produce distortive conflicts-of-law that affect capital flows and contract design?
matches.specific_contribution: Noting the rise of minimally documented Eurodollar deposits and competing home- and host-state claims, the article cautions that such jurisdictional conflicts constrain effective contractual risk design in transnational banking.
matches.generalized_contribution: Conflicting jurisdictional claims and sparse documentation can constrain contract design in cross-border finance.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do legal ambiguities and doctrinal vagueness (e.g., in 'pari passu', 'loan' definitions, or damages measures) cause litigation, market uncertainty, and suboptimal contracting outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The article describes how outdated legal doctrines, inconsistent judicial treatment, and sparse documentation in the Eurodollar wholesale market create uncertain risk allocation between home offices and foreign branches, leading to numerous depositor–bank disputes in the 1980s cases it reviews.
matches.generalized_contribution: Indeterminate cross-border banking law and weak contractual documentation generate inconsistent case outcomes, heightened litigation risk, and uncertainty over parties’ obligations.

matches.theme_name: Can contractual drafting (currency clauses, pari passu, waiver language, amendment thresholds) be designed to reliably reduce cross-border enforcement uncertainty and interjurisdictional conflict?
matches.specific_contribution: Drawing on 1980s disputes over foreign-branch deposits and conflicting home- and host-country controls, the article offers tentative guidelines and presumptions for how banks and depositors can allocate and limit cross-border enforcement risk by contract, including clarifying applicable law and avoiding double liability.
matches.generalized_contribution: Contractual allocation of risk—through clear choice-of-law and liability delimitations—can be structured to mitigate interjurisdictional enforcement conflicts in cross-border financial deposits.

matches.theme_name: Does the availability and legal treatment of cross-border asset attachment and situs rules determine creditor recovery probabilities and thus influence lending terms?
matches.specific_contribution: The article examines, through cases on Eurodollar deposits at foreign branches, how uncertainty over the situs of deposits and the interplay of home- and host-country controls determines whether depositors can reach a bank’s home office or are constrained by foreign-branch restrictions.
matches.generalized_contribution: Creditor recovery in cross-border bank-deposit disputes hinges on situs characterizations and the effectiveness of conflicting national controls across jurisdictions.

matches.theme_name: Is the expanding exercise of domestic prescriptive or extraterritorial jurisdiction over foreign sovereign acts legitimate and effective in governing cross-border economic obligations?
matches.specific_contribution: Reviewing European courts’ consideration of U.S. economic sanctions targeting Eurodollar deposits in foreign branches, alongside cases on home-office liability despite host-country controls, the article distills the practical limits and conflicts in states’ attempts to project domestic controls extraterritorially over cross-border banking.
matches.generalized_contribution: Judicial treatment of extraterritorial economic controls in cross-border banking reveals inherent limits and conflict when domestic law seeks to govern foreign-branch transactions.

matches.theme_name: Would greater doctrinal clarity (narrowed exceptions, precise rules) improve predictability enough to sustain cross-border lending and reduce costly strategic behavior?
matches.specific_contribution: Synthesizing inconsistent 1980s cases on cross-border bank deposits, the article proposes tentative guidelines and presumptions to allocate risk between multinational banks and depositors and to clarify which law governs when home- and host-country controls conflict.
matches.generalized_contribution: Clear conflict-of-laws presumptions and contractual risk-allocation rules can improve predictability in cross-border banking relationships and reduce disputes arising from inconsistent judicial approaches.

matches.theme_name: What is the role of governing-law clauses and the extraterritorial reach of major legal systems (e.g., US law) in constraining sovereign policy space?
matches.specific_contribution: The article examines European courts’ consideration of U.S. economic sanctions aimed at restraining Eurodollar deposits in foreign branches of U.S. banks, and explores when a bank’s home office may remain liable despite host-country controls, highlighting judicial limits on the reach of national laws in cross-border banking.
matches.generalized_contribution: Foreign judicial scrutiny shapes and constrains the effective extraterritorial reach of national economic controls over international banking transactions, thereby affecting states’ policy space.

matches.theme_name: Do exculpatory and limitation-of-liability clauses, together with sovereign-immunity doctrines, unduly restrict private claimants' remedies and distort bargaining in high-stakes international transactions?
matches.specific_contribution: The article examines cases and offers tentative guidelines on when multinational banks can, through contractual risk allocation and by complying with the law of the deposit’s foreign branch, limit exposure and avoid double liability amid conflicting home- and host-country controls.
matches.generalized_contribution: Contractual risk-allocation terms and adherence to applicable branch law can, under certain conditions, effectively limit intermediaries’ liability when overlapping national controls conflict.

matches.theme_name: How does mismatch between legal form and economic substance (label vs function) affect enforcement, creditor remedies, and regulatory treatment?
matches.specific_contribution: The article highlights that Eurodollar deposits are denominated like U.S. dollars yet operate outside the U.S. regulatory regime, and—together with multinational branch structures and placeless intangibles—this mismatch helps produce conflict-of-law uncertainty and uneven enforcement of depositor claims.
matches.generalized_contribution: Divergence between monetary labels and regulatory substance generates conflict-of-law uncertainty that complicates creditor remedies and liability allocation.

matches.theme_name: To what degree does forum-shopping and strategic exploitation of legal uncertainty alter creditor litigation strategies and restructuring outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The article highlights that depositors in cross-border bank deposit disputes may try to invoke whichever governing law (branch or home-office) favors them, and notes that recent U.S. and English decisions have tended to let depositors prevail.
matches.generalized_contribution: Opportunities to select favorable governing law or forum in cross-border banking disputes can shape creditor success and litigation outcomes.

matches.theme_name: Does enforceability of exculpatory or limitation-of-liability clauses in consumer, broker, and financial contracts protect market activity or undermine accountability and market integrity?
matches.specific_contribution: Surveying 1980s cases on Eurodollar deposits at foreign branches, the article observes that depositors almost always win, indicating that contractual risk-allocation devices and bank efforts to limit exposure are often ineffective when conflicting governmental controls are at issue.
matches.generalized_contribution: In cross-border banking disputes involving regulatory conflicts, courts’ tendency to favor depositors limits the effectiveness of contractual limitations on bank liability.

matches.theme_name: Can contract clauses be designed to allocate macro- or systemic-shock risk (pandemics, exchange controls, MAE/MAC events) effectively without creating excessive moral hazard or perverse incentives?
matches.specific_contribution: Examining 1980s cases on Eurodollar deposits at foreign branches amid conflicting sovereign controls and minimal documentation, the article offers tentative guidelines and presumptions for contractually allocating depositor–bank risks in a setting where courts frequently favor depositors.
matches.generalized_contribution: Contractual guidelines and presumptions can allocate cross-border deposit risks under exchange controls and sanctions, but sparse documentation and judicial tendencies to favor depositors limit the reliability of such clauses.

matches.theme_name: Do contractual devices (insurance, covenants, staged payments, MAC/force-majeure language) adequately allocate risk for large, systemic shocks, or is public intervention required?
matches.specific_contribution: Through disputes over Eurodollar deposits affected by U.S. sanctions and foreign monetary controls, the article shows that state-imposed measures often collide with private risk allocations, with courts frequently siding with depositors.
matches.generalized_contribution: In systemic-shock settings such as exchange controls and sanctions, government measures can unsettle or override private contractual risk allocation, limiting the adequacy of ex ante clauses absent public-law coordination.

matches.theme_name: When and on what grounds should domestic courts review or abstain from adjudicating claims arising from foreign sovereign acts (act-of-state and comity doctrines)?
matches.specific_contribution: By surveying European and American cases on Eurodollar deposits, the article shows that courts often rule for depositors despite foreign economic controls, illuminating limits on judicial deference to foreign sovereign acts in cross-border banking disputes.
matches.generalized_contribution: In cross-border banking cases, domestic courts often prioritize depositor claims over conflicting foreign sovereign controls, indicating constrained judicial deference to foreign public acts in this context.

matches.theme_name: How do legal and institutional shocks (financial crises, regime change, pandemics) drive changes in contractual practice and market pricing?
matches.specific_contribution: The article notes that the computer and telecommunications revolution and the drive for speed in wholesale markets have led to the near disappearance of deposit documentation, heightening legal uncertainty when disputes arise.
matches.generalized_contribution: Institutional and technological shifts can erode contractual documentation practices, increasing legal uncertainty and exposing contract design gaps during periods of stress.

matches.theme_name: How does judicial interpretive flexibility (vague standards vs precise rules) affect predictability and market behavior in high-stakes transactional and sovereign debt litigation?
matches.specific_contribution: Reviewing 1980s cases on Eurodollar deposits at foreign branches, the article observes that courts’ inconsistent and expectation-focused reasoning yields unsatisfying, depositor-favoring outcomes and offers tentative guidelines and presumptions to clarify applicable law and allocate risk.
matches.generalized_contribution: In cross-border banking disputes, vague and inconsistent judicial approaches undermine predictability and skew outcomes, warranting clearer presumptions and contractual risk-allocation rules to guide market actors.

matches.theme_name: How does crisis-time, time-pressured contract drafting affect the prevalence of unintended or overbroad clauses that bind parties in subsequent disputes?
matches.specific_contribution: The article notes that in the Euromarket’s high-volume, low-margin environment, documentation for wholesale deposits has largely disappeared, which later hampers clear loss allocation and yields unsatisfying judicial outcomes when disputes arise.
matches.generalized_contribution: Accelerated, lightly documented financial contracting increases the risk of indeterminate obligations that complicate later dispute resolution.

matches.theme_name: How does legal and drafting complexity affect transaction costs, negotiability, and the likelihood of litigation or deal failure?
matches.specific_contribution: In the Eurodollar wholesale market, the near absence of deposit documentation and the complexity of multi-jurisdictional legal regimes lead courts to deliver unsatisfying and hard-to-predict loss allocations, with party-intent arguments often proving ineffective.
matches.generalized_contribution: Sparse documentation and cross-border legal conflicts increase ambiguity and lead to unpredictable, often unsatisfactory judicial outcomes and elevated dispute risk.

matches.theme_name: Do exculpatory and limitation-of-liability clauses meaningfully shift litigation risk and welfare among contracting parties and third parties?
matches.specific_contribution: Surveying 1980s U.S. and English cases on deposits at foreign branches, the article observes that depositors nearly always prevail, indicating banks cannot reliably limit exposure or shift risk through compliance with local controls or contractual risk allocation.
matches.generalized_contribution: Courts often decline to enforce contractual or legal mechanisms that would meaningfully shift deposit-loss risk from financial institutions to customers in cross-border deposit disputes.

papers.node_id: 82templrev1!!ARTICLE: DISPUTING BOILERPLATE
papers.title: ARTICLE: DISPUTING BOILERPLATE
papers.abstract:
Sovereign bond contracts are thought to consist mostly of boilerplate. That is, except for a handful of custom terms, the contracts are assumed to adopt highly standardized provisions that are functionally identical to those used in other bond contracts.The assumption of standardization extends to enforcement-related terms, including terms in which the issuer consents to be sued in the event of a default. Thus, the "standard" choice of forum term is presumed to call for litigation in foreign courts, typically in New York (for New York-law bonds) or England (for English-law bonds).
To describe sovereign bond contracts as "standardized," or "boilerplate," is to invoke significant theoretical baggage. For a variety of reasons, standardized terms may be "sticky."Parties who adopt a standard term may obtain benefits, while those who depart from the standard may incur costs, and these benefits and costs may induce even sophisticated parties to select a standard term over a custom term that matches their unique preferences. Thus, the presumed choice of forum standard may not evidence a preference for litigation over arbitration among participants in the sovereign debt markets. This is because the litigation term is thought to be a sticky default.
The assumptions underlying this "stickiness" explanation, however, are largely untested. Do sovereign bonds really contain standardized dispute resolution terms, and do these terms indeed eschew arbitration for litigation? If so, why attribute these contracting practices to the stickiness of forum selection terms rather than, say, a widely held preference for litigation? This Article explores these questions. In the process, it provides the first systematic empirical look at the manner in which sovereign bond contracts structure the process of enforcing sovereign debt obligations. This analysis reveals a richer and more nuanced picture of how some of the world's most sophisticated contracting parties structure the dispute resolution process, and of the likely impact of standardization on their choices.
Part I begins with an introduction to this unique contracting context, one in which the threat of legal enforcement plays a relatively minor role. Part I also introduces the presumptive standard set of choice of forum and other enforcement-related terms. That standard eschews arbitration in favor of litigation before creditor-friendly courts in New York or England. Part I closesby exploring a common explanation for the widespread use of this presumed standard. This explanation posits that bond contracts choose litigation not because market participants prefer it to arbitration, but because forum selection clauses are sticky.
The foregoing discussion suggests the ambiguity inherent in highly standardized contracts. Do parties simply prefer the standard, or does standardization deter contract innovation and change? Answering these questions requires some prior belief as to the parties' likely preferences, as well as an analysis of the contracts themselves. Part II engages these questions, beginning with an assessment of the merits of arbitration as a means of resolving sovereign debt disputes. I do not purport to offer a definitive resolution. I suggest, however, that few participants in the sovereign debt markets presently have strong reasons to prefer arbitration. That conclusion implies that arbitration clauses may appear infrequently in sovereign bond contracts for reasons having little or nothing to do with contract stickiness.
Part II next reports findings from an analysis of sovereign bond contracts, including at least one issuance from virtually every major (and most minor) issuers of New York-or English-law bonds over the last twenty years. As it turns out, enforcement-related terms vary to a surprising degree across the different issuers in my sample. With respect to choice of forum terms, more than twenty percent of the issuers depart in some way from the presumptive standard, including nearly ten percent whose bonds include arbitration clauses. Different issuers also vary in the degree to which they waive sovereign immunity from suit, from execution, or both. This variance across issuers, however, coexists with intra-issuer contracting stasis. The issuers in my sample may choose nonstandard enforcement terms, but they rarely change their own established contracting practices.
Part III explores the implications of these findings. Contrary to the stickiness explanation, actual contracting practices suggest that market participants generally prefer litigation to arbitration in this context. Most issuers provide for litigation but include broad sovereign immunity waivers in their bond contracts. This practice captures some of the advantages claimed for arbitration, without incurring the potential costs and uncertainty associated with a relatively untested, and unsubsidized, disputing forum. Moreover, when there are unique reasons to prefer arbitration - as when the issuer's courts are unlikely to enforce foreign court judgments - many (though not all) issuers provide for it. And although issuers rarely change their existing dispute resolution terms, they presently have little reason to do so.
Part III closes by briefly situating these findings within the broader body of research into sovereign debt and, more generally, contract innovation and change. At a basic level, the findings serve as a reminder that actual contracting practices are often more diverse than expected. This is especially true across the different issuers in the sample, suggesting that robust models of sovereign debt contracting practices must take into account a more heterogeneous set of terms than has previously been thought to exist. The findings also implicate a larger debate over when and where contract change is likely to occur. Much contractsscholarship focuses on innovation by larger and "high-status" players - those whose economic strength and reputational capital make them ideal "first movers." But the variance in enforcement-related terms tells a different story. In particular, the use of arbitration by relatively minor players in the sovereign debt world calls for greater attention to the forces that drive innovation among less-established and lower-status players.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do choice-of-law and forum-selection clauses determine the enforceability of claims against sovereigns?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a comprehensive sample of New York- and English-law sovereign bonds over two decades, the article shows that most issuers route disputes to New York or English courts and pair this with broad sovereign-immunity waivers, while a notable minority employ arbitration when their domestic courts are unlikely to recognize foreign judgments—evidence that forum and waiver clauses meaningfully shape enforcement options against sovereigns.
matches.generalized_contribution: Forum-selection and sovereign-immunity waiver terms materially determine how and where claims against sovereigns can be enforced, with arbitration used chiefly when judgment recognition in courts is doubtful.

matches.theme_name: Do the legal norms and contracting practices centered in major financial hubs (New York, London) produce convergence in sovereign-debt contract terms worldwide, and under what mechanisms?
matches.specific_contribution: Despite a presumptive New York/England litigation standard, the study finds substantial cross-issuer variation—over twenty percent deviate and nearly ten percent adopt arbitration—coexisting with intra-issuer stasis and innovation by lower-status issuers.
matches.generalized_contribution: Dominant New York/London norms do not produce full convergence in sovereign-debt enforcement terms; heterogeneous practices persist, shaped by issuer characteristics and path dependence.

matches.theme_name: How do enforcement realities (asset location, capital controls, extraterritorial remedies) interact with contractual clauses to determine practical recoveries from sovereign or cross-border defendants?
matches.specific_contribution: The paper links clause selection to enforcement realities: issuers typically choose litigation plus broad immunity waivers to capture some benefits attributed to arbitration without its uncertainty, and turn to arbitration when their courts are unlikely to enforce foreign judgments.
matches.generalized_contribution: Contracting parties tailor dispute-resolution clauses to enforcement constraints, using immunity waivers and forum choice to enhance judgment enforceability and resorting to arbitration when judgment recognition is uncertain.

matches.theme_name: Can contractual drafting (currency clauses, pari passu, waiver language, amendment thresholds) be designed to reliably reduce cross-border enforcement uncertainty and interjurisdictional conflict?
matches.specific_contribution: Most issuers draft for litigation and include broad sovereign-immunity waivers to secure some of arbitration’s advantages while avoiding the perceived costs and uncertainty of relatively untested arbitral fora, adding arbitration clauses only where specific recognition risks exist.
matches.generalized_contribution: Tailored forum-selection and sovereign-immunity waiver language can reduce cross-border enforcement uncertainty and calibrate dispute resolution to anticipated recognition risks.

matches.theme_name: How do cross-border legal conflicts-choice-of-law, extraterritorial reach, and conflicting forum judgments-shape enforceability and predictability in international financial contracts?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a broad sample of New York- and English-law sovereign bonds over two decades, the article shows that issuers predominantly channel disputes to creditor-friendly foreign courts and pair this choice with broad sovereign-immunity waivers, resorting to arbitration chiefly when foreign court judgments are unlikely to be enforced.
matches.generalized_contribution: In cross-border sovereign debt contracting, parties design forum and immunity terms to manage multi-jurisdictional enforceability, favoring reliable foreign courts and turning to arbitration primarily when recognition and enforcement risks are high.

matches.theme_name: Do judicial doctrines-such as act-of-state, sovereign immunity, and abstention/comity-unduly limit creditors' remedies in cross-border disputes and require doctrinal reform to balance politics and predictability?
matches.specific_contribution: The study reports that most issuers pair litigation clauses with broad waivers of sovereign immunity—from suit and, in some cases, execution—thereby capturing some of arbitration’s advantages without abandoning courts.
matches.generalized_contribution: Broad contractual waivers of sovereign immunity commonly mitigate doctrinal limits on creditor remedies in transnational debt disputes.

matches.theme_name: Do exculpatory and limitation-of-liability clauses, together with sovereign-immunity doctrines, unduly restrict private claimants' remedies and distort bargaining in high-stakes international transactions?
matches.specific_contribution: Across a wide sample of sovereign bonds, issuers frequently include broad waivers of sovereign immunity alongside litigation clauses, lessening jurisdictional barriers to recovery rather than expanding them.
matches.generalized_contribution: Routine inclusion of sovereign-immunity waivers in sovereign debt contracts tends to limit barriers to private claimants’ remedies rather than exacerbate them.

matches.theme_name: Do dispute-resolution architectures that shift authority to international fora create unintended incentive distortions or enforcement gaps?
matches.specific_contribution: The article finds that market participants generally avoid arbitration—viewed as relatively untested and unsubsidized—in favor of litigation in New York or England, using arbitration mainly when foreign judgments may not be enforced.
matches.generalized_contribution: Sovereign debt contracts typically rely on national courts and employ arbitration only as a contingency when recognition and enforcement risks make litigation impractical.

matches.theme_name: How do bargaining power asymmetries and repeat-player advantages shape non-price contract terms and the distribution of surplus in sovereign and major corporate transactions?
matches.specific_contribution: The article finds that relatively minor sovereign issuers disproportionately adopt arbitration clauses and other nonstandard enforcement terms, indicating that innovation in these non-price provisions is occurring among less-established and lower-status players rather than expected high-status first movers.
matches.generalized_contribution: Innovation in non-price sovereign bond terms can originate with lower-status or less-established parties, not solely with high-status repeat players.

matches.theme_name: To what degree do soft-law norms, reputation, and market practice substitute for enforceable legal remedies in cross-border finance?
matches.specific_contribution: The article situates sovereign debt contracting in a setting where the threat of legal enforcement plays a relatively minor role.
matches.generalized_contribution: Formal legal enforcement plays a relatively minor role in sovereign debt finance.

matches.theme_name: Does the extraterritorial reach of national legal regimes and conflicting jurisdictional claims produce distortive conflicts-of-law that affect capital flows and contract design?
matches.specific_contribution: It reports that when an issuer’s courts are unlikely to enforce foreign court judgments, many issuers opt for arbitration rather than litigation.
matches.generalized_contribution: Limits on cross-border judgment recognition lead parties to choose arbitration over foreign-court litigation in sovereign bond contracts.

matches.theme_name: Why do standardized contractual clauses ('boilerplate') persist despite inefficiencies, and what institutional or market mechanisms overcome this lock-in?
matches.specific_contribution: Analyzing two decades of New York- and English-law sovereign bonds, the paper finds substantial cross-issuer variation in enforcement terms (including some use of arbitration) alongside pronounced intra-issuer stasis, indicating persistence reflects issuer preferences more than clause stickiness and that innovation often comes from lower-status issuers.
matches.generalized_contribution: Persistence of standardized enforcement clauses in sovereign bonds stems more from issuer-specific preferences and path dependence than universal lock-in, with change often initiated by lower-status market participants.

matches.theme_name: How do inconsistent conflict-of-laws rules and varying domestic adjudicative practices affect cross-border payment disputes, the localization of bank deposits, and asset-recovery strategies?
matches.specific_contribution: Across issuers, dispute-resolution and immunity terms vary—over 20% depart from the litigation-in-New York/England presumption and nearly 10% use arbitration—with arbitration more likely where the issuer’s courts are unlikely to enforce foreign judgments and with differing waivers from suit and execution affecting enforcement strategy.
matches.generalized_contribution: Variation in forum-selection, arbitration usage, and immunity waivers reflects adaptation to cross-border recognition and enforcement environments, with arbitration favored when local courts resist foreign judgments.

matches.theme_name: What is the role of governing-law clauses and the extraterritorial reach of major legal systems (e.g., US law) in constraining sovereign policy space?
matches.specific_contribution: Most issuers of New York- or English-law bonds provide for litigation in creditor-friendly New York or English courts and include broad sovereign-immunity waivers, while some opt for arbitration when court-judgment recognition is doubtful.
matches.generalized_contribution: Governing-law and forum-selection choices that favor New York or England, often paired with immunity waivers, shape sovereigns’ exposure to external legal enforcement, with arbitration used tactically where judgment recognition is uncertain.

matches.theme_name: What practical limits do asset-sheltering, jurisdictional immunity, and political constraints impose on extraterritorial enforcement of claims against states?
matches.specific_contribution: The study documents widespread inclusion of broad waivers of sovereign immunity from suit (and variably from execution) to enhance enforceability, notes that legal enforcement plays a relatively minor role, and observes a shift to arbitration where foreign judgments are unlikely to be enforced.
matches.generalized_contribution: Contractual waivers of jurisdictional and execution immunity and tailored forum choices are used to mitigate practical obstacles to enforcing claims against sovereigns amid generally limited legal enforceability.

matches.theme_name: What can large-scale, contract-by-contract textual and empirical analyses reveal about the gap between drafted language and actual functional allocations of risk?
matches.specific_contribution: A contract-by-contract empirical review shows that many issuers pair litigation with broad sovereign-immunity waivers that capture some advantages of arbitration, indicating that different textual formulations can produce similar functional allocations of enforcement risk.
matches.generalized_contribution: Large-sample textual analyses can show that formally distinct dispute-resolution clauses may functionally allocate enforcement risk in similar ways.

matches.theme_name: Do standardized contract forms and drafting defaults systematically shape non-price deal terms and bargaining outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a comprehensive sample of New York- and English-law sovereign bonds over two decades, the article finds substantial cross-issuer variation in enforcement terms (with over 20% departing from the presumed forum standard and nearly 10% using arbitration) alongside intra-issuer stasis, and concludes that choices largely reflect a preference for litigation rather than sticky boilerplate defaults.
matches.generalized_contribution: Observed diversity across parties and stable issuer-specific practices indicate that standardized defaults do not uniformly dictate non-price terms, as party preferences and context often prevail over boilerplate stickiness.

matches.theme_name: Does the availability and legal treatment of cross-border asset attachment and situs rules determine creditor recovery probabilities and thus influence lending terms?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a 20-year sample of New York- and English-law sovereign bonds, the paper shows that issuers tailor enforcement terms—most choosing litigation with broad waivers of sovereign immunity from suit and execution, and some adopting arbitration when foreign judgments would not be enforced—indicating that cross-border enforceability considerations drive drafting choices.
matches.generalized_contribution: Cross-border enforceability and immunity-from-execution rules materially shape sovereign bond enforcement terms, with parties favoring litigation plus broad immunity waivers except where barriers to enforcing foreign judgments make arbitration preferable.

matches.theme_name: What are the trade-offs between standardized boilerplate and bespoke drafting for transaction costs, liquidity, and fairness?
matches.specific_contribution: From a two-decade sample of New York- and English-law sovereign bonds, the paper finds that while standardized litigation clauses dominate, issuers customize—including by adding arbitration—when specific enforcement risks warrant it, and many pair litigation with broad immunity waivers to capture arbitration’s benefits without its costs and uncertainty.
matches.generalized_contribution: In sovereign debt, standardized litigation terms serve as efficient defaults, but bespoke dispute-resolution clauses emerge when issuer-specific enforcement constraints make customization relatively more valuable than arbitration’s added cost and uncertainty.

matches.theme_name: Can empirical contract-level datasets reveal patterns of clause prevalence and evolution that should inform doctrinal or regulatory reform?
matches.specific_contribution: Analyzing at least one issuance from virtually every major and most minor sovereign issuer over twenty years, the paper documents substantial cross-issuer variation and intra-issuer stasis in enforcement terms, with over 20% departing from the presumed standard and nearly 10% using arbitration.
matches.generalized_contribution: Contract-level datasets can reveal heterogeneity across parties and persistence within parties in dispute-resolution terms, challenging assumptions of boilerplate uniformity.

matches.theme_name: How do market conditions, bargaining power, and counterparty composition drive adoption and specific wording of non-price clauses (MAE/MAC, covenants, break fees) in M&A and lending contracts?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a two-decade sample of New York- and English-law sovereign bonds, the article shows that issuers mostly opt for litigation with broad sovereign-immunity waivers, choose arbitration selectively when foreign-court judgment enforcement is doubtful, and otherwise display issuer-specific but path-dependent drafting of enforcement terms.
matches.generalized_contribution: Adoption and wording of enforcement clauses in sovereign debt are driven by issuer-specific enforcement risks and cost-benefit assessments, yielding cross-issuer heterogeneity and within-issuer path dependence.

matches.theme_name: How do norms, professional networks, and market practice diffuse contractual innovations (like new clause language) across jurisdictions and market segments?
matches.specific_contribution: The study documents substantial cross-issuer variation alongside intra-issuer stasis in enforcement terms and finds that relatively minor issuers are the ones adopting arbitration, indicating that innovation can originate with lower-status players.
matches.generalized_contribution: Contractual innovations in sovereign debt can originate with lower-status market participants and diffuse unevenly, with heterogeneity across issuers and stickiness within issuers.

matches.theme_name: How do secondary markets and market-level standardization affect the diffusion of contract terms, the formation of expectations, and the potential for contagion across financial contracts?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a comprehensive sample of New York- and English-law sovereign bonds over two decades, the article shows substantial cross-issuer variation in enforcement terms (over one-fifth depart from the presumed standard and about one-tenth include arbitration) alongside issuer-level stasis, indicating that widespread litigation clauses reflect party preferences more than boilerplate stickiness and that innovations such as arbitration tend to appear among lower-status issuers.
matches.generalized_contribution: Apparent boilerplate can mask significant cross-firm heterogeneity with within-firm inertia, with standard terms reflecting shared preferences rather than pure path dependence and innovation sometimes originating from lower-status market participants.

papers.node_id: 53vandjtransnatll1637!!ARTICLE: Mozambican Illegal Debts: Testing the Odious Debt Doctrine
papers.title: ARTICLE: Mozambican Illegal Debts: Testing the Odious Debt Doctrine
papers.abstract:
In June 2019, the Constitutional Council of Mozambique declared a financial transaction made in contravention of constitutional norms related to the national budget invalid.The transaction concerned a loan of $ 850 million contracted by Ematum, a Mozambican state-owned fishing company, with Credit Suisse and guaranteed by the Mozambican government.
The judgment of the Mozambican Constitutional Council was just the tip of the iceberg of a complicated financial scheme articulated in three separate transactions to state-owned enterprises arranged by two banks: the Russian VTB Capital PLC and the SwissCredit Suisse.In addition to the Ematum loan, there were two other loans to state-owned enterprises: a $ 622 million loan to ProIndicus to perform coastal surveillance (from Credit Suisse) and a $ 535 million loan to theMozambique Asset Management company (MAM) to build and maintain shipyards (from VTB).All these loans were backed by guarantees from the Mozambican government. Of the three loans, only the one made to Ematum was publicly disclosed and subsequently converted into loan participation notes (LPNs). These LPNs were, in turn, legally extinguished in April 2016 through an exchange for $ 727 million of eurobonds issued by the Mozambican government.
Following the disclosure by the Mozambican government of the existence of these debts, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and bilateral donors suspended their financial support to Mozambique. As a result, the local currency depreciated by about 65 percent within six months and economic growth plummeted to 3.8 percent in 2016 from 6.6 percent the previous year.In this context, the Mozambican government announced its intention to restructure all its external commercial debt.Since then, no payment on this debt has been made, causing the country's credit profile to be downgraded and the cost of financing to rise.
Making matters even more complicated, in 2016 and in 2017 the country's administrative court (Tribunal Administrativo) declared the state guarantees of the Ematum, ProIndicus, and MAM loans illegal for violating the Constitution and budgetary laws.A special commission within Parliament arrived at a similar conclusion, and an independent audit report was subsequently published highlighting numerous irregularities in borrowing and using funds.In December2018, several charges for indictment were brought before the District Court for the Eastern District of New York against multiple individuals, including a former Mozambican minister, for having allegedly conspired to defraud investors through numerous material misrepresentations and omissions.Further, Mozambique brought a lawsuit against Credit Suisse and VTB in the English High Court alleging the invalidity of the secret loans.
The judgment rendered by the Constitutional Council in June 2019 must be seen in this framework. It was based on a claim filed by the Budget Monitoring Forum, the Platform of Civil Society Organizations, and another two thousand citizens to declare the Ematum transaction unconstitutional. This request was based on Article 179(2)(p) of the Mozambican Constitution,under which Parliament has the exclusive competence to authorize the contraction of loans and other financial transactions and fix the upper limits of state guarantees. The Ematum transaction, instead, was arranged by the government and merely approved by the Mozambican Parliament by means of anex postresolution.
The Mozambican Parliament opposed the claim of the applicants, arguing that the resolution was a political act and, thereby, was not justiciable before the Constitutional Council.
