papers.abstract:
INTRODUCTION"Who are these guys that just keep coming?"--Treasury Secretary Henry M. Paulson Jr., speaking of the serial collapse of U.S. financial institutions.
"Who are these guys that just keep coming?"--Treasury Secretary Henry M. Paulson Jr., speaking of the serial collapse of U.S. financial institutions.
Many people now claim that they knew that a financial crisis was coming, but it does not appear that those working for the government were among them. Perhaps they should have been--the government was certainly very close to the problem. Federal Reserve macroeconomic policy, inadequate regulation of the two government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs) the Federal National Mortgage Association (Fannie Mae) and the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation (Freddie Mac) and other regulatory failures with respect to the mortgage-origination industry, financial institution oversight, ratings agencies, and the securitization market all played their part in creating an unprecedented real estate and credit bubble.
But as part of the solution, the government's contribution was much more fitful. When the real estate bubble popped, with catastrophic implications for the financial institutions that facilitated property purchases, the credit market, and, eventually, all of the participants in the worldwide financial system, the federal government reacted slowly, and thenuncertainly, and finally on an emergency and massive basis.
What, exactly, was the government trying to do to respond to the crisis? Observers will differ on the quality and wisdom of its actions for years to come, but we think that its response to the financial crisis was driven by the legal constraints on the government institutions that handled the crisis--and by the creative, and principally transactional, ways that the government managed those legal constraints. As the crisis developed, the government forced the sales of one of the five largest investment banks, the largest thrift in the country, and a number of consumer banks.It permitted an even larger investment bank and another of the country's largest thrifts to fail. The government also took over the country's largest insurer and nationalized the two government-sponsored enterprises that mortally suffered from the popping of the housing bubble.
When these efforts failed to prevent a cascading "run" on financial institutions, the government decided, in the course of less than a month, to create through congressional action an unprecedented $ 700 billion asset purchase program. The government then turned this authorization into a massive investment in the country's largest financial institutions. It capstoned the investment by forcing the nation's nine largest remaining financial institutions to accept $ 125 billion of government equity--a partial nationalization which the United States had never seen before. Nor did the government stop there. It flooded the global markets with liquidity and entered the commercial paper market on a massive scale. And the bailouts would continue with the rescue of Citigroup and Bank of America, two of the nation's largest financial institutions. These actions would mark the largest government economic intervention in history, and left former Treasury Secretary Henry M. Paulson Jr., Federal Reserve Board Chair Ben S. Bernanke, and former President of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and current Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner, the apparent leaders of this government effort, in control of much of the financial economy.
Although the government never, throughout this period, acted as if it felt very constrained by the law that limited its actions, we think that its legal constraints help to explain a great deal of the government response. For example, even though the crisis first evinced itself in the struggles of Bear Stearns, an investment bank overseen by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), it was the Board of Governors of the Federal ReserveSystem (Federal Reserve) that failed that bank and forced its sale, with the Treasury Department participating in the process. The other big financial institution collapses that preceded the government's implementation of the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of 2008 (EESA)were largely coordinated by the Treasury Department and the Federal Reserve--regulators who did not manage these institutions. These government agencies acted because they had the resources and the flexible legal authority to do so, while they concluded that the primary supervisors of the collapsing institutions were at best unnecessary and at worst helpless in the face of the looming crisis.
We think that the government's novel efforts during the financial crisis can be usefully analyzed in two ways. First, the government has been doing deals--the sorts of deals that it usually leaves to the private sector.The dealmaking ethos permeated even the staffing of the government's response--its financial crisis team was comprised largely of investment bankers, led primarily by Secretary Paulson, a veteran dealmaker who served as the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Goldman Sachs Group, Inc.In this Article, we show how these deals were done and how the government stretched, and in some cases appeared to overstretch, its legal authority to make those deals happen. Second, the government, as a matter of administrative law, has been exploring the outer limits of its permissible authority in what it views as a time of crisis and, in so doing, conducted the management of the crisis through the two institutions least constrained by the law--the Treasury Department and the Federal Reserve. We analyze how the government's response both pushed and was shaped by the law at its disposal.
Doing deals and aggressively reinterpreting regulatory authority are not unrelated activities. Dealmakers use contract to avoid some legalconstraints and often prefer to focus on arms-length negotiation, rather than regulatory authorization, as the source of legitimacy for their actions. We think that one useful way to characterize the government's role would be as that of an extraordinarily vigorous dealmaker, with some of the bad, as well as good, implications of governance by deal. For example, the early set of deals concluded by the government's team were done on tough terms for their targets; the government as "buyer" maximized its leverage over distressed institutions. Sometimes the government walked away from the table--as it did with Lehman Brothers--an act that dealmakers often do to bolster their reputation for future deals. And the government often acted in this phase of the crisis as dealmakers do--conclude it, forget it, and move on to the next deal. But when the government's deal-to-deal response appeared to be failing, the Treasury Secretary, at the urging of the Chairman of the Federal Reserve, decided that it needed a more comprehensive and systematic approach to preventing systemic fallout from the collapse of the housing bubble as well as the continuing and speeding collapse of the financial economy.This holistic approach was planned as one kind of deal, where the government would purchase distressed assets from financial institutions, and turned into another kind of deal, where the government purchased sizable stakes in these financial institutions instead of buying their hard-to-price-and-sell troubled assets.
All of this suggests at least a weak sort of process consistency in the government response to the crisis. This is a consistency that many observers have concluded that the government has lacked; and to be sure, we agree with Richard Posner that there were "a series of improvisations" in the government's actions.But perhaps this unusual consistency also offers a coherent explanation of the government's apparently incoherent response to the crisis. Dealmakers of the investment-banker variant, after all, do not much care about the consistency between deals. In the process they decide quickly, negotiate hard, consider transaction and other costs to the best they can, and then call it a day.Moreover, although contract, securities, corporate, and other forms of law play an important role in deals, strict legal compliance has never been the principal focus of the dealmaker. Rather, risks and legal constraints must be weighed against each other in pursuit of the ultimate private goal--a completed deal. That perspective,too, characterized the government's response to the crisis. Time and again, the government structured deals that pushed its legal authority to the very edge and beyond in pursuit of, and bound by, its own political, economic, and, perhaps, sociological interests.
To be sure, that legal authority made a difference with how the government structured its deals. It did so largely through the Federal Reserve, to begin with, because that agency had the resources and regulatory flexibility to serve in that role. But the Federal Reserve's legal authority was stretched as far as possible as these deals evolved. And again, here the government acted as dealmakers do--structuring the latest deal with a view toward precedent from prior transactions but willing to deviate as circumstances dictated. In the first three parts of our Article, we analyze just what the government did when it chose to act by deal.
We then turn in the final part of our Article to an evaluation of the government's approach and its implications for legal scholarship. For example, while administrative law scholars spend much of their time thinking about how the D.C. Circuit and Supreme Court might review government administrative decisions, it is worth noting that the response to the financial crisis has had nothing to do with the courts. Instead, it has been concentrated entirely in the Executive Branch and independent agencies--although aficionados of presidential control will have a difficult time identifying any particularly important presidential role in the construction and implementation of the bailout, which appears to have been conducted by the Treasury Secretary and Chairman of the Federal Reserve with some congressional blessing. Nor can one find much of a role for states in this epic corporate reorganization and insurance crisis, even though state law is the basis of corporate and insurance regulation.
But if courts and states are the missing players in the administrative law paradigm, the new process of regulation by deal exemplifies regulatory trends that are more familiar and increasingly important. In adopting a form of policymaking unlikely to be subject to judicial review (especially before congressional passage of the EESA), the government adopted a new governance model of administration, one exemplified, as many other more-prosaic initiatives are, by public-private partnerships and regulatory action positioned outside of the range of judicial review. Government by deal is not open government, and it rejects some of the usual values of administrative law, such as predecision notice to affected parties and the public; measured, unhasty action; and comment-ventilated policymaking.
Perhaps most interestingly, even as the regulation-by-deal paradigm semi-nationalized some traditional private financial services in the United States, it also contributed to the privatization of government functions, which, during this period, were in many ways "run like a business" ratherthan as a regulator. The government was doing deals and taking stakes in profit-making institutions.In this way, government by deal is not wholly unlike the government reinvention that analysts ranging from Tom Peters to Al Gore have urged on it.
Moreover, this study informs dealmaking theory. The deals the government and its lawyers structured reaffirmed the limitations of dealmaking and deal lawyering. Dealmaking is a path-dependent process--lawyers and transaction participants rely upon network and signaling effects, structuring the current deal on the basis of the old one to advantage themselves with the benefits of prior precedent and to illustrate their capability.But lawyers can overrely on this precedent to forgo innovation, resulting in an agency cost that injects inefficiencies into the dealmaking process. These inefficiencies are reinforced by the transaction costs of lawyering in high-pressure, time-sensitive environments, which can result in drafting mistakes and other errors.In structuring bailouts these principles were ably on display. The quick time frames of the government's deals resulted in both mistakes and unintended consequences. Moreover, even though lawyers and participants were freed from the bounds of prior precedent, they still looked to that precedent to structure deals. But this account also shows the beauty of dealmaking and the circumstances under which innovation can occur. Despite the errors, innovation was a stronger force than normal, showing the potential of lawyers and dealmakers to create more internally efficient structures when they are not constricted by normal agency and signaling costs. We alsoexplore the implications of the deal paradigm the government chose--venture capital instead of private equity--even though it appeared that the sort of fundamental restructuring, and often shrinking, promised by private equity was a better fit for the government, taxpayers, and, perhaps, market stability.
It is worth observing that the government has concluded distressed deals before--indeed, the underused "prompt corrective action" regime is premised on these sorts of distressed deals.And governments have increasingly participated as market actors--sovereign wealth funds are an example--though our government rarely does so. Governments, though again, not the government of the United States, have nationalized firms and industries before. But this regulation by deal is new, and it is new in size, scale, and scope.
Our account is a preliminary one, and it is meant to provide a basis for further explaining what, precisely, the government did as a matter of law, and an evaluation of whether what it did worked. It is too soon to pass a final judgment on the empirical soundness of the government's strategy or to adjudge its use of the law as comprehensively good or bad.What we do here is show precisely how the government's response was constrained by the law as it existed when the crisis hit and how it used the law it had, rather than the one it needed, culminating in the decision to seek further authority from Congress and then quickly reinterpreting that authority to make more deals.
In what follows, we evaluate the government's response to the crisis through a blow-by-blow, or historical, account. The gathering crisis pushed the government to rely on its traditional tools of economic control and financial regulation as it began to spread. Once Bear Stearns failed, those tools were abandoned and bailouts--or deals--became the new norm. We analyze each deal or nondeal in some detail and then dissect the bailout statute itself and the way the government interpreted, and then reinterpreted, it. Finally, we analyze the actions of the all-too-maligned SEC, as well as the other agencies involved in the government's deals. The result is a comprehensive review of the government's actions during the financial crisis. In doing so, we hope to inform and guide the coming legal debate about the validity of the government's actions and any future regulatory reform.

matches.theme_name: How do legal and institutional shocks (financial crises, regime change, pandemics) drive changes in contractual practice and market pricing?
matches.specific_contribution: In response to the 2008 crisis, the U.S. government abandoned routine regulatory tools in favor of transaction-based “regulation by deal” and rapidly sought and reinterpreted statutory authority (including the EESA) to structure novel interventions.
matches.generalized_contribution: Severe institutional shocks can drive actors to shift from standard regulatory approaches to contract-like transactional solutions and aggressive legal reinterpretations.

matches.theme_name: Do contractual devices (insurance, covenants, staged payments, MAC/force-majeure language) adequately allocate risk for large, systemic shocks, or is public intervention required?
matches.specific_contribution: The article shows that private market arrangements and existing regulatory tools proved insufficient during the 2008 crisis, necessitating unprecedented public interventions—liquidity support, capital injections, and deal-driven rescues—to stabilize the financial system.
matches.generalized_contribution: Large systemic shocks can exceed the capacity of ex ante private contracts and require flexible, large-scale public backstops to maintain stability.

matches.theme_name: Do lawyers, deal teams, and legal intermediaries (as repeat players) add measurable economic value through drafting and structuring beyond mere documentation?
matches.specific_contribution: Drawing on the bailout transactions, the article demonstrates that lawyers and deal teams both generated value through innovative structuring under pressure and imposed costs through path dependence, agency frictions, and drafting errors, with the venture-capital-style approach illustrating these tradeoffs.
matches.generalized_contribution: Repeat-player legal and deal intermediaries can add economic value by innovating structures but also risk destroying value via path dependence, agency costs, and mistakes, especially in high-pressure settings.

matches.theme_name: How do agency problems among intermediaries (banks, law firms, underwriters, trustees) distort contract terms and affect post-signing enforcement and renegotiation outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: In the crisis bailouts, the government's deal lawyers and transaction participants relied on precedent and signaling in ways that created agency costs and inefficiencies, and the high-pressure timelines produced drafting mistakes and other errors that affected deal terms.
matches.generalized_contribution: Agency frictions and signaling among transactional intermediaries, especially under time pressure, distort deal structures and invite drafting errors that impose inefficiencies.

matches.theme_name: How do domestic courts, international arbitration, and official institutions (e.g., IMF) interact to determine bargaining leverage and the legality of restructuring plans?
matches.specific_contribution: The crisis response occurred almost entirely within the Treasury and Federal Reserve and was positioned to avoid judicial review, leaving courts and states with virtually no role in determining legality or leverage.
matches.generalized_contribution: Executive-led, court-avoiding crisis interventions displace judicial fora in shaping bargaining leverage and the legal landscape.

matches.theme_name: How do market conditions and relative bargaining power among actors determine debt terms, restructuring allocations, and recovery outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: Early in the crisis the government, acting as a powerful buyer, imposed tough terms on distressed institutions and even walked away from Lehman to bolster future bargaining reputation, before pivoting to large-scale capital injections.
matches.generalized_contribution: In systemic crises, dominant state actors can use superior bargaining power to exact stringent terms or withhold support, thereby determining allocations and outcomes across restructurings.

matches.theme_name: How does crisis-time, time-pressured contract drafting affect the prevalence of unintended or overbroad clauses that bind parties in subsequent disputes?
matches.specific_contribution: Because deals were executed on quick time frames, the government's bailout contracts contained drafting mistakes and produced unintended consequences.
matches.generalized_contribution: Accelerated crisis-time contracting increases the incidence of drafting errors and unanticipated constraints that later shape performance and disputes.

matches.theme_name: Do professional intermediaries (law firms, underwriters, trustees, advisors) introduce agency costs that bias contract design and risk allocation?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article shows that the government's crisis-era deals, structured by its lawyers under extreme time pressure, were path-dependent and signaling-driven, producing agency-cost inefficiencies, drafting mistakes, and unintended consequences even as they enabled unusual innovation.
matches.generalized_contribution: Professional deal intermediaries operating under time pressure and repeat-player dynamics tend to rely on precedent in ways that create agency-cost inefficiencies and drafting errors, though such conditions can also spur innovation.

matches.theme_name: How do bargaining power asymmetries and repeat-player advantages shape non-price contract terms and the distribution of surplus in sovereign and major corporate transactions?
matches.specific_contribution: In its crisis deals, the U.S. government used its dominant bargaining position to impose tough non-price terms—most notably forcing large banks to accept equity stakes—and even walked away from Lehman to bolster future leverage, with precedent dependence and time pressure shaping contract design and outcomes.
matches.generalized_contribution: In high-stakes transactions, powerful repeat players use leverage and reputational strategies to dictate non-price terms (such as equity injections), while precedent dependence and time pressure shape contractual structure and surplus allocation.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do information asymmetries and signaling affect creditor decision-making and pricing in sovereign and complex financial contracting?
matches.specific_contribution: In recounting the bailouts, the article observes that deal lawyers and participants relied on network and signaling effects and prior precedent, which both constrained innovation and, under urgent time pressures, produced drafting mistakes and inefficiencies.
matches.generalized_contribution: In complex, time-pressured transactions, network and signaling effects steer contract structuring toward precedent, often entrenching inefficiencies and occasional errors.

matches.theme_name: Do legal-opinion practices and interpretive uncertainty among advisors increase transaction costs and systematically shape how contracts are drafted and priced?
matches.specific_contribution: In the U.S. financial-crisis bailouts, lawyers and deal participants working under time pressure and legal uncertainty relied on precedent, incurred significant transaction costs, and made drafting mistakes that shaped the structure of government deals.
matches.generalized_contribution: Under high uncertainty and time pressure, legal-advisory practices increase transaction costs, promote path-dependent drafting, and elevate error risk that materially influences contract design.

matches.theme_name: What role do lawyers, underwriters, and other intermediaries play in creating, diffusing, and entrenching contractual innovations and standard clauses?
matches.specific_contribution: Reviewing bailout transactions, the article shows that deal lawyers relied on network and signaling effects and prior precedents to structure agreements—entrenching templates and agency costs—while crisis conditions also enabled notable contractual innovation.
matches.generalized_contribution: Intermediaries use precedent and reputational networks to diffuse and entrench standard terms, but shocks can relax these constraints and spur contractual innovation.

matches.theme_name: Why do standardized contractual clauses ('boilerplate') persist despite inefficiencies, and what institutional or market mechanisms overcome this lock-in?
matches.specific_contribution: In reviewing crisis-era bailouts, the article notes that dealmaking is path-dependent, with lawyers relying on precedent and network/signaling effects that can entrench inefficient structures, though the exigencies of the crisis also enabled atypical innovation.
matches.generalized_contribution: Path dependence and professional signaling can lock in inefficient contractual and deal structures, but acute shocks that relax agency and signaling constraints can catalyze departures from standardized practices.

matches.theme_name: How does legal and drafting complexity affect transaction costs, negotiability, and the likelihood of litigation or deal failure?
matches.specific_contribution: Reviewing fast-paced bailout transactions, the article observes that time-pressured, precedent-driven drafting and lawyering produced agency-cost inefficiencies and drafting mistakes with unintended consequences, even as the loosened constraints sometimes enabled more efficient innovations.
matches.generalized_contribution: Time-pressured, precedent-driven contract drafting increases transaction costs and execution risk through agency-cost inefficiencies and drafting errors, although reduced constraints can also spur more efficient innovation.

matches.theme_name: What are the trade-offs between standardized boilerplate and bespoke drafting for transaction costs, liquidity, and fairness?
matches.specific_contribution: In recounting the crisis bailouts, the article notes that government deal lawyers’ path-dependent reliance on prior precedent and signaling created agency-cost inefficiencies and drafting mistakes under extreme time pressure, while relaxing those constraints allowed innovative, more internally efficient structures to emerge.
matches.generalized_contribution: Precedent-driven, standardized deal practices can introduce agency-cost inefficiencies and error risks in high-pressure transactions, whereas tailored innovation can yield more internally efficient arrangements when not constrained by signaling and path dependence.

matches.theme_name: How do norms, professional networks, and market practice diffuse contractual innovations (like new clause language) across jurisdictions and market segments?
matches.specific_contribution: In the government's crisis-era bailout deals, lawyers and participants relied on networks and precedent to structure successive transactions—creating path dependence, agency-cost resistance to innovation, and some drafting errors—yet the urgency of the crisis also enabled unusually rapid innovation and more efficient structures.
matches.generalized_contribution: Network and signaling effects and reliance on prior deal templates create path dependence that can impede contractual innovation, but shocks that relax agency and signaling constraints can accelerate the diffusion of more efficient structures.

papers.node_id: 70lawcontempprob7!!ARTICLE: RENEGOTIATING THE ODIOUS DEBT DOCTRINE
papers.title: ARTICLE: RENEGOTIATING THE ODIOUS DEBT DOCTRINE
papers.abstract:
Following the United States' invasion and subsequent occupation of Iraq,the U.S. government argued that the successor government in Iraq was not responsible for Iraq's Saddam-era debt under the purported doctrine of odious-regime debt. This purported doctrine apparently excused - by operation of law - all successor regimes from repaying debts that were incurred by oppressive predecessor regimes.Some human-rights groups liked this idea and promoted the purported legal doctrine through websites and publications.Soon, the global media joined in.It had become fashionable to suggest that debtors be released from oppressive prior debts.
Fads pass. When they do, calmer heads may acknowledge the truism that when an entity is a creditor, it rather likes to be repaid. But when it is a debtor, it finds little pleasure in repaying loans and might even claim that its debts are repugnant or odious.Law, and the legal scholars that shape it, should appraisesuch claims of odiousness and determine the appropriate international response.
This article presents a three-part response. The first part of the response, detailed in Part II below, addresses the purported rule that oppressive debts of a predecessor government do not bind its successor. Even assuming that positivism is the correct focal lens, state practice does not support a purported doctrine of odious-regime debts.
Part III demonstrates that the purported doctrine of odious-regime debts inadequately supports the human-rights policies that its proponents identify as its normative basis. The purported doctrine is both overinclusive and underinclusive. It is overinclusive because the purported rule would eviscerate creditors' rights, even in situations where doing so could destabilize global markets, harm millions of people dependent on these markets for their livelihoods, and cause creditors to deny much-needed fresh loans to successor governments. It is underinclusive because the purported rule does not address non-debt commercial obligations that might debilitate the successor government if their repayment terms exceeded the capacity of the successor government's economy to meet them.
Part IV proposes that the problem of succession of debts should be reframed more broadly as a problem of succession to all commercial obligations. A solution to this broader problem is to abandon arid formalism in favor of understanding and adjusting the global decisionmaking process. The international response to claims that a debt is an odious-regime debt is more subtle than a brute doctrinal approach. Creditors, debtors, and other influential international actors exchange claims and counterclaims backed by varying degrees of power and authority. Eventually, outcomes are reached that tend to balance global stability with the human rights of the citizens of the successor entity. Commercial arrangements are generally preserved, but commercial obligations are adjusted on terms that would allow the successor entity's economy to recover from the trauma of succession.
A Doctrinal Appraisal of the Purported Doctrine of Odious-Regime Debts
The issue of how to address claims that postsuccession debts are odious is important because successions occur with some regularity. States are essentially self-governing territories of individuals.Just as humans fail, so too do their efforts to govern. When the ruling elite of a territory fails to properly govern with sufficient frequency or intensity, the governed may, by force or peaceably, replace the ruling elite with new leaders and authority structures.
There have been numerous successions in the twentieth century alone. Some of these have involved changes in the international legal personality of a state or changes in territory, such as the independence of East Timor or the secession of Montenegro from Serbia and Montenegro. Others have involved fundamental changes of government, such as the communist revolutions in China and the Soviet Union and the military coup d'etat in Burma. On occasion, foreign powers may undermine the ruling elite of a state. The most overt example of such meddling occurs through invasions, or, as it is more coyly termed today, "regime change." This was the case with the recent successions in Afghanistan and Iraq.
It would not be beyond the realm of possibility to anticipate foreign-engineered successions in the future - in North Korea, Iran, or other states that may have allegedly gravitated towards an imaginary "axis of evil."Independence movements in provinces such as Aceh in Indonesia, Chechnya in Russia, and Transnistria in Moldova may succeed in these territories. Should more fundamentalist notions of Islam find more followers in secular states with significant Muslim populations, more successions may occur.
In successions, large debts could be subject to claims of odiousness. When the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, it owed $ 67 billion in external debts.When Saddam Hussein was forcibly removed from power in Iraq, his regime had incurred $ 140 billion in external debt.Cuba, which will not be forever governed by Fidel Castro, reportedly owed about $ 40 billion in 2002.Given the frequency of successions and the magnitude of debt that could be at stake, the college of international jurists should propose appropriate international responses to the purported odious debt doctrine.
The idea of odious debts is broad. When the U.S. government and human-rights groups invoked the purported doctrine of odious debts, they were in fact referring only to a narrow species of odious debts that in international legal theory is known as regime debts. In order to determine the meaning of the purported doctrine of regime debts, it is necessary to clarify the meanings of doctrine or legal rules, state and government successions, and odious debts generally as opposed to regime debts specifically.

matches.theme_name: When, if ever, should successor states be relieved of predecessor debts on grounds of odiousness, illegitimacy, or regime change?
matches.specific_contribution: The article finds that state practice does not support a categorical odious‑regime debt doctrine excusing successors from predecessor debts and instead proposes that obligations generally be preserved but adjusted through international bargaining to balance global stability with human rights.
matches.generalized_contribution: Relief from predecessor debts on odiousness grounds is not established as a rule; continuity should be the baseline with negotiated adjustments to reconcile market stability and human rights.

matches.theme_name: How do regime change, state succession, redenomination, or political transitions affect which sovereign obligations remain binding and how courts and markets treat repudiation or odious-debt claims?
matches.specific_contribution: The article explains that, after regime change, state practice does not recognize a blanket odious‑debt defense, broad repudiation would unsettle markets and restrict new lending, and real‑world outcomes tend to be negotiated adjustments that preserve most commercial arrangements.
matches.generalized_contribution: Successor liability generally persists despite regime change, with markets penalizing sweeping repudiation and obligations typically restructured through negotiation rather than excused by an odious‑debt defense.

matches.theme_name: Are private-law doctrines (agency, trust, odious-debt, successor-state rules) appropriate and effective tools for resolving state-succession and repudiation claims?
matches.specific_contribution: The article concludes that the purported odious‑regime debt doctrine lacks support in state practice and is both overinclusive and underinclusive as a tool for allocating liabilities after political change.
matches.generalized_contribution: Odious‑debt doctrines do not provide a coherent, legitimate, or workable basis for resolving state‑succession and repudiation claims.

matches.theme_name: What are the political-economy trade-offs between repudiating/forgiving sovereign debt (odious or illegal debt doctrines) and preserving future access to international capital?
matches.specific_contribution: The article argues that a broad odious‑debt rule would eviscerate creditor rights, destabilize global markets, harm populations dependent on those markets, and deter fresh loans to successor governments.
matches.generalized_contribution: Categorical repudiation on odiousness grounds risks market instability, social harm, and reduced future credit for successor states.

matches.theme_name: Are negotiated, policy-oriented processes through multilateral institutions more effective than formal international-law doctrines in resolving sovereign debt crises?
matches.specific_contribution: The article proposes abandoning a brute doctrinal approach in favor of a policy‑oriented process in which creditors, debtors, and other international actors negotiate adjustments that balance global stability with human rights, generally preserving commercial arrangements while easing terms.
matches.generalized_contribution: Policy‑oriented negotiation among international actors is more effective than formal odious‑debt doctrines for resolving succession‑related sovereign obligations.

matches.theme_name: How should legal rules allocate continuity, assets, and liabilities across political transitions (regime change, secession, state dissolution) to protect vulnerable populations while preserving market access?
matches.specific_contribution: The article recommends treating succession as to all commercial obligations, with continuity as the default and adjustments calibrated to enable economic recovery while safeguarding human rights and global market stability.
matches.generalized_contribution: Post‑transition rules should generally maintain continuity of obligations but modify terms to protect vulnerable populations and economic stability.

matches.theme_name: What institutional design best balances creditor enforcement rights and debtor-state welfare during sovereign restructurings (e.g., new-money priority, funding of essential services)?
matches.specific_contribution: The article contends that a categorical odious‑regime debt rule would eviscerate creditor rights and destabilize markets, and instead proposes a flexible, power‑aware international process in which commercial arrangements are generally preserved but obligations are adjusted to allow the successor economy to recover while balancing global stability with human rights.
matches.generalized_contribution: Flexible, process‑based adjustment that preserves commercial arrangements while easing burdens to support recovery better balances creditor enforcement with debtor welfare than categorical odious‑debt nullification.

matches.theme_name: Which institutional or doctrinal reforms (statutory sovereign bankruptcy, coordinated creditor fora, harmonized conflict-of-laws rules) are feasible and likely to improve restructuring speed, predictability, and fairness?
matches.specific_contribution: The article argues that state practice does not support a legal doctrine canceling odious‑regime debts and that such a rule is normatively overinclusive and underinclusive, advocating instead a broader, non‑formalist approach that adjusts all commercial obligations through international bargaining to balance stability and human rights.
matches.generalized_contribution: Formal codification of an odious‑debt cancellation rule is neither grounded in state practice nor normatively sound, whereas a broader, non‑formalist process for adjusting successor commercial obligations offers a more workable path to balanced outcomes.

matches.theme_name: Should courts or legislators prioritize textual formalism or pragmatic crisis-management when resolving disputes implicating sovereign obligations?
matches.specific_contribution: Part IV proposes abandoning arid formalism in favor of a flexible, power-aware global decisionmaking process that preserves most commercial arrangements while adjusting sovereign obligations to balance global stability with human rights and enable post-succession recovery.
matches.generalized_contribution: Pragmatic crisis-management that flexibly adjusts sovereign obligations to balance systemic stability and human rights is preferable to strict textual formalism in disputes over sovereign obligations.

matches.theme_name: How do market conditions and relative bargaining power among actors determine debt terms, restructuring allocations, and recovery outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The article explains that creditors, debtors, and other influential international actors exchange claims backed by varying degrees of power and authority, yielding outcomes that largely preserve commercial arrangements while adjusting obligations to allow economic recovery.
matches.generalized_contribution: Relative bargaining power among states, creditors, and international actors shapes restructuring outcomes that preserve core arrangements while selectively adjusting obligations to balance stability with recovery needs.

matches.theme_name: To what degree do soft-law norms, reputation, and market practice substitute for enforceable legal remedies in cross-border finance?
matches.specific_contribution: Part IV proposes reframing succession debts as a problem of succession to all commercial obligations and abandoning formal doctrine in favor of a global decisionmaking process in which creditors, debtors, and other influential actors negotiate adjustments that preserve commercial arrangements while enabling economic recovery.
matches.generalized_contribution: Non-binding, process-based coordination among international actors can substitute for rigid legal rules in governing successor obligations by preserving commerce while tailoring relief to balance stability and human rights.

matches.theme_name: How does the legal enforceability of sovereign obligations and the practical cost of cross-border enforcement affect foreign investment and cross-border capital flows to sovereigns/markets?
matches.specific_contribution: The article warns that a blanket odious-debt rule would eviscerate creditors' rights, destabilize global markets, and lead creditors to deny much-needed fresh loans to successor governments.
matches.generalized_contribution: Reducing the enforceability of sovereign obligations through broad odious-debt exemptions diminishes investor willingness to lend and threatens market stability and capital access for successor states.

matches.theme_name: Would greater doctrinal clarity (narrowed exceptions, precise rules) improve predictability enough to sustain cross-border lending and reduce costly strategic behavior?
matches.specific_contribution: Rather than refining a doctrinal rule on odious debts, the article urges abandoning arid formalism in favor of a broader, flexible decisionmaking process to adjust successor obligations.
matches.generalized_contribution: Greater doctrinal precision is not the preferred tool for sustaining cross-border lending in cases of state succession; flexible, non-formal processes that balance stability and human rights are more suitable.

matches.theme_name: What are the welfare trade-offs of prioritizing orderly, negotiated restructuring (stability and debtor rehabilitation) over strict creditor protections?
matches.specific_contribution: The article contends that a categorical odious‑regime debt rule would be overinclusive—eviscerating creditor rights, destabilizing markets, and deterring fresh lending—while a process‑oriented approach that preserves commercial arrangements but adjusts obligations can better balance global stability with human rights and enable successor economies to recover.
matches.generalized_contribution: Blanket invalidation of predecessor debts risks undermining creditor rights, market stability, and future lending, whereas negotiated adjustments that preserve contracts while easing terms can better reconcile stability, human rights, and debtor rehabilitation.

matches.theme_name: Can private ordering, market-level contractual design, and intermediaries substitute effectively for statutory or multilateral interventions in solving cross-border collective-action problems?
matches.specific_contribution: The article proposes replacing a rigid odious-debt doctrine with a broader, negotiated international process in which creditors, debtors, and other influential actors adjust commercial obligations to preserve arrangements and enable recovery.
matches.generalized_contribution: Ad hoc international bargaining among creditors, debtors, and public actors can adjust obligations to balance market stability and human-rights concerns without relying on rigid legal rules.

matches.theme_name: How do bargaining power asymmetries and repeat-player advantages shape non-price contract terms and the distribution of surplus in sovereign and major corporate transactions?
matches.specific_contribution: In addressing odious-debt claims after regime change, the article describes a process in which creditors, debtors, and other influential international actors negotiate on the basis of unequal power and authority to preserve commercial arrangements while adjusting obligations to balance market stability and human rights and enable economic recovery.
matches.generalized_contribution: During sovereign transitions, bargaining among actors with unequal power shapes non-price adjustments to obligations, preserving core commercial arrangements while reallocating terms to balance systemic stability with humanitarian concerns.

papers.node_id: 62washlrev397!!ARTICLE: RETHINKING THE ACT OF STATE DOCTRINE: AN ANALYSIS IN TERMS OF JURISDICTION TO PRESCRIBE.
papers.title: ARTICLE: RETHINKING THE ACT OF STATE DOCTRINE: AN ANALYSIS IN TERMS OF JURISDICTION TO PRESCRIBE.
papers.abstract:
The act of state doctrine requires United States courts to refrain from questioning the validity of acts done by a foreign sovereign within its own territory.This seemingly simple statement has caused hopeless confusion in the courts,has aroused endless scholarly debate,and has provokedvehement criticism from the bar.Recent cases applying the doctrine to foreign sovereign acts affecting intangible property have raised the level of conceptual confusion to new heightsand have triggered yet another flurry of critical commentary.
A basic cause of confusion about the doctrine is that courts and commentators disagree about the nature and scope of the doctrine.For instance, thedoctrine has been called a special rule of choice of law,a doctrine of judicial deference based on the principle of separation of powers,and a doctrine of nonjusticiability similar to the political question doctrine.Critics of the act of state doctrine point out that the existence of these inconsistent theories has confounded the courtsand judicial application of these discordant theories has led to arbitrary and unjust results.According to some critics, the act of state doctrine should be abolished altogether.
This article proposes a new conception of the act of state doctrine.The basic approach of this new conception is that the act of state doctrine should be analyzed in terms of international law principles governing a sovereign state'sjurisdiction to prescribe rules of law.  As used here, jurisdiction to prescribe refers to the appropriate authority of a state "to make its law applicable to the activities, relations, or status of persons, or the interests of persons in things."In analyzing questions of prescriptive jurisdiction,this article employs the useful and important approach set forth by the recently adopted Restatement of Foreign Relations Law of the United States (Revised).
To illustrate this approach, suppose that a forum court is called upon to resolve a dispute involving foreign sovereign acts.  The court determines that under international law the foreign legal system has the appropriate authority to make its law applicable to those acts.In this case, the foreign sovereign has committed acts over which it has proper jurisdiction to prescribe.  The court of the forum state is bound to apply the law of the foreign sovereign to determine the legal consequences of those acts and may not question the results unless they are contrary to international law.On the other hand, suppose that the forum court determines that under international law the legal system of the forum state has the appropriate authority to make its law applicable to the acts in question.  In this case, the foreign sovereign has committed acts over which the forum state has proper jurisdiction to prescribe.The legal status of the acts under the foreign sovereign's own legal system is irrelevant to the adjudication of the dispute by the forum court.Rather, the legal consequences of the acts of the foreign sovereign are determined solely by the laws of the forum state.  Otherwise, the foreign sovereign would, in effect, be amending legal relationships that should be governed by the legal system of the forum state.
Since modern international law contemplates broad and overlapping bases of jurisdiction to prescribe, both the forum and the foreign sovereign will frequently have concurrent bases to exercise prescriptive jurisdiction over the same persons, things, or conduct.In these cases, each sovereign state should evaluate the relevant competing interests by a standard of reasonableness and one state should defer to the other if the other state has a greater interest at stake.
Admittedly, in certain cases, an analysis in terms of jurisdiction to prescribe will be scarcely easier than an analysis based upon a current theory of the act of state doctrine.Nonetheless, this approach can be justified because it offers jurisprudential and legal advantages over the current theories comprising act of state jurisprudence.
, the doctrine of jurisdiction to prescribe incorporates the descendants of positivist concepts of power and absolute territoriality -- the original underpinnings of the act of state doctrine.By building upon contemporary versions of the doctrine's original foundations, an analysis of the act of state doctrine in terms of jurisdiction to prescribe remains faithful to the doctrine's origins and accommodates the needs of the modern international legal and economic order.
, jurisdiction to prescribe is a fundamental and powerful concept that plays an increasingly important role as international business transactions multiply and nations, such as the United States, seek to regulate such transactions across national boundaries.  Developing agreed-upon rules of prescriptive jurisdiction should enhance understanding of the extraterritorial reach of the federal antitrust and securities laws, an area where attempts by the United States to exercise extensive prescriptive jurisdiction has led to international tension and resentment.In addition, the concept of jurisdiction to prescribe has broad explanatory power.  The act of state doctrine and the doctrine of absolute and restrictive sovereign immunity, now considered discrete and independent theories, can be analyzed under this single, unified approach.Also, most of the exceptions to the act of state doctrine can be incorporated directly into the main analysis in terms of jurisdiction to prescribe.The development of a single and comprehensive theory, applicable to areas now considered governed by independent legal doctrines and exceptions, offers the advantages of economy and simplicity.
, the doctrine of jurisdiction to prescribe is governed by rules of international law, now recognized as part of the federal law of the United States.According to legal scholars, the act of state doctrine "is probably the single most important reason for the arrested development of international law in the United States."A theory of the act of state doctrine basedupon jurisdiction to prescribe will allow United States courts to contribute to the development of international law.Moreover, the proposed new conception of the act of state doctrine satisfies the judicial concern that the doctrine should be governed by federal law, a concern that has profoundly influenced the doctrine's previous development.
, an act of state analysis in terms of jurisdiction to prescribe will bring much needed analytical clarity to current act of state disputes involving intangible property and contract rights.  Since traditional act of state analysis offers little guidance in this area, courts and commentators propose conflicting and confusing new approaches to the application of the act of state doctrine to sovereign defaults on private loans and sovereign expropriations of foreign bank branches or deposits.Moreover, given the likelihood of increasing numbers of international business transactions involving intangible property and contract rights, it will prove useful to invest scholarly and judicial energy into developing principles regulating the competence of nations to prescribe rules of law governing intangible property.
Part I of this article sets forth a history and development of theories of the act of state doctrine.  This section traces the major shifts in the jurisprudential and legal foundations of the doctrine that occurred between its birth in the nineteenth century and its reemergence in the latter half of the twentieth century.  These shifts contributed to the development of incompatible theories of the doctrine.  Part II demonstrates that each of these current theories is seriously flawed for various jurisprudential, legal, and practical reasons.  Part III first proposes and defends an analysis of the act of state doctrine in terms of jurisdiction to prescribe, and argues that the proposed new conception of the doctrine will serve a valuable and unique function in the modern international legal order.  Part III then applies an act of state analysis in terms of jurisdiction to prescribe to major act of state cases and to recent cases involving intangible property.

matches.theme_name: Do judicial doctrines-such as act-of-state, sovereign immunity, and abstention/comity-unduly limit creditors' remedies in cross-border disputes and require doctrinal reform to balance politics and predictability?
matches.specific_contribution: Diagnosing arbitrary and unjust outcomes under conflicting act-of-state theories, the article proposes a reform grounded in international-law rules of prescriptive jurisdiction that unifies related doctrines and incorporates most exceptions to improve predictability in disputes that can include sovereign defaults and bank deposit cases.
matches.generalized_contribution: Replacing fragmented act-of-state approaches with an international-law-based prescriptive-jurisdiction framework can reduce arbitrariness and enhance predictability in cross-border disputes involving state acts.

matches.theme_name: Is the expanding exercise of domestic prescriptive or extraterritorial jurisdiction over foreign sovereign acts legitimate and effective in governing cross-border economic obligations?
matches.specific_contribution: The article contends that domestic exercises of prescriptive jurisdiction over foreign sovereign acts are legitimate when the forum has authority under international law to prescribe, that foreign law should govern when the foreign state has that authority, and that overlapping claims should be resolved by a reasonableness test with deference to the state with the greater interest.
matches.generalized_contribution: Domestic and extraterritorial regulation of foreign sovereign acts is appropriate and effective when tied to international-law criteria of prescriptive authority and moderated by reasonableness-based deference.

matches.theme_name: When and on what grounds should domestic courts review or abstain from adjudicating claims arising from foreign sovereign acts (act-of-state and comity doctrines)?
matches.specific_contribution: It offers a rule-of-decision for act-of-state cases: apply the foreign state’s law when that state has proper prescriptive jurisdiction and do not question the result unless contrary to international law; apply forum law when the forum has prescriptive jurisdiction; and, where both do, balance interests and defer to the state with the stronger interest.
matches.generalized_contribution: Courts should calibrate review and deference in cases implicating foreign public acts by applying international-law rules on prescriptive jurisdiction and interest-balancing reasonableness.

matches.theme_name: Does the extraterritorial reach of national legal regimes and conflicting jurisdictional claims produce distortive conflicts-of-law that affect capital flows and contract design?
matches.specific_contribution: The article notes that expansive U.S. assertions of prescriptive jurisdiction in antitrust and securities law have generated international tension and argues that agreed rules of prescriptive jurisdiction would clarify such laws’ extraterritorial reach.
matches.generalized_contribution: Conflicting or expansive extraterritorial jurisdictional claims create international frictions that can be mitigated by clear, widely accepted rules on prescriptive jurisdiction.

matches.theme_name: Do fragmented or indeterminate cross-border legal regimes create enforcement gaps that justify doctrinal or institutional reform for sovereign debt?
matches.specific_contribution: Finding deep confusion in act-of-state jurisprudence—especially for intangible property and sovereign default disputes—the article proposes a unified prescriptive-jurisdiction framework to replace patchwork doctrines and exceptions.
matches.generalized_contribution: Fragmented cross-border doctrines create uncertainty that justifies unified reform grounded in international-law rules of prescriptive jurisdiction.

matches.theme_name: Do exculpatory and limitation-of-liability clauses, together with sovereign-immunity doctrines, unduly restrict private claimants' remedies and distort bargaining in high-stakes international transactions?
matches.specific_contribution: By reframing the act of state doctrine and sovereign immunity within a single prescriptive-jurisdiction analysis, the article delineates when courts must defer to foreign sovereign acts and when they may adjudicate claims, thereby clarifying the scope of private remedies in cross-border disputes involving intangible property.
matches.generalized_contribution: Analyzing sovereign-act and immunity issues through prescriptive-jurisdiction rules clarifies and limits the circumstances in which private claimants can obtain remedies against sovereign-related conduct.

matches.theme_name: Does the extraterritorial reach of national regulatory regimes create irresolvable conflicts in cross-border financial enforcement?
matches.specific_contribution: The article observes that expansive U.S. assertions of prescriptive jurisdiction in antitrust and securities have produced international tension, and contends that applying international-law rules of prescriptive jurisdiction—with reasonableness and deference in cases of overlap—can manage such conflicts.
matches.generalized_contribution: Conflicts generated by extraterritorial regulatory reach can be mitigated when courts apply international-law limits and reasonableness balancing in prescriptive jurisdiction.

matches.theme_name: What is the role of governing-law clauses and the extraterritorial reach of major legal systems (e.g., US law) in constraining sovereign policy space?
matches.specific_contribution: Grounding act-of-state analysis in prescriptive jurisdiction, with deference to the state with the greater interest, cabins the extraterritorial application of dominant national laws and respects foreign authority over domestic acts.
matches.generalized_contribution: Applying prescriptive-jurisdiction and reasonableness standards constrains extraterritorial application of national laws and mediates their impact on sovereign policy space.

matches.theme_name: How do inconsistent conflict-of-laws rules and varying domestic adjudicative practices affect cross-border payment disputes, the localization of bank deposits, and asset-recovery strategies?
matches.specific_contribution: Applying a prescriptive-jurisdiction framework to act-of-state questions provides analytical clarity for disputes over sovereign defaults, expropriations of bank branches, and the legal status of foreign deposits and other intangible property.
matches.generalized_contribution: Using prescriptive-jurisdiction rules reduces choice-of-law inconsistency in cross-border payment and deposit disputes and clarifies where such assets and claims are legally situated.

matches.theme_name: When do sovereign emergency measures (nationalization, exchange controls) constitute a compensable 'taking' under contract or international law?
matches.specific_contribution: By applying its prescriptive-jurisdiction framework to disputes involving sovereign defaults and expropriations of foreign bank branches or deposits, the article indicates when courts must give effect to the foreign sovereign’s law and when they may scrutinize such acts as contrary to international law.
matches.generalized_contribution: Using prescriptive-jurisdiction rules to decide whose law governs helps delineate the legal consequences of sovereign emergency measures affecting property, including when judicial review under international law is appropriate.

matches.theme_name: Would greater doctrinal clarity (narrowed exceptions, precise rules) improve predictability enough to sustain cross-border lending and reduce costly strategic behavior?
matches.specific_contribution: The article maintains that a prescriptive-jurisdiction analysis brings analytical clarity, unifies related doctrines, and develops agreed rules that enhance understanding of extraterritorial regulation in cross-border transactions.
matches.generalized_contribution: Greater doctrinal clarity through precise prescriptive-jurisdiction rules improves predictability in cross-border legal disputes and can reduce friction from overlapping regulatory claims.

matches.theme_name: How do cross-border legal conflicts-choice-of-law, extraterritorial reach, and conflicting forum judgments-shape enforceability and predictability in international financial contracts?
matches.specific_contribution: The article reconceives the act of state doctrine as an application of international-law rules on prescriptive jurisdiction, directing courts to apply the law of the sovereign with proper prescriptive authority (or the forum’s law where it has that authority) and to defer on reasonableness grounds in cases of concurrent jurisdiction, thereby bringing clarity to disputes over intangible property and contract rights, including sovereign defaults.
matches.generalized_contribution: Grounding act-of-state analysis in international prescriptive-jurisdiction rules clarifies which law governs cross-border sovereign acts and increases predictability for contracts and financial claims exposed to multiple legal systems.

matches.theme_name: How does judicial interpretive flexibility (vague standards vs precise rules) affect predictability and market behavior in high-stakes transactional and sovereign debt litigation?
matches.specific_contribution: The article argues that conflicting theories of the act of state doctrine have yielded arbitrary and unpredictable results, and that re-grounding the doctrine in international law’s jurisdiction-to-prescribe framework would provide analytical clarity and more determinate outcomes, including in disputes over sovereign defaults on private loans and other intangible-property cases.
matches.generalized_contribution: Unifying vague, competing doctrines under a jurisdiction-to-prescribe analysis increases clarity and predictability in high-stakes cross-border transactional and sovereign debt disputes.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do legal ambiguities and doctrinal vagueness (e.g., in 'pari passu', 'loan' definitions, or damages measures) cause litigation, market uncertainty, and suboptimal contracting outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The article shows that competing and inconsistent theories of the act of state doctrine have produced hopeless confusion and arbitrary, unjust judicial results, and proposes a prescriptive-jurisdiction framework grounded in international law to restore clarity and predictability, particularly in disputes over intangible property and contract rights.
matches.generalized_contribution: Conflicting doctrinal theories create litigation confusion and arbitrary outcomes, and clear prescriptive-jurisdiction rules can reduce such uncertainty.

matches.theme_name: How do cross-border regulatory measures (sanctions, capital controls, deposit freezes) alter contractual rights, remedies, and the incentives of creditors and debtors?
matches.specific_contribution: By directing courts to apply the law of the state with prescriptive jurisdiction—and to balance competing interests when jurisdiction overlaps—the article supplies a rule-of-decision for cases where sovereign measures (including defaults or expropriations affecting bank deposits) alter private contract and intangible-property rights across borders.
matches.generalized_contribution: A prescriptive-jurisdiction framework determines when courts should give effect to foreign or forum regulatory acts that impinge on private contracts, thereby shaping cross-border rights and remedies.

matches.theme_name: How does legal and drafting complexity affect transaction costs, negotiability, and the likelihood of litigation or deal failure?
matches.specific_contribution: The article contends that inconsistent theories of the act of state doctrine have produced confusion and arbitrary results in litigation, and proposes a unified, prescriptive-jurisdiction framework to bring analytical clarity and simplify adjudication, especially in disputes over intangible property and contract rights.
matches.generalized_contribution: Reducing doctrinal fragmentation by applying coherent jurisdiction-to-prescribe principles can improve analytical clarity and simplify adjudication in cross-border disputes involving intangible property and contracts.

papers.node_id: 1989columbuslrev307!!SYMPOSIUM: RETHINKING LEGAL OPINION LETTERS: SAME THOUGHTS ON THE ECONOMICS OF LEGAL OPINIONS
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: RETHINKING LEGAL OPINION LETTERS: SAME THOUGHTS ON THE ECONOMICS OF LEGAL OPINIONS
papers.authors: THOMAS L. AMBRO + AND J. TRUMAN BIDWELL, JR. ++
papers.abstract:
Legal opinions rendered to third parties have become an integral part of major commercial transactions.  Nonetheless and despite the growing body of literature on legal opinions, relatively little attention has been paid to the question of how or whether such opinions add value to a transaction.This article will examine the ways in which a third party legal opinionmay, or may not, give value to the recipient and suggest that the necessity for and scope of an Opinion should be measured in part on the basis of a cost/benefit analysis.
The value of an Opinion, like beauty, is all too often in the eye of the beholder.  The Opinion frequently tracks many of the representations and warranties in the relevant contract.  Is the law firm that is rendering the Opinion providing a separate guarantee of the accuracy of the representations and warranties?  Clearly not.  What then is the value of the Opinion to the recipient?  Why not simply rely on remedies for breach of contract if the representations or warranties turn out to be inaccurate?
Perhaps the justification most frequently heard for requesting Opinions is that "I want the other side's counsel to bless the deal, and I want them to tell me that it works." In this context the value of a third party opinion is primarily the assurance or reassurance itgives to counsel advising the opinion recipient.  Properly worded, the opinion induces disclosures and identifies legal risks, i.e. those pitfalls or possible areas of concern or doubt that the recipient's counsel wants to know about in completing his due diligence and advising his client.  The assumption seems to be that, absent the requirement for an Opinion, counsel from whom the Opinion is requested would not focus on the transaction in sufficient detail to ensure its success.  We doubt this is so, since the lawyer will want to ensure that the transaction works because it is in the interest of his client.  If it is agreed, as we believe it should be, that an Opinion is essentially a lawyer's view of how a court would decide a particular issue (i.e., the "deal works"), then only the unwary lawyer will be held liable for an Opinion.  Perhaps more pitfalls arise where the lawyer's Opinion is more factual than legal, but even there the careful lawyer will protect himself with appropriate diligence or limitations on the scope of his diligence.  Furthermore, at least when dealing with a substantial client, if it turns out that a representation or warranty is untrue, not only is the client's pocket deeper than the lawyer's, but the case is much easier to prove.
Thus, are there not instances in which each side should look to its own counsel? Restraints on requests for Opinions are certainly less when the cost is borne by the opposing party, and avoiding the tensions created when one's own counsel renders an opinion to the other party may on appropriate occasions have merit.
Whether the Opinion was from one's counsel or from another party's counsel, the scope of the Opinion should always be weighed against the objective of keeping costs to a minimum.  Since businessmen find it difficult to justify the expense of Opinions they often neither understand nor find useful, it is in the interest of both client and lawyer that the scope of the lawyer's Opinion be clear and that the time and costs invested in the production of an Opinion be kept within reasonable parameters.  Lawyers need to guide their clients as to how to spend money most intelligently in getting (and giving) the assurances that business diligence requires.
We note that increasing attention is being devoted to the subject of legal opinions by bar associations, scholars and practitioners.Most of these efforts are aimed at standardizing opinions and achieving consensus on language and format.  These efforts will, if successful, reduce the cost of Opinions.  To the extent that agreement is reached on standardized formats of Opinions for particular transactions, many hours of negotiation will be saved.  As importantly, the temptation to ask for Opinions that one would not give oneself will be removed.  Finally, from the lawyer's perspective, Opinions will cease to be a trap for the unwary -- particularly for the lawyer who does not regularly participate in transactions in which Opinions are issued.  It may be noted that to this end the American Bar Association has formed a Committee on Legal Opinions, whose first task has been to prepare an accord on Opinions in commercial transactions.  It is hoped that this accord will set a standard that will reduce the time spent negotiating Opinions and promote agreement on the meaning of Opinion terms.
