matches.generalized_contribution: Mandatory contractual constraints are unlikely to correct inefficiencies arising from bargaining-power imbalances.

matches.theme_name: Do professional intermediaries (law firms, underwriters, trustees, advisors) introduce agency costs that bias contract design and risk allocation?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article identifies a two-stage contracting process in which principals set price and then delegate design details to lawyers, and cautions that the exercise of bargaining power in this delegated stage may distort nonprice terms.
matches.generalized_contribution: Delegation of contract drafting to professional intermediaries can introduce agency-driven distortions in nonprice terms when bargaining power is exercised after price is set.

matches.theme_name: How do agency problems among intermediaries (banks, law firms, underwriters, trustees) distort contract terms and affect post-signing enforcement and renegotiation outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article observes that when contract design is delegated to lawyers after principals agree on price, principal–agent frictions allow bargaining power to shape and potentially skew nonprice terms.
matches.generalized_contribution: Agency frictions with professional intermediaries can bias contractual risk allocation by enabling late-stage bargaining power to influence drafting choices.

matches.theme_name: Do lawyers, deal teams, and legal intermediaries (as repeat players) add measurable economic value through drafting and structuring beyond mere documentation?
matches.specific_contribution: The article identifies a two-stage contracting process in which lawyers draft design details after principals set price, and explains that bargaining power exercised at this stage can distort nonprice terms away from efficiency.
matches.generalized_contribution: Delegating contract design to lawyers after price-setting enables powerful parties to shape nonprice terms in ways that may reduce efficiency.

matches.theme_name: What role do lawyers, underwriters, and other intermediaries play in creating, diffusing, and entrenching contractual innovations and standard clauses?
matches.specific_contribution: The article suggests that the party with greater bargaining power has stronger incentives to invest effort and resources in innovating and developing contractual opportunities, influencing which nonprice terms are created.
matches.generalized_contribution: Greater bargaining power concentrates the creation of contractual innovations in the hands of stronger parties, shaping which terms emerge.

matches.theme_name: Do exculpatory and limitation-of-liability clauses meaningfully shift litigation risk and welfare among contracting parties and third parties?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article shows that under asymmetric information and extreme allocations of bargaining power, parties may adopt inefficiently one-sided nonprice terms—such as warranty disclaimers or limitations on remedies—that sacrifice aggregate surplus to reallocate risk and surplus shares.
matches.generalized_contribution: Unequal bargaining power under asymmetric information can induce inefficient remedy-limiting or disclaimer clauses that reduce overall welfare to shift risk and surplus between parties.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do information asymmetries and signaling affect creditor decision-making and pricing in sovereign and complex financial contracting?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article explains that information asymmetries and shifts in pricing (e.g., higher interest rates) can intensify adverse selection and moral hazard in lending, prompting the use of stricter covenants and other nonprice terms as screening or signaling devices, with unequal bargaining power exacerbating inefficiencies.
matches.generalized_contribution: In financial contracting, information asymmetry and price levels shape the use and stringency of screening and signaling terms, with greater asymmetry and higher prices leading to tighter contractual controls and potential inefficiencies when bargaining power is one-sided.

matches.theme_name: How do information asymmetries-adverse selection and moral hazard-shape the design of contractual devices (collateral, covenants, disclosure) in sovereign and corporate lending?
matches.specific_contribution: The article explains that when market interest rates are high, the heightened severity of adverse selection and moral hazard leads lenders to use tighter and more extensive covenants in loan agreements.
matches.generalized_contribution: Greater expected adverse selection or moral hazard induces the adoption of stricter nonprice contractual devices, such as covenants, to screen and constrain borrowers.

matches.theme_name: Do material adverse effect/change (MAE/MAC) clauses operate primarily as true risk-allocation devices or as strategic deal-termination levers in M&A transactions?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article notes that material adverse change clauses in mergers and acquisitions agreements fluctuate over time between buyer-friendly and seller-friendly versions as market conditions and bargaining power shift.
matches.generalized_contribution: MAE/MAC clause stringency varies with market conditions and bargaining power, reflecting their use as negotiable levers in dealmaking.

papers.node_id: 85geowashlrev57!!ARTICLE: The Inefficient Evolution of Merger Agreements
papers.title: ARTICLE: The Inefficient Evolution of Merger Agreements
papers.abstract:
Transactional law accounts for approximately 32% of Am Law 50 firm revenue, nearly as much as litigation, and is an outsized driver of profitability and prestige for elite firms.Transactional lawyers draft the terms contained in documents that delineate the rights and duties of parties involved in trillions of dollars of transfers every year.Thiswork product has staggering importance, as the legally operative terms in these agreements have the potential to meet or frustrate the economic motivations of enormous transfers of capital in the United States and world economies.
Despite its economic importance, there has been little empirical work on the overall legal drafting process in transactional law.Most articles about transactional drafting deal either with pedagogical issues in teaching legal drafting or with specific substantive aspects of law.In contrast, the process by which transactional lawyers draft documentsthat shape capital flows of trillions of dollars remains understudied.
This study seeks to fill this gap by analyzing the evolution of public company merger agreements in a dataset encompassing 12,000 agreements over a twenty-year period. Using computer textual analysis, it is possible to identify the precedent (an earlier merger agreement) which serves as the template for the drafting of each deal.This approach allows us to construct comprehensive "family trees" of merger agreements which can show how agreements are created and how they change over time.
This innovative approach allows us to explore the extent to which the transactional drafting is driven by a rational process that minimizes the cost of deal documentation and risk to clients, or by an ad hoc process that increases billable hours and risk. This study shows that a high level of "editorial churning"--unnecessary and ad hoc edits that appear to be cosmetic rather than substantive--takes place in legal drafting. This churning appears to go far beyond the necessary deal-specific edits,with over half of merger agreement text being routinely rewritten even though the substantive provisions of merger agreements have similar features.
This Article demonstrates that public merger agreement terms are not based off a common "form" agreement, but rather are the product of an "evolution" over many generations. This is true even within large law firms where drafts are based on prior agreements rather than standardized form language. The absence of even firmspecific forms has led to haphazard and inconsistent lawyering, as lawyers add significant amounts of extraneous information to each deal and inadvertently retain deal-specific information from prior deals.
This fact underscores the inefficiency of current deal drafting processes and undercuts the argument that merger agreements are distinctively crafted (at great expense) to suit the needs of clients. This Article argues that the remarkable heterogeneity of acquisition agreements reflects lawyers' tendency to use precedents that they are more familiar with or that relate to the particular client they are dealing with, rather than those that may be more readily adapted to the transaction at hand. The result is a path-dependent process of deal-term evolution that thwarts standardization even within firms, and leads to systematic inefficiencies in the acquisition agreement drafting process which raises costs and risk to clients.
The high degree of drafting inefficiency suggests the desirability of transitioning to greater standardization of acquisition agreements.This Article provides an approach that could assist that process by enabling drafters to see the edits that have been made over the past few generations of a draft lineage so that they can more easily reverse non-standardized text embedded in a precedent document. This approachwould help transform acquisition agreements from opaque, byzantine documents into easily comparable agreements that would entail lower costs to produce and create higher legal certainty. This Article suggests how private equity firms (or trade associations representing the private equity industry) could take the lead in the standardization process based on their repeat-player interaction with law firms.
Although this study focuses on the public company merger context, this Article's argument may extend to a far broader spectrum of transactional contexts. If there is evidence of systematic inefficiency in the merger agreement context where there is transparency of the end product, one would expect there would be an even greater risk of non-standardization and editorial churning in other transactional contexts where there is little to no transparency of the deal documents.Deal lawyers face a paradox--standardization reduces transaction costs and thus helps their clients, but also may cut into the bottom line of their firm's revenues.This Article argues that, just as merger agreement standardization may allow transactional lawyers to focus on where they can add value to a merger or acquisition, the same logic applies in other transactional contexts. But a similar challenge exists across transactional law, as lawyers have every temptation to stick with the lucrative status quo unless clients themselves push for greater standardization across the spectrum of transactional law contexts.
Part I provides the background to transactional practice necessary to understand the approach of this Article and sets out the method by which this study was conducted. Part II analyzes the dataset of merger agreements and discusses the empirical findings of this study. Part III offers some steps toward solutions that will better integrate legal practice with the needs of modern capital markets.

matches.theme_name: Do lawyers, deal teams, and legal intermediaries (as repeat players) add measurable economic value through drafting and structuring beyond mere documentation?
matches.specific_contribution: Analyzing 12,000 public-company merger agreements, the study finds pervasive editorial churning and reliance on familiar precedents rather than optimal forms, producing inefficiencies that raise client costs and risk and undermining claims that bespoke drafting adds distinctive value.
matches.generalized_contribution: Repeat-player transactional drafting practices often add cost and risk rather than measurable economic value due to ad hoc editing and precedent-driven choices.

matches.theme_name: How does legal and drafting complexity affect transaction costs, negotiability, and the likelihood of litigation or deal failure?
matches.specific_contribution: The paper shows that extensive non-standard, extraneous, and inconsistent drafting—driven by editorial churning and lack of standardized forms—raises transaction costs and legal risk, while standardization would lower costs and increase legal certainty.
matches.generalized_contribution: Greater drafting complexity and heterogeneity increase transaction costs and legal risk, whereas standardization reduces them and improves certainty.

matches.theme_name: What are the trade-offs between standardized boilerplate and bespoke drafting for transaction costs, liquidity, and fairness?
matches.specific_contribution: The study finds that bespoke, precedent-driven drafting produces path-dependent heterogeneity and inefficiency in merger agreements, and proposes standardization tools to lower production costs and improve legal certainty.
matches.generalized_contribution: Standardized boilerplate delivers efficiency and certainty compared to bespoke, precedent-driven drafting that imposes unnecessary costs.

matches.theme_name: Do professional intermediaries (law firms, underwriters, trustees, advisors) introduce agency costs that bias contract design and risk allocation?
matches.specific_contribution: Evidence of widespread ad hoc editing and reliance on familiar precedents indicates that law firms’ incentives and habits bias contract design toward non-standard, inefficient terms that increase client costs and risk.
matches.generalized_contribution: Professional intermediaries’ incentive structures and familiarity biases introduce agency costs that sustain suboptimal drafting and shift cost and risk to clients.

matches.theme_name: Do standardized contract forms and drafting defaults systematically shape non-price deal terms and bargaining outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The article notes the absence of firm-level forms and suggests that standardized templates and lineage-tracking tools would make agreements more comparable and legally certain.
matches.generalized_contribution: Providing standardized forms and drafting defaults can shape non-price terms by promoting comparability and legal certainty across deals.

matches.theme_name: Why do standardized contractual clauses ('boilerplate') persist despite inefficiencies, and what institutional or market mechanisms overcome this lock-in?
matches.specific_contribution: The paper attributes the persistence of inefficient, non-standard clause language to path-dependent reliance on familiar precedents and billable-hour incentives, and proposes that repeat players like private equity firms can catalyze standardization.
matches.generalized_contribution: Path dependence and agency incentives lock in inefficient clause language, and change can be driven by powerful repeat players and standardization tools.

matches.theme_name: Can empirical contract-level datasets reveal patterns of clause prevalence and evolution that should inform doctrinal or regulatory reform?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a 12,000-agreement, 20-year corpus of public-company merger contracts and textual lineage mapping, the study identifies extensive editorial churning, path-dependent evolution from precedents, and lack of standardization that motivate concrete standardization tools and reforms.
matches.generalized_contribution: Large empirical corpora of contracts can reveal drafting inefficiencies and evolutionary lineage patterns that inform doctrinal or market-based standardization reforms.

matches.theme_name: What role do lawyers, underwriters, and other intermediaries play in creating, diffusing, and entrenching contractual innovations and standard clauses?
matches.specific_contribution: Analyzing drafting lineages shows that transactional lawyers build new merger agreements by copying and cosmetically editing familiar precedents rather than firm-wide forms, producing path-dependent diffusion and persistent heterogeneity of terms.
matches.generalized_contribution: Intermediaries’ reliance on familiar templates and precedent copying drives the spread and persistence of contract terms and can impede standardization.

matches.theme_name: What can large-scale, contract-by-contract textual and empirical analyses reveal about the gap between drafted language and actual functional allocations of risk?
matches.specific_contribution: Textual analysis shows that over half of merger agreement text is routinely rewritten despite substantively similar provisions, indicating cosmetic variation not matched by substantive change and adding cost and risk for clients.
matches.generalized_contribution: Corpus studies can detect extensive wording changes that do not correspond to substantive shifts in rights and risk allocation.

matches.theme_name: Does diffusion of standardized contract clauses across jurisdictions reduce transaction costs and improve predictability for investors?
matches.specific_contribution: Building on evidence of inefficiency and heterogeneity, the article contends that greater standardization—and tools to surface and reverse nonstandard edits—would lower drafting costs and increase legal certainty.
matches.generalized_contribution: Adoption of standardized clauses reduces transaction costs and improves ex ante predictability for market participants.

matches.theme_name: How do agency problems among intermediaries (banks, law firms, underwriters, trustees) distort contract terms and affect post-signing enforcement and renegotiation outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The study links widespread editorial churning and precedent-driven drafting to lawyers’ incentives, noting that standardization would cut client costs but threatens billable revenue, so lawyers may resist efficiency unless pushed by repeat-player clients.
matches.generalized_contribution: Agency conflicts in legal intermediation can steer drafting toward inefficient, nonstandard terms that increase client costs and risk and persist absent countervailing client pressure.

matches.theme_name: How do bargaining power asymmetries and repeat-player advantages shape non-price contract terms and the distribution of surplus in sovereign and major corporate transactions?
matches.specific_contribution: The article notes that repeat-player clients such as private equity firms could spearhead standardization of merger agreements, while law firms’ revenue incentives encourage continuation of inefficient, non-standard drafting that increases client costs and risk.
matches.generalized_contribution: Repeat-player counterparties can leverage their position to press for standardized contracting practices, but intermediary incentives can entrench inefficient drafting that disadvantages clients.

matches.theme_name: How do norms, professional networks, and market practice diffuse contractual innovations (like new clause language) across jurisdictions and market segments?
matches.specific_contribution: Using textual analysis of 12,000 public company merger agreements, the study maps precedent-based family trees and finds that language diffuses through path-dependent copying with extensive cosmetic “editorial churning” and minimal standardization even within firms.
matches.generalized_contribution: Contract terms diffuse primarily through precedent copying within professional networks, yielding path-dependent heterogeneity and limited standardization rather than coherent, form-driven convergence.

papers.node_id: 55urichlrev565!!SYMPOSIUM FEATURE: MERGERS, MACS, AND COVID-19
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM FEATURE: MERGERS, MACS, AND COVID-19
papers.abstract:
On May 20, 2020, Forescout Technologies filed a lawsuit seeking a declaratory judgment against Advent International.Forescout and Advent had signed a merger agreement in early February, some three months before.By May, it was becoming apparent toForescout that Advent was suffering buyer's remorse: a deal that looked good prior to the onset of a global pandemic looked less wonderful after the U.S. economy ground to a halt in an effort to battle the spread of COVID-19. Forescout's lawsuit sought a declaratory judgment from the court that COVID-19 did not represent a material adverse event and an order that Advent proceed to closing of the transaction.Ultimately, Forescout and Advent settled the litigation through a renegotiation downwards of the merger price and the transaction moved forward to closing.The Forescout litigation was one of a small number of cases that followed the onset of COVID-19 in the spring of 2020 in which buyers sought to walk away from merger agreements citing a material adverse effect.While the Forescout story is consistent at first glance with the conventional wisdom that parties use material adverse effect/material adverse change ("MAE/MAC") clauses in merger agreements to facilitate renegotiation, the paucity of such efforts following the COVID-19 outbreak should cause us to re-evaluate that conventional wisdom.This Article argues that the ambiguity that often serves the corporation law well has, by now, dissipated with respect to MAE/MAC clauses, and there has been a fundamental change in the role of the MAE/MAC since 2001. The lack of ambiguity surrounding modern MAE/MAC clauses has, as a result, fundamentally changed the role MAE/MAC clauses play in merger agreements. Rather than act as a quasi-force majeure clause, with the seller bearing the burden of adverse shock, modern MAE/MAC clauses allocate exogenous risks to the buyer and endogenous risks to the seller consistent with the role described by Professors Gilson and Schwartz.Consequently, conventional wisdom that describesMAE/MAC clauses as contractual devices that potentially facilitate efficient renegotiations in the face of adverse shocks is overstated.
The sudden onset of COVID-19 in spring 2020 was, and remains, a tsunami-like event. It was totally unexpected and swept across the economy with frightening speed. It also threatens to extend well into the foreseeable future. COVID-19 is precisely the kind of adverse event that the MAE/MAC clause in merger agreements is intended to protect signatories against. The COVID-19 outbreak gives us a unique opportunity to evaluate the role the MAE/MAC clause plays in merger contracting. Most transactions pending at the outset of the COVID-19 outbreak in the U.S. closed notwithstanding the massive disruption brought on by the pandemic. In a small number of transactions, buyers refused to close, citing a MAE/MAC as the reason not to move forward with the merger. In three of those transactions, the parties sought to litigate the question of a MAE/MAC (i.e., Simon v. Taubman,LVMH v. Tiffany,and Forescout Technologies), but ultimately settled their litigation by renegotiating the terms of their merger agreement. In Mirae's acquisition of Anbang's hotel assets, a court refused to declare a MAE/MAC, but permitted the buyer to walk away for breach of a seller's covenant.In another transaction, the parties agreed to terminate the transaction voluntarily (i.e., Victoria's Secret) rather than renegotiate or litigate the issue of whether there had been a MAE/MAC.
The MAE/MAC provision is one of a number of risk-shifting clauses in the merger contract. In most cases, the MAE/MAC does this by assigning the risk of exogenous material adverse events between signing and closing to the buyer and the risk of endogenous material adverse events to the seller.Because the MAE/MAC assigns the risk to the party best able to bear it, one can reasonably conclude that the MAE/MAC is an efficient term. Where there has been a MAE/MAC, the buyer is permitted to terminate the transaction and walk away, or the parties can renegotiate the terms of the agreement in order to facilitate an efficient transaction. Where there has been an adverse event that does not rise to a MAE, the buyer bears the risk of loss. However, because the MAE/MAC provision can act as a fulcrum for potential efficient renegotiations, the conventional wisdom is that the MAE/MAC provision has a subsidiary function as a renegotiation clause in the face of any adverse shock.
By now, it is clear, however, that courts are extremely reticent to permit a buyer to simply point to an adverse event between signing and closing and walk away from a transaction. Notwithstanding courts' reluctance, the conventional wisdom remains that following an adverse event, a buyer may lean on these clauses, and the threat of litigation, to push sellers to renegotiate the terms of merger agreements. This conventional wisdom overestimates the degree of judicial ambiguity surrounding modern MAE/MAC provisions. Where the parties overestimate judicial ambiguity, buyers may be able to take advantage of bargaining dynamics to hold up the seller and shift the cost of adverse shocks, at least in part, to sellers rather than bear them themselves. Renegotiating in the absence of a true MAE/MAC represents an inefficient ex post distribution of transaction surplus.
This Article seeks to illustrate the role MAE/MACs play in the merger agreement and understand how they may affect bargaining dynamics that accompany renegotiations of merger agreements. In particular, this Article adds to the literature on merger contracting by observing that the conventional wisdom with respect to the role played by MAE/MACs misapprehends the role of a modern MAE/MAC provision.
This Article proceeds in the following manner. Part I situates the discussion of the MAE/MAC as a lever for renegotiation by providing an overview of the conventional wisdom with respect to the role of MAE/MAC clauses following the occurrence of an adverse shock. Part II provides an overview of the MAE/MAC clause in merger agreements, including an analysis of the work MAE/MAC clauses are intended to accomplish in the contracting process. Part III provides an overview of the current state of the doctrine with respect to MAE/MAC clauses in Delaware. Part IV discusses the experience of merger parties with renegotiations in the wake of the COVID-19 outbreak. Specifically, this Part asks why there were so few renegotiations following the outbreak and how the conventional wisdom with respect to the role of MAE/MAC in renegotiations misapprehends its role. Finally, Part V summarizes and concludes.

matches.theme_name: Do material adverse effect/change (MAE/MAC) clauses operate primarily as true risk-allocation devices or as strategic deal-termination levers in M&A transactions?
matches.specific_contribution: Using the COVID-19 episode and contemporary Delaware doctrine, the article argues that modern MAE/MAC clauses primarily allocate risk—exogenous shocks to buyers and endogenous risks to sellers—and that their use as strategic termination or renegotiation levers is overstated.
matches.generalized_contribution: Modern MAE/MAC clauses function chiefly as risk-allocation devices rather than as opportunistic deal-termination tools.

matches.theme_name: To what degree do contract design choices (termination rights, MAC/MAC clauses, break fees) allocate completion risk in mergers and acquisitions, and how do they affect bargaining dynamics under asymmetric power?
matches.specific_contribution: The article explains that because courts are highly reluctant to find a MAE/MAC and modern clauses assign exogenous shock risk to buyers and endogenous risk to sellers, these terms structure completion risk and limit buyers’ leverage to force renegotiations, as evidenced by the few COVID-era renegotiations.
matches.generalized_contribution: By allocating shock risk and operating under judicial reluctance to excuse performance, MAE/MAC and termination rights shape completion incentives and curb opportunistic renegotiation pressure.

matches.theme_name: Can contract clauses be designed to allocate macro- or systemic-shock risk (pandemics, exchange controls, MAE/MAC events) effectively without creating excessive moral hazard or perverse incentives?
matches.specific_contribution: Using the pandemic as a test case, the article contends that MAE/MAC provisions allocate systemic-shock risk to buyers and did not generally permit walkaways during COVID-19, indicating these terms can handle macro shocks without serving as quasi–force-majeure outs.
matches.generalized_contribution: Well-specified MAE/MAC terms can effectively allocate systemic-shock risk without broadly enabling deal exits.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do judicial interpretations of boilerplate contractual language shape market practice and subsequent contract drafting?
matches.specific_contribution: The article observes that Delaware courts’ reticence to find a MAE/MAC and the dissipation of ambiguity have constrained buyers’ ability to rely on boilerplate MAE/MAC language to avoid closing or force renegotiation.
matches.generalized_contribution: Clear and consistently applied judicial interpretations of MAE/MAC clauses reduce parties’ reliance on them as exit or bargaining devices.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do legal ambiguities and doctrinal vagueness (e.g., in 'pari passu', 'loan' definitions, or damages measures) cause litigation, market uncertainty, and suboptimal contracting outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The article argues that modern MAE/MAC clauses and clearer Delaware doctrine have largely eliminated ambiguity, as evidenced by the small number of COVID-era MAE disputes, and that only misperceived ambiguity enabled some buyer hold-up and inefficient renegotiation.
matches.generalized_contribution: Increased doctrinal clarity and clearer clause drafting reduce litigation and renegotiation driven by legal uncertainty, though misperceived ambiguity can still invite opportunistic and inefficient bargaining.

matches.theme_name: How does the degree of clause specificity (precise proxies vs vague standards) in contracts affect ex-post renegotiation costs, adaptability to shocks, and judicial interpretation?
matches.specific_contribution: By clearly allocating exogenous risks to buyers and endogenous risks to sellers, modern MAE/MAC clauses, reinforced by courts’ reluctance to excuse performance, have curtailed the use of MAEs as a general renegotiation lever after shocks.
matches.generalized_contribution: More specific risk-allocation drafting narrows judicial escape routes and reduces ex-post renegotiation leverage following adverse shocks.

matches.theme_name: How do bargaining power asymmetries and repeat-player advantages shape non-price contract terms and the distribution of surplus in sovereign and major corporate transactions?
matches.specific_contribution: The article notes that when parties overestimate judicial ambiguity around MAE/MAC provisions, buyers can exploit bargaining dynamics to hold up sellers and shift the costs of shocks, producing inefficient ex post surplus distribution.
matches.generalized_contribution: Perceived legal uncertainty can create bargaining advantages that enable opportunistic surplus shifting in renegotiations.

matches.theme_name: How does legal and drafting complexity affect transaction costs, negotiability, and the likelihood of litigation or deal failure?
matches.specific_contribution: Because modern MAE/MAC clauses and Delaware doctrine have shed much of their prior ambiguity, buyers rarely have a credible walk‑away or litigation threat after exogenous shocks like COVID‑19, reducing post‑signing renegotiation leverage and producing few disputes as most deals closed and only a small number litigated or modestly renegotiated.
matches.generalized_contribution: Reduced ambiguity in standardized risk‑allocation clauses lowers post‑signing renegotiation leverage and litigation risk after adverse shocks, decreasing deal‑failure likelihood and related transaction costs.

matches.theme_name: When and to what extent should courts reinterpret or override standardized contract language to achieve equitable outcomes without sacrificing contractual certainty?
matches.specific_contribution: The article reports that Delaware courts have largely clarified MAE/MAC doctrine and are extremely reticent to let buyers walk away based on general adverse events, reducing ambiguity and increasing contractual certainty around standardized MAE/MAC language.
matches.generalized_contribution: Consistent, reticent judicial interpretation of standardized MAE/MAC clauses reduces ambiguity and promotes contractual certainty over equitable reallocation in response to unforeseen shocks.

matches.theme_name: How does judicial interpretive flexibility (vague standards vs precise rules) affect predictability and market behavior in high-stakes transactional and sovereign debt litigation?
matches.specific_contribution: The article argues that ambiguity around MAE/MAC clauses has largely dissipated and that courts are highly reluctant to find a MAE, increasing predictability and limiting buyers’ ability to use vagueness to walk away or force renegotiations.
matches.generalized_contribution: Reduced judicial ambiguity and clearer contractual risk allocation increase predictability in major transactions and curtail strategic behavior premised on vague standards.

matches.theme_name: Do legal-opinion practices and interpretive uncertainty among advisors increase transaction costs and systematically shape how contracts are drafted and priced?
matches.specific_contribution: The article notes that parties’ overestimation of judicial ambiguity around MAE/MAC clauses can enable buyers to threaten hold-up renegotiations, creating inefficient ex post costs when no true MAE exists.
matches.generalized_contribution: Perceived interpretive uncertainty can invite costly, strategic renegotiation efforts even when contractual language and doctrine would not support relief.

matches.theme_name: Would greater doctrinal clarity (narrowed exceptions, precise rules) improve predictability enough to sustain cross-border lending and reduce costly strategic behavior?
matches.specific_contribution: By showing that modern MAE/MAC doctrine is comparatively clear and that courts rarely credit MAE defenses, the article indicates that clearer rules enhance predictability and diminish buyers’ scope for opportunistic renegotiation after shocks like COVID-19.
matches.generalized_contribution: Greater doctrinal clarity increases transactional predictability and reduces costly strategic behavior following adverse shocks.

matches.theme_name: Do standardized contract forms and drafting defaults systematically shape non-price deal terms and bargaining outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The article contends that modern, standardized MAE/MAC clauses allocate exogenous risks to buyers and endogenous risks to sellers, and this allocation—rather than a renegotiation lever—shapes bargaining outcomes, as reflected in limited COVID-19-era renegotiations.
matches.generalized_contribution: Standardized risk-allocation terms in deal templates shape non-price outcomes and bargaining leverage by predetermining how shocks are borne.

papers.node_id: 77chikentlrev59!!SYMPOSIUM: THEORY INFORMS BUSINESS PRACTICE:WHY CONTRACTS ARE WRITTEN IN "LEGALESE"
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: THEORY INFORMS BUSINESS PRACTICE:WHY CONTRACTS ARE WRITTEN IN "LEGALESE"
papers.abstract:
Drafting and negotiating complex business contracts is difficult. It requires prodigious memory capacity as well as imagination. How does the lawyer know what the contract ought to cover besides the bare promises to buy and sell or borrow and lend?
Not surprisingly, lawyers have come up with a production process by which each lawyer can access the accumulated wisdom of many: the "form." The form is typically not a form in the "fill-in-the-blanks" sense; rather, it is an actual contract the lawyer or someone she works with has used in one or more previous transactions.
Over time, the form evolves, mostly for the better. Many mistakes, especially those with serious consequences, get corrected. Contingencies discovered "the hard way," through painful and expensive experience, are addressed. And other improvements are made. But the results are far from perfect. The imperfections chiefly are unnecessary length and complexity - the very attributes often bemoaned in popular accounts.Sometimes the imperfections are more serious: ambiguities that go uncorrected. As I will argue, the production process, meant to help lawyers learn quickly and efficiently from their experience and from that of others, leads, perhaps intractably, to these imperfections. For expository purposes, I characterize contract drafting and negotiating as a production process, addressing a question to which there's admittedly an obvious answer: Why aren't contracts drafted from scratch? My answer frames my account of the contract production process, illustrating how multiple iterations do not always improve, and sometimes even worsen, the form. My interest in considering contract forms is twofold. First, I want to show how rational, and, what some would consider irrational,elements can combine to create a serviceable, but arguably second-best, product. Work on "standardized" or "boilerplate" contract terms has considered these issues.My workfocuses on an overlapping but distinct phenomenon: the persistence of redundancy and the ubiquity of cumbersome, inartful, and sometimes imprecise drafting.
, and more generally, I want to illustrate that the demarcation between path-dependence and network-effect explanations on the one hand, and efficiency explanations on the other hand, may be more complex and nuanced than present literature acknowledges. Path-dependence and network-effect explanations explain how inefficient, "second-best" phenomena come about and survive. These types of explanations are increasingly becoming popular in the literature. By contrast, efficiency explanations present the phenomenon being explained as "first best." The debate between path-dependence theorists and efficiency theorists is sometimes couched, with only slight exaggeration, as a debate as to whether history matters in explaining the types of phenomena law and economics considers. Path-dependence theorists argue that it does; efficiency theorists ostensibly argue that it does not. The "same" phenomenon can be either the product of a path-dependent process (and hence second best or inefficient) or efficient depending on how the phenomenon itself is described. I show how business contracts can be characterized as second best, needing history as an explanation or, indeed, an excuse; or, alternatively, business contracts can be viewed as closer to efficient. The description of the phenomenon is critical.
This Article proceeds as follows. Part II explains the production process by which complex business contracts are drafted and negotiated in large law firms. It models the process as a way of imparting to each lawyer the accumulated wisdom of her predecessors. Part III considers how economic and psychologicaldynamics operate in the contract drafting and negotiating process. Indeed,some of the dynamics fall comfortably within the rubric of rational self-interest maximization. Others perhaps represent departures from "rationality," as that term commonly is used in economics. Part IV summarizes the imperfections of complex contracts. It considers why the form production process might persist despite these imperfections, stressing switching costs attributable to network and other effects. It also considers certain specialization benefits to the form production process. Finally, it compares other costs and benefits of retaining the process versus switching. Part V concludes, addressing why multiple iterations don't make contracts "perfect."
. Contract Drafting and Negotiation: Genesis and Use of the Form
In Anatomy of a Merger, James Freund, a leading merger and acquisition lawyer in New York, includes a playlet describing a mock acquisition transaction, in which Suggestive Software, Ltd. is acquired by Proliferating Products, Inc.In one scene, taking place on Friday, December 27, the junior associate, Peter Preppie, is being lambasted by his supervisor, the partner Perry Prudent, for having done a rotten job in his first draft of the acquisition agreement:
PRUDENT: Merry Christmas, Pete. Now look fella, you'll just have to forgive my candor but time's short and this draft of the Proliferating-Suggestive agreement is an inferior job. The problem is that you just didn't think! You walked out of here, you went into the library, you grabbed that Screwloose binder off the shelf, you had a photocopy made of the final contract, and you marked it up for purposes of this draft. Don't you realize that the final Screwloose agreement represented the culmination of three weeks of intensive negotiation on the part of a pretty smart seller's attorney? You've got to start with the first draft of the Screwloose contract.
All that stuff in there about their right to defend lawsuits, and all those materiality and knowledge caveats - they have no place in the first draft of an agreement to buy Software; plus which you forgot about the omission of the tax representation in Screwloose because of that special problem of theirs. And then you left in all that valuation language - average closing price, etc. - which was fine in the Screwloose deal where the pricing was based on the market price over a two-week period right before the closing, but is completely inapplicable here since we're using a fixed number of shares. You have to think, boy.
And then, in the one place you did a little thinking, Pete, it seems to me you went too far. I know it's possible that they'll repeal the Copyright Act some day, but it doesn't really rise to a level of probability sufficient to warrant three pages of provisions conditional upon that event.
Get this thing fixed up, and let me see it first thing Monday.
This passage, meant in jest, nevertheless captures quite well a junior lawyer's initiation into contract drafting. Indeed, in large-firm practice, complex contracts are drafted and negotiated using a process that permits much of the work to be done by somewhat more experienced versions of Preppie. Such a process makes eminent sense. A new product, custom-crafted for the client from a form, can be produced quickly, and at far lower cost than a product crafted from scratch. The form design enables the product to be produced by lower-paid, less-senior and less-experienced lawyers. Given the complex nature of the task, and the quick turnaround time typically required, even the most experienced lawyer would have difficulty remembering every step and detail; the form is a useful reminder. The form also preserves the benefits of experience with its provisions, both in the transacting community and, sometimes, in judicial decisions. The form simplifies the mechanical task as well: a lawyer "marks up" a form, using the existing structure and changing only what's needed. A contract for client #2 is created quickly from client #1's contract; global searches change the names and some other words. The remaining changes are input mechanically, and the new contract quickly emerges from the laser printer.
Within the present structure, it is hard to imagine drafting any other way. Without a form, how would most junior lawyers have any idea of what a contract should address? They have never bought a multimillion-dollar company or taken out a multimillion-dollar loan.And they are not trained to reason by far-flung analogy, which might permit them to use information from their past experiences in quite different contexts. Furthermore, many conventions, such as drafting conventions, have arisen; intuiting such conventions would be impossible. Seniority and increasing judgment help. But evenFreund would probably not want to draft from scratch.Ready access to others' experience is crucial.
Returning to Freund's playlet: Preppie, who is quite inexperienced, nevertheless has major drafting responsibility for the contract. Prudent, Freund's alter ego, presumably told Preppie to use the form from the Screwloose transaction, a transaction on which Prudent himself had worked.If Prudent had not worked on a similar transaction in the recent past, he would tell Preppie to get a form from another senior lawyer Prudent trusted,and who had worked on a similar transaction recently. Preppie decides how to "mark up" the form - what to retain, what to change, and what to add. Prudent reviews Preppie's draft, as described in the quote above; Preppie then revises it and sends it to the other side. Prudent and Preppie both attend the negotiations. Preppie's principal role is as scribe; he drafts the agreed-upon changes and sends out the revised agreements to the multi-person distribution list. Prudent probably wants to see important changes before Preppie sends out the revised draft. However, Prudent probably trusts Preppie to make minor changes without supervision.
In this playlet, Prudent does the negotiations himself. However, except in the largest transactions, someone as senior as Prudent (and with as high a billing rate) would be unlikely to do the bulk of the negotiations. Indeed, in many cases, someone at an early stage in his career - say, a midlevel to senior associate - might do a great deal of the negotiation, and perhaps all of it. One can readily imagine a similar conversation in which a still comparatively junior Preppie reports back to Prudent as to the results of the negotiations. Prudent asks which of the contested points Preppie won, Preppie responds, and Prudent perhaps rants that Preppie succeeded only on the lessimportantpoints but failed on the more important ones. Preppie then is sent back to negotiate further. Over time, Preppie comes to understand what is important and what is not, and what sorts of arguments win and lose.
Like any junior lawyer, Peter Preppie needs to learn how to draft and negotiate contracts. In the passage I quoted, Prudent is doing a reasonable job of teaching him. He tells Preppie to think about which form to use, and to think while marking up the form. He also tells Preppie to consider the differences between the deal for which Preppie is drafting the contract and the deal for which the contract form was used.
The lesson Prudent is teaching Preppie is much more complex than it appears. Preppie will presumably know, as would just about anyone in Preppie's position, not to have three pages describing consequences of the repeal of the Copyright Act next time he gives Prudent a first draft. He will almost certainly know not to give such a draft to any other senior lawyer. But Prudent wants Preppie to learn a far more general lesson: he wants Preppie to learn not to write in new provisions addressing contingencies as remote as the repeal of the Copyright Act. Which contingencies are as remote as repeal of the Copyright Act? How is Preppie to know? The generic instruction "think" is scarcely much of a guide. But, coupled with a few examples, it may be the best Prudent can do - Preppie will have to look to his imagination and judgment, and, as time goes on, experience, hopefully not so hard-won as in his encounter with Prudent. Prudent speaks as though "thinking" were a matter of brawn rather than brains - something you could simply do by trying to do it. But Preppie's problem, as Prudent surely would agree, is not lack of effort. After all, Preppie produced this draft quite quickly, in the week that included Christmas Day. Preppie's problem is that he doesn't know what to think about - and there may be no good way to tell him.
This dynamic extends far beyond determinations about which contingencies to include in a contract. Learning effectively from experience requires generalizing to an experience's salient features. There is no formula to determine which features of an experience are salient. Overgeneralizing is common in everyday life, and can sometimes take the form of superstition (I'd better not do X because the last time I did X...). Undergeneralizing is common as well, and is a particular peril for the corporate lawyer. A lawyer suffers professionally if she addresses in the B contract a bad outcome that occurred in the A transaction but not a similar bad outcome that actually occurs in the B transaction. ("We prohibited liens on property the company purchased for more than $ 200,000; we didn't prohibit liens on property the company purchased for less but improved so that their aggregate expenditure exceeded $ 200,000.")
The 1967 movie Bedazzledillustrates the difficulties of learning from experience. In the movie, Stanley Moon sold his soul to the Devil for seven wishes. All Stanley wanted was to win over Margaret, the waitress from Wimpy's. He tried various ways of accomplishing this end, but every time the Devil managed to grant his wish in fact but violate it in spirit. For instance, Stanley had always been tongue-tied around Margaret; for his first wish, he asked the Devil to make him articulate. Stanley wanted to converse so well with Margaret that she'd fall in love with him. As the wish progresses, Margaret is passionate about conversation, emboldening Stanley to take the next step and suggest romance; needless to say, her passions don't carry over into the romantic realm. His next wish is that she be very physical; she is, but with everyone except Stanley. Next, he wishes for them to be in love; they are, but they are married to other people. And so on. Each time, Stanley crafts his wish precisely, so as to prevent what has gone wrong before. But after several wishes, he is no closer to landing Margaret than he was when the Devil discovered him trying to hang himself in despair.
Stanley is undergeneralizing from his experience. He should have learned to think about not just what had gone wrong, but what else could have gone wrong - what sort of thing the thing that went wrong was. And what sort of thing did not go wrong but could have.
There is no one correct level of generalization. More generally, there is no one correct level of effort to be spent determining what acontract should provide for. In some transactions, the contract's words may be particularly crucial. For instance, the more devilish the other side is known to be, the more effort one may need to spend; reputational forces will not constrain a devilish party from taking advantage of every gap in the contract, no matter how tiny. But at a certain point, the effort may not be worthwhile: the Devil can always find a way to grant Stanley's wish in fact but violate the spirit, no matter how well-crafted the wish had been.
Prudent is trying to impart a much more general lesson: that Preppie should defer to the form, but not unthinkingly - not "too much." But again, how is Preppie to know how much is too much? And it's not as though he can learn this lesson once and for all. He presumably will learn the lesson better and better as time goes on; nevertheless, he will likely continue to err for a long time in his career. Some lawyers by temperament (risk lovers? overconfident?) might tend to defer too little; in my experience, most will defer too much.
The form provides a baseline from which to determine what the contract should address. For instance, when Preppie is trying to determine whether a contingency is sufficiently likely that it warrants being addressed in a contract he's drafting, he will naturally apply a different standard for contingencies the form already addresses. Consider why: deleting a provision is an affirmative act. Why do it without a good reason? But thinking of new contingencies takes effort - brawn - as well as brains; Preppie simply might not think of new contingencies as remote as some of those already addressed in the form (or, for that matter, he might not think of new contingencies far less remote than those already in the form).
When Prudent reviews Preppie's draft, he presumably focuses more on deviations from the form - on things he is not used to seeing. Prudent's reviewing strategy is sensible and intuitive. He trusts the lawyers in his firm who created and "vetted" the form.He therefore feels no need to review their work: the form - that is, the contract given to Preppie to mark up. But Prudent has no reason at this point to trust Preppie.Thus, whatever Preppie's done by himself willwarrant particular scrutiny. But if each person skips over the more familiar provisions quickly, assuming her (competent) predecessors have considered it, many provisions may never have been vetted. Nevertheless, given Prudent's billing rate, he is likely acting in his client's best interest by conducting only the more abbreviated review. A review from scratch would be quite costly; the likelihood that Prudent would detect anything warranting this cost is small.
If something goes wrong later, both Preppie and Prudent can argue that they acted reasonably, in accordance with an industry-wide standard: the form production process.Preppie, Prudent, and Prudent's firm will look very bad if they do not provide for a commonly provided-for remote contingency that actually occurs; they will not look nearly as bad if they do not provide for an equally remote contingencynot commonly provided for.
Thus, Preppie accords a rebuttable presumption to provisions in the form. For particular provisions, he weighs whether the presumption has been rebutted. The presumption will not be rebutted for benign provisions (such as the typical boilerplate about references to one gender including the other and captions of provisions not being part of the meaning of the provision); saving trees (or secretarial overtime or shipping charges) will not be a sufficient counterweight. His best guess may be that a provision seems benign, but he's not completely sure: the calculation will favor keeping the provisions. Indeed, Preppie will make as few changes as possible. Hewill often favor "band-aids," requiring the least tinkering possible, over a more elegant, structural solution. The paradigm band-aid says "anything else in this agreement to the contrary notwithstanding" or other words to that effect. Preppie has been told that the form - the contract he's marking up - "works": that the provisions, in the aggregate, create internally consistent rights and duties, and cover the appropriate universe of events and contingencies. He will worry that any larger changes might make the contract not work.
Preppie's deference to the form accords with lawyers' preferences generally, including lawyers on the other side in the Suggestive transaction. A lawyer used to seeing an article entitled Representations and Warranties immediately preceding an article entitled Covenants and Agreements will find it easier to review a document with these same articles in this order. Indeed, lawyers often use other forms, as well as mental "forms," to compare forms they are asked to review: in this respect, the reviewing process is similar to the drafting process. Consider again Prudent's description of the problems with Preppie's first draft: Prudent depicts himself and Preppie as using physical (and mental) forms as a baseline, checking off inclusion of all the usual items, noting deviations, and limiting in-depth consideration mostly to those deviations.
After the transaction closes, neither Preppie nor Prudent will have any incentive to review the final contract as signed, to "clean up the form," replacing band-aids with more elegant solutions, and, more generally, incorporating the insights they may have gotten during time-pressured negotiating or drafting sessions. Who would such a review benefit? Probably not the client, especially given what such a review would cost.Moreover, since drafting and negotiating is almost always done in the heat of the moment, the form likely would not stay "clean" for long, unless the firm were willing to commence an expensive, regular form-cleaning process.Finally, Prudent and Preppie probably have moved on to other transactions. And Preppie would just as soon not see the contract in the cold light of day, where, he thinks, all the mistakes he's made will become glaringly obvious.
In Prudent's next transaction, he probably will tell the junior lawyer assigned to him, Josephine Preppina,to ask Preppie for the Suggestive contract. And the process will unfold very much as it did with Preppie. Or perhaps he will work again with Preppie; the process will still unfold substantially as it does above, since Preppie is still far from having unlocked the mysteries of drafting and negotiating contracts.
In the next part, I analyze the dynamics behind the story I have just told. I discuss the incentives of firms, and lawyers within firms, at both the junior and senior levels, to use the form production process. I described above how this same process leads to the notoriously cumbersome, difficult to read, inartfully drafted contracts. I identify below economic and psychological factors accounting for this result.

matches.theme_name: Why do standardized contractual clauses ('boilerplate') persist despite inefficiencies, and what institutional or market mechanisms overcome this lock-in?
matches.specific_contribution: Modeling large-firm form-based drafting, the article explains that the process persists despite redundancy, complexity, and ambiguities because of switching costs tied to network and other effects, specialization benefits, and lawyers’ economic and psychological incentives, while cautioning that some observed “inefficiencies” may be second-best or near-efficient depending on how the phenomenon is described.
matches.generalized_contribution: Boilerplate persists because network effects, switching costs, specialization gains, and professional and cognitive incentives entrench existing forms, and the efficiency versus path-dependence divide is more nuanced than commonly assumed.

papers.node_id: 6jempiricallegalstud818!!ARTICLE: Contractual Complexity and the Cognitive Load of R&D Alliance Contracts
papers.title: ARTICLE: Contractual Complexity and the Cognitive Load of R&D Alliance Contracts
papers.abstract:
Interorganizational contractual arrangements, such as those set up to govern interfirm alliances, have become important mechanisms through which firms exchange products, services, and knowledge. Mayer and Argyresand Sampsonargue that sophisticated contractual relationships are an increasingly important feature of the business landscape, particularly where high technology is involved. While previous research has focusedpredominantly on the manner in which firms govern these relationships, legal scholars, economists, and business scholars have more recently begun to study "the actual formalized documents that we call contracts . . . . "These studies have generally been based on transaction cost economics and property rights theory, which has led to an extensive examination of particular control rightsand/or ownership rights.
As markets become ever more complex, so do the contracts that are devised to transfer risks, align incentives, effectively distribute gains from trade, and structure expost adjustments in these markets over prolonged periods of time. An understanding of contract design is thus essential for individuals and companies alike to succeed effectively in an increasingly dynamic business environment. Most research on alliances ignores the underlying contracts that govern the terms of the relationship. Several authors have called for a more in-depth investigation of contract structure and have in that sense attempted to describe contracts in terms of the degree of "complexity."Measures that authors have used to determine contractual complexity include the length of contracts in terms of the number of pages,the "number" of kilobytes of information in contracts,or the number of provisions in contracts and their stringency.This brings us to the point of why some contracts are relatively complex or simple.
Whether contracts always mirror the complexity of the market is questionable. One reason that parties may not draft complex contracts is that drafting such documents can be extremely costly. Factors such as information asymmetries, monitoring dynamics, cognitive limitations, trust, and reputation effects may encourage parties to evade writing increasingly complex documents.
The understanding of the complexity of contracts is relevant as complexity has a signaling function regarding the costs that companies face in terms of designing, writing, implementing, controlling, and enforcing contracts that govern the relationship with their contractual partners.The concept of contractual complexity is not only relevant for the parties whose business interests are represented in the contracts, but also for other parties, such as lawyers, courts, and policymakers involved in the drafting and enforcement of contracts.
Lawyers who draft contracts should carefully consider the appropriate level of detail of their documents.Complexity evolves over time, facilitated by the rapid technological advancement of computer systems and programs, allowing law firms and legal departments of multinational corporationsto collect and store large data sets of contracts. Clauses are frequently added, but it is questionable whether more detail is always good.
The contract drafter must remain aware that too much of the text is preserved in each new incarnation of the contract. The pervasive and rash use of forms enhances contractual complexity--both in terms of length and comprehensiveness--an attribute often bemoaned in accounts with practitioners. Where lawyers argue that a person can never plan too carefully for contingencies, businesspeople complain that strict planning efforts interfere with the interests of valuable deals. Complexity can show distrust and overwhelm the cognitive abilities of parties, absorb resources, and have other negative consequences,and parties should always be aware of the contextual embeddedness of complexity. Lawyers should be careful to evaluate complexity when drafting contracts. Individuals drafting contracts must acknowledge that the ability of lawyers and laypeople to comprehend contracts and to understand the interdependencies of various elements of a contract is limited. The incidence of mistakes increases with the length of contracts, the interrelatedness of provisions, and the complex language of the latter. When complexity is positively related to a misunderstanding of contract (terms), complexity may increase the potential for contractual disputes. In that case, contractual complexity can be seen as a major cause of litigation. Whether and to what extent contractual complexity leads to more "mistakes" and, subsequently, litigation is not easily verifiable due to a lack of data.
Courts should also take account of the relative complexity of contracts. The design of a contract and its relative complexity signals information about the contracting practices and processes. An interesting point to be made, for example, is whether different levels of complexity should give rise to a differentiated enforcement or interpretation of contracts. Eggleston et al. link the complexity of contracts to the interpretive techniques used by the court.In general, a court can take either a more liberal or more literal approach to the interpretation of a contract. Using the liberal approach, the court will attempt to discern the parties' general contractual goals and attempt to maximize the value of the contract by relying on its own judgment. In contrast, givena more literal interpretation technique, the court will adhere strictly to the text of the written document in order to determine parties' rights and obligations. To interpret a contract properly, the court should regard complexity. There are different factors that may determine the degree of contractual complexity, such as reputation and trust, information asymmetries, contracting costs, and prior experience. Although it may be difficult for the court to discern to what degree these factors influence the complexity of the contract, these factors and, thereby, complexity do reveal information as to the contract's source, purpose, and value. For example, Schwartzargues that when a simple contract arises from a complex environment, courts should use a literal interpretation technique, since the simple contract was then a conscious choice. Eggleston et al., on the other hand, argue that the complexity of the environment should be a reason for a more liberal interpretation; a simple contract given a complex environment may be inefficient.
A greater understanding of the complexity of contracts also substantiates the debate on the proper content and role of contract law. As contract law is largely nonmandatory, firms contract in the realm of the freedom of contract and often develop rules tailored to their particular needs. Subsequently, contract terms vary depending on parties' characteristics and goals, their shared understanding, transaction costs, the characteristics of the transaction, and the background legal regime. When parties opt out of default rules, writing increasingly complex documents, this may be an indication of the suboptimality of such rules.
Although the complexity of contracts has received quite some attention in the literature, the actual understanding and conceptualization of contractual complexity as such remains a challenge. First, complexity is typically one of those concepts that is often used, yet difficult to define. Also, attempts to measure complexity are laden with intricacies. As stated by Kades,"scholars have not had an easy time defining complexity, and some have been disarmingly honest about this difficulty. One author admitted that he wastempted to define complexity by averring, 'I know when I read it.'"Our own understanding of complexity is influenced by Simon, who defines complexity in terms of the "large number of parts that interact in a nonsimple way, . . . [where] . . . the whole is more than the sum of its parts, not in an ultimate, metaphysical sense but in the important pragmatic sense that, given the properties of the parts and the laws of their interaction, it is not a trivial matter to infer the properties of the whole."
For contracts, this implies that the more complex contracts are, the more they are characterized by many parts, for example, provisions, with a large number of interdependencies.More complex contracts also refine and increase the number of events, enforcement mechanisms, and clauses that would otherwise be sparsely mentioned in a less complex contract.A higher degree of interdependency between provisions in a contract increases the information-processing costs, caused by the limits of human cognition.Kadesargues that for legal rules, "the length and detail of . . . rules, along with their interconnectedness, . . . are directly related to their elaborative complexity" and as such this complexity goes beyond the mere length of contracts.In that light, it becomes apparent that straightforward measures of length of contracts are probably not sufficient to fully capture the construct of complexity.
In related work, some scholars from the field of law and economics, for example, Schuckand, in particular, Eggleston et al.,suggest that objective measures of the complexity of contracts should be complemented by subjective measures related to the degree of cognitive load of contracts, that is, the degree of difficulty that people face when they attempt to understand contracts.In other words, these authors argue that the complexityof contracts has to be seen from a multidimensional perspective where both objective and subjective dimensions are taken into account. To better comprehend contractual complexity, as discussed above, we therefore follow up on these suggestions to include both subjective and objective elements within the construct of contractual complexity as we investigate the feasibility of a multidimensional measure of the complexity of contracts.
Given this general goal of our article, we attempt to make several contributions to the existing literature. First, we investigate whether different objective measures of complexity, such as the number of words, the number of pages, and the number of kilobytes, of contracts are substitutes or complements. Second, we introduce a new measure of contractual complexity that has both an objective element, for example, the length of contracts, and a subjective element based on the perception of the cognitive load of contracts. Third, our study also has some interesting interdisciplinary features, in the sense that we build on the understanding of the complexity of contracts in business, economics, and law in combination with an understanding of the role of cognitive load as developed in the psychology and education literatures.
The empirical analysis that we present is based on a combination of a sample of nearly 400 R&D alliance contracts in the biopharmaceutical industry and a measurement of the perception and assessment of the cognitive load of these contracts. Our findings indicate that diverse objective measures of contractual complexity, based on the length or size of contracts, are interchangeable. In addition, objective and subjective measures do indeed refer to different dimensions of contractual complexity, where the cognitive load of contracts carries both objective and subjective characteristics. Our expanded conception thus allows contractual complexity to vary simultaneously across an objective as well as a subjective dimension.
The remainder of the article is organized as follows: in the next section we give an overview of the different measures of contractual complexity currently discussed in the literature. This is followed by an introduction of the concept of cognitive load as this has been defined and researched in the psychology and education literatures. Methods and research design are discussed in the next section, after which we present the findings of our research. Finally, the section with the discussion and conclusions not only discusses our findings in the context of the literature on cognitive load, bounded rationality, and contractual complexity, but also suggests some steps for further research that link up to other recent contributions that advocate an in-depth understanding of the content of interfirm contracts.

matches.theme_name: How does legal and drafting complexity affect transaction costs, negotiability, and the likelihood of litigation or deal failure?
matches.specific_contribution: The article explains that longer, more interdependent, and linguistically complex contracts raise cognitive load, absorb resources, increase misunderstanding, and may heighten the risk of disputes and litigation, though direct verification is limited by data constraints.
matches.generalized_contribution: Greater contractual complexity increases information-processing costs and can raise negotiation and enforcement frictions, misunderstandings, and downstream dispute risk.

matches.theme_name: Can empirical contract-level datasets reveal patterns of clause prevalence and evolution that should inform doctrinal or regulatory reform?
matches.specific_contribution: Using nearly 400 biopharma R&D alliance contracts alongside cognitive-load assessments, the study shows that objective length/size metrics are interchangeable and distinct from perceived cognitive burden, introducing a multidimensional measure that can better map contracting practices relevant to debates over default rules.
matches.generalized_contribution: Empirical, multidimensional measures combining objective contract length with perceived cognitive load can track contract-structure patterns useful for informing doctrinal discussions about defaults and reform.

matches.theme_name: Do professional intermediaries (law firms, underwriters, trustees, advisors) introduce agency costs that bias contract design and risk allocation?
